noticias.titulo: Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests
noticias.resumen: Female protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, a rights group says.
noticias.texto:
Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests
- Published
Taraneh Rahimi is on death row in Iran.
In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.
She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.
He says Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.
When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi says, speaking from the US.
He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.
Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.
The figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini says.
The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".
It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".
It said death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".
The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.
It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) says it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.
The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it says totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.
The twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.
Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which says Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.
Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.
Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, says both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".
Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".
According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.
Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.
Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.
She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.
Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.
"As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her says.
In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.
The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it says is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.
The woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing."
Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".
In response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".
At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.
She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".
Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, says "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".
Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.
However, Sato says as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".
In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.
The death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned â though two of those have been sent for retrial. She says she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".
Sato says there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.
Women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression."
The Iranian embassy said judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh."
Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.
Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.
Nourmohammadi says the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.
Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he says.
Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he says, and they tell her they plan to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope."

noticias.titulo: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause, BBC understands
noticias.resumen: Text of the treaties will be published this afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
noticias.texto:
New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause, BBC understands
- Published
The government and the EU are set to publish the texts of two treaties that were agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.
The treaties will be published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation which is designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
The BBC understands the deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.
Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.
The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the long-term UK-EU relationship.
The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.
New assessments of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country are also expected.
- EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme 
  - Published16 hours ago
- Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students 
  - Published16 hours ago
- Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU 
  - Published14 hours ago
Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports.
The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.
Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.
Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."
"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."
The BBC understands that a plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.
The treaty text will also contain finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules.
Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, will also be detailed in the legislation.
Such powers could enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.
Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".
Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.
Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.
Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

noticias.titulo: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
noticias.resumen: The Starmind constellation aims to be the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for AI computing power.
noticias.texto:
Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
- Published
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it, external as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan" and astronomers in the US said it would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky.
There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.
Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.
Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.
Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd., said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed.
Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them.
"That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said.
Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision.
It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky".
It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects," meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky."
"Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet," Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the nonprofit group Earthjustice, said in a statement.
The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.
The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.
New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.
An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.
Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.
Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

  - Published16 hours ago
- Bezos' Blue Origin announces satellite rival to Musk's Starlink 
  - Published22 January

noticias.titulo: DR Congo demands answers over Ugandan general's threats
noticias.resumen: Gen Kainerugaba threatened a rebel takeover of a mineral-rich area in DR Congo in controversial X posts.
noticias.texto:
DR Congo demands answers over Ugandan general's threats
- Published
The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.
In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo. He insisted that Uganda's military involvement was purely driven by security concerns.
The DR Congo's foreign ministry summoned Uganda's envoy to explain the remarks, describing them as "particularly serious" and damaging to diplomatic relations.
The Ugandan government has yet to respond.
The diplomatic row comes despite close military ties between the neighbours.
Their forces have been conducting joint operations against the Islamic State-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in eastern DR Congo since 2021.
Uganda has also recently been involved in efforts to mediate between the Congolese government and an armed group led by former warlord Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.
- The Ugandan general who lobs grenades on Twitter 
  - Published30 October 2022
In his posts, Gen Kainerugaba accused the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group operating in eastern DR Congo, of targeting members of the Bahima ethnic community.
The Bahema are a traditionally cattle-herding community mainly based in DR Congo's north-eastern Ituri province.
They have historical and cultural ties to the Bahima people of neighbouring Uganda.
He also threatened a rebel takeover of Walikale, in North Kivu province, while defending Uganda's military presence in DR Congo.
Walikale is rich in mineral resources , including some of the country's largest tin deposits and several major gold mines.
Gen Kainerugaba's X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, has since become inaccessible.
It is unclear whether he deactivated it, as he has done in the past, or whether the platform had suspended it.
During the same week he declared: "My tweets in Uganda are directives that must be obeyed."
The posts followed reports that a DR Congo military aircraft had allegedly been shot down by rebels, with foreign mercenaries reportedly among those on board.
Gen Kainerugaba criticised the reported presence of foreign mercenaries in DR Congo.
"These remarks, which are particularly serious, have caused a major media incident and undermine the necessary restraint that must prevail in relations between sovereign states," the DR Congo foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
"The Congolese government expects the Republic of Uganda to clarify its official position and take the necessary measures to prevent such transgressions from recurring in the future".
The ministry added that DR Congo remained committed to regional peace and stability but would defend its dignity and institutions against "any form of provocation or interference".
It is not the first time Gen Kainerugaba's social media posts have strained relations between the two countries.
In February last year, he threatened to seize the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia, claiming that members of the Bahima ethnic community were being attacked.
In 2024, DR Congo also summoned Uganda's diplomatic representative after the general made threats against foreign mercenaries operating in eastern DR Congo.
The 52-year-old general, widely seen as a potential successor to his father Yoweri Museveni, has become known for his provocative social media posts.
In 2022, he sparked a diplomatic row with neighbouring Kenya after threatening to invade the country and capture its capital, Nairobi, prompting his father to apologise forn the remarks.

noticias.titulo: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
noticias.resumen: The musician, who co-wrote some of the band's biggest hits, had been treated for prostate cancer.
noticias.texto:
Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
- Published
Andy Taylor, the guitarist for the pop group Duran Duran, has died at the age of 65.
Born in Tynemouth, he co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits, including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film; and also worked with artists like Robert Palmer, Rod Stewart and Belinda Carlisle.
In a statement, his bandmates said Taylor had fought "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer" and "passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23 November".
His wife, Tracey, said the musician "was the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day".
- Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off 
  - Published11 hours ago
The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.
He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.
The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.
Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.
"Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," said his bandmates Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor (his bandmates were unrelated, despite sharing the same last name).
"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.
"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.
"Our thoughts are with his wife Tracey, his children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and grandson Albie. They all loved him deeply and we ask that their privacy be respected at this very difficult time."
Sir Rod Stewart, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, paid tribute to his "dear pal".
"We made some good music together and at the same time had some outrageous fun," Sir Rod posted on Instagram.
Duran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs.
Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly launched MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.
They became so popular in the States that the press labeled them the leaders of a "Second British Invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.
During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station.
The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran, after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.
"We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.
"We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."
He went on to play on Robert Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.
After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.
In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.
When the group took the stage, singer Simon Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.
Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.
"Andy never took the easy musical route," said Le Bon in a personal statement marking his friend's death.
"His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later.
"There's a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart. It'll never close up; I won't let it. I will miss him & love him for all my days."
Taylor is survived by his wife, Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982.
"For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first," she wrote in her statement.
"Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home."
She continued: "Andy faced the last few years with so much courage and determination. He never gave up, fighting until the very end, never losing his love of life.
"The kindness and support shown to him by fans from all over the world throughout his illness brought him immense comfort and strength, and for that we will always be grateful."

noticias.titulo: Thirteen dead as mine disaster highlights illegal hunt for gold
noticias.resumen: Indonesian authorities say another 13 are missing in the illegal gold mine, which flooded on Monday.
noticias.texto:
Thirteen dead as mine disaster highlights illegal hunt for gold
- Published
It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground.
Rais, 50, had been working as an illegal gold miner in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province. On Monday night, he and 25 other miners were digging in an open-pit mine about 100m (328ft) deep, when torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood the two shafts.
Authorities on Thursday confirmed that 13 people had died and their bodies were recovered from the site. At least 13 more are thought to still be missing.
Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing, with personnel using ropes to access the depths of the dark, narrow and slippery mine shafts, which are continually being flooded from below.
Above ground, ambulances and medical personnel are ready and waiting to transport victims.
"We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement on Wednesday.
"The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely."
Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia, but remains widespread in rural parts of the mineral-rich archipelago.
Multiple studies show that over the past ten years the illegal industry has rapidly flourished, often in correlation with rising gold prices. In early 2026, those prices reached an all-time high â spurring a gold rush that prompted mine operators across the country to expand their operations.
This included state-owned mining company Aneka Tambang (Antam), which owns the business permit for the area in which this week's flooded mine is located. Antam have said the mine was not theirs and was operating without their authorisation.
On Wednesday, while rescue operations there were underway, West Java Regional Police separately announced that they had uncovered 24 cases of illegal mining across the province between October and November alone.
But Bisman Bakhtiar, Executive Director of the Center for Energy and Mining Law Studies, told the BBC earlier this year that the actual number of illegal mines in Indonesia is higher than the government's figures.
"[The government figures are] what's been recorded. That means there must be more than that," he said, noting that law enforcement operations have had little impact on the sector.
"It's still very massive and very big because this has been going on for a very long time."
Others allege that the illegal industry is underpinned by corruption.
Laode M Syarif, former deputy chairman of the Corruption Eradication Committee, said that unofficial mining is difficult to eradicate because every illegal mine has "backing", usually from "police and military or high-ranking officials in local and provincial governments".
"As long as these backers are not dealt with firmly, illegal mining will continue," he said.
In many cases, though, the allure of these mines is simple: they offer an economic lifeline to people with few other viable prospects.
Despite the value of gold having dipped in recent months, countless illegal miners throughout Indonesia are still eagerly digging for paydirt.
But the lack of regulation and poor construction in the pits also means accidents are relatively common â whether from landslides, floods, or exposure to hazardous gases, all of which have claimed lives in recent years.
Earlier this year, in the same area as this week's flooded mine, 11 illegal gold miners reportedly died after a carbon monoxide leak inside a shaft.
Elsewhere, in West Sumatra, nine people were killed at an illegal gold mine in May after heavy rain triggered the collapse of a 30-metre cliff, burying 12 miners in total.
There are numerous reports of other such incidents across the Indonesian archipelago. But the illegal nature of the small-scale gold mining sector obfuscates the true number of casualties.
Even this week, when asked how many miners were in the pits in Bogor when they flooded, M Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency, said the total casualty figure "is still unclear".
"Some say 20 people, others say 29 people," Hamdani told Indonesian news outlet Detik. "The problem is that no one reported it and no one wants to report it."
The Indonesian Ombudsman on Thursday urged law enforcement officials to conduct a thorough investigation of the incident and to address the larger systemic issue behind it.
"This should be a momentum for all parties to resolve the [illegal gold mining] problem comprehensively, not just taking action after the incident or closing the holes discovered," said Abdul Ghoffar, a member of the Indonesian Ombudsman.
"We need to uncover the entire [illegal gold mining] chain," he continued. "We must not allow only the miners in the field to be seen and prosecuted, while those who control the activities, provide capital and facilities, store, and market the mined products remain untouched.
"Law enforcement must target the actors and networks that keep this illegal activity going."
As rescue operations continue and more bodies are recovered, the picture is becoming less murky. But even if there are survivors among those who remain missing, time may be running out.
More than three days since the shafts flooded, the relatives of the anonymous men in the mines are desperately waiting to hear whether their loved ones survived.
As she waits for news of her father, Rani says: "I hope he's found soon."

noticias.titulo: Guinea orders residents to clean up the capital months after deadly rubbish dump collapse
noticias.resumen: The capital's main rubbish dump has been closed since the disaster, leading to rubbish piling up in the streets.
noticias.texto:
Guinea orders residents to clean up the capital months after deadly rubbish dump collapse
- Published
Guinea has ordered residents to do a mass clean-up of the capital, Conakry, months after a rubbish landfill collapsed, killing dozens of people.
Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah on Wednesday announced a deadline of 31 December to clear rubbish in the city and its suburbs, which has seen an increase in illegal dumping in recent months.
In August heavy rains caused a landslide at the capital's main waste dump, with the rubbish collapsing onto homes killing 31 people and injuring others.
The site in the city's Dar es Salaam area was subsequently closed permanently, which has led to piles of rubbish accumulating outside homes and on the streets.
At a public forum on sanitation, Sanitation Minister Aboubacar Camara said Conakry was generating about 3,000 tonnes of waste every day.
He said much of the garbage was ending up in the streets because of weaknesses in the collection system.
The prime minister called on local authorities to become more involved in organising waste collection, saying this could become a way to create jobs.
"The state will do its part, but the municipalities must also organise themselves to ensure waste collection and provide jobs for young people," the prime minister said.
"Conakry must be completely clean by the end of December," he added, relaying a directive from the country's president, Mamady Doumbouya.
He cited measures the government was taking to improve waste collection and recycling, including a national sanitation fund that would guarantee financing for the sector.
Camara said talks had been finalised with a waste collection operator, with a plan for equipment to move waste from transit and sorting centres to a new disposal site in BaretodÃ©, outside the capital.
The August tragedy at the Dar es Salaam landfill was not the first - 10 people were killed at the same site in 2017.
The government had ordered people living close to the site to move, but many residents chose to stay.
According to the prime minister, the government now plans to transform the closed waste site into an urban park.

noticias.titulo: FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, causing brief suspension of flights at airport
noticias.resumen: The brief stoppage came on the eve of the US Thanksgiving holiday, one of the busiest travel days of the year.
noticias.texto:
FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, causing brief suspension of flights at airport
- Published
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) temporarily halted flights bound for Miami International Airport in Florida after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway on Wednesday evening.
Departures heading to Miami were grounded just after 20:15 local time (01:15 GMT) and all but one runway at the airport was closed, according to the FAA advisory. Flights resumed again about 90 minutes later.
The airliner that ran past the runway arrived from Memphis. No injuries have been reported. The FAA is investigating the incident.
The ground stop came on the day before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year in the US.
Flight delays in Miami reached one hour but appeared to be declining later Wednesday night.
At 21:41 local time, the FAA confirmed that "flights will be resuming shortly".
Passengers scheduled to travel on Wednesday night were encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport.
"We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," Miami-Dade Aviation Department spokesman Greg Chin said in a statement to the BBC.
The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travellers in the country over this holiday week, according to the American Automobile Association.
The Miami-Dade area is also under a flood watch until late Wednesday night. Periods of heavy rain throughout the day are expected to cause flooding, according to the US National Weather Service.
A nationwide ground stop earlier this month halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

noticias.titulo: California warns of flooding as King Tides peak over Thanksgiving
noticias.resumen: Parts of the Canadian province of British Columbia may also be affected by the storms and flooding, which come as millions of people travel for the holiday.
noticias.texto:
California warns of flooding as King Tides peak over Thanksgiving
- Published
Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.
Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.
The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding.
Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US.
Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.
Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.
Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area.
In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.
In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding.
Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data.
King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day.
While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by the strongest El NiÃ±o weather pattern on record.
Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said.
On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding.
Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said.
"Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added.
The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina.
The US department store chain Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened.
The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.
Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia.
Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada said.
King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too.

  - Published12 October

noticias.titulo: Two screenings of Pakistani TV show cancelled in India after backlash
noticias.resumen: The show, Dar-e-Nijaat, has become a sensation in India but is now embroiled in a political row.
noticias.texto:
Two screenings of Pakistani TV show cancelled in India after backlash
- Published
Until Wednesday, the weekend plans of some television enthusiasts in the Indian city of Bengaluru involved dressing up, having an elaborate dinner and finding out what happens next in the lives of a wildly popular fictional Pakistani couple.
Then geopolitics intervened.
Two private screenings of Dar-e-Nijaat (Door to Salvation), a Pakistani television drama that has become something of a sensation on Indian social media, were called off after an online backlash and police scrutiny.
The serial, which airs on Pakistan's ARY Digital, is available to Indian viewers through some YouTube channels, though the broadcaster's official channel is blocked in India.
The controversy comes amid a renewed appetite for Pakistani entertainment in India, even though cultural engagement remains a sensitive issue following a brief but intense military confrontation between the two nuclear-armed neighbours in May last year.
A similar gathering in Delhi, featuring quizzes and even a virtual interaction with the show's director, had already divided opinion online last week.
In Bengaluru, one screening, scheduled for Saturday at a restaurant, offered a Persian and Arabic dinner alongside two episodes of the serial for a small ticket charge. The other - scheduled at a private theatre and meant only for family members - asked guests to dress in their "best Pakistani ensemble".
As promotional posters circulated online, several social media users questioned the appropriateness of such gatherings and called for police intervention. Both events have since been called off.
The backlash has coincided with calls to block the release of another Pakistani drama in India.
The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi demanding that Netflix's upcoming Pakistani series, Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo (Gather whatever is left), be barred from release in India.
Featuring Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan, Sanam Saeed and other stars with many Indian fans, the series is Pakistan's first Netflix original. Its global premiere is scheduled for 4 December.
In its letter to Modi on Tuesday, the AICWA argued that releasing the series in India would disregard the sentiments of families affected by terrorism. India has long accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism, an allegation Islamabad denies.
The association has also sought permanent legislation prohibiting Pakistani entertainment content in India. Netflix is yet to clarify whether the series will be available to Indian subscribers.
The developments have revived an old debate in India over whether cultural ties with Pakistan should be kept separate from political differences.
India and Pakistan share a rich cultural heritage, but relations between them have often been fraught since they were carved out of British India as independent nations in 1947.
And cultural exchanges have often been among the first casualties of political tensions. Pakistani ghazal singers with devoted audiences in India have periodically found themselves unable to perform there. Indian films, immensely popular in Pakistan, have disappeared from its cinemas. Artistic collaborations have flourished during periods of relative calm, only to unravel when tensions flare again.
The early 2010s were a particularly fertile period. Pakistani singers Atif Aslam and Rahat Fateh Ali Khan were among the most recognisable voices in Hindi cinema. The launch of the television channel Zindagi in 2014 brought Pakistani serials into Indian living rooms, introducing viewers to stories whose language and emotional worlds were familiar, but whose treatment of everyday life often felt refreshingly different.
By 2016, Fawad Khan was appearing in some of Bollywood's most prominent productions. But attacks on Indian security forces in Uri that year and in Pulwama in 2019, both of which India blamed on Pakistan-based militant groups, narrowed the space for cultural collaboration. Pakistan - which has constantly denied any involvement - also imposed restrictions on Indian entertainment.
Even as formal exchanges dwindled, Pakistani dramas found new audiences in India on YouTube, while music continued to travel across the border through streaming platforms.
But the events of last year disrupted even this relatively informal relationship.
On 22 April 2025, militants killed 26 people, most of them tourists, in Pahalgam in Indian-administered Kashmir. India blamed Pakistan-linked militants; Islamabad denied involvement. In May, India launched military strikes on what it described as terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir. Four days of fighting followed before a ceasefire was announced.
Amid widespread anger in India, the government asked streaming platforms to discontinue Pakistani-origin content, while social media accounts of several Pakistani celebrities were blocked.
Fawad Khan's much-anticipated return to Hindi cinema with Abir Gulaal was thwarted when the film was denied permission for release in India. Criticism of India's military action by Pakistani artistes fuelled further anger.
For much of the past year, Indian audiences have encountered Pakistan on screen largely through the prism of national security. In December, millions flocked to watch Dhurandhar, Aditya Dhar's espionage thriller, whose success inspired a fascination with the gangsters, spies and political intrigues of Karachi.
But in recent months, a more familiar kind of fascination with Pakistan has begun to resurface.
Pakistani songs like Alfaaz have become hugely popular on Indian social media, while Dar-e-Nijaat, a story about marriage, heartbreak and domestic life, has found an enthusiastic audience.
Written by the celebrated Urdu novelist Umera Ahmed, the serial revolves around the marriage of Zaryab (Durefishan Saleem), a young woman recovering from a romantic betrayal, and Abu Bakar (Sheheryar Munawar), a deeply religious man.
Though the drama explores questions of faith and redemption, it is Abu Bakar's tenderness towards his wife that has earned him perhaps the highest accolade in the contemporary vocabulary of courtship: a "green flag".
It was this enthusiasm for the drama that prompted the organiser of one of the screenings in Bengaluru to plan an event at a private theatre in her apartment complex.
What she had envisaged as a small family gathering, she said, had been interpreted quite differently once the invitation found its way onto X.
"My family was saying why should we cancel?" she said. But ultimately, she decided to call it off.

noticias.titulo: Israeli attacks on Gaza kill senior education official, seven other people
noticias.resumen: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirms killing of Khaled Abu Nada, undersecretary of Education Ministry.
noticias.texto:
Israeli attacks on Gaza kill senior education official, seven other people
Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirms killing of Khaled Abu Nada, undersecretary of Education Ministry.
Israeli attacks have killed at least eight Palestinians across the Gaza Strip, including a senior education official and his wife, according to health officials, as attacks continued despite the ceasefire in the enclave.
Khaled Abu Nada, undersecretary of Gaza’s Ministry of Education, and his wife were killed in an air strike in western Deir el-Balah, medics at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital said on Thursday. Six other people were wounded, several of them critically.
“Without prior warning, Israeli Apache helicopters fired two missiles directly and in succession at this residential apartment,” Al Jazeera’s Ashraf Abu Amra said, reporting from Deir el-Balah. He said the area was crowded with hundreds of tents sheltering displaced families, and that the strike came during dawn prayers.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz said the attack killed Abu Nada, whom they said was “a Hamas figure responsible for the group’s economy and education portfolios”.
In northern Gaza, a drone attack on a group of people in Gaza City’s Shati refugee camp killed three people and wounded four, al-Shifa Hospital said, and a separate strike on the Tuffah neighbourhood killed three people. Another drone attack on the Nassr neighbourhood wounded several people.
The deaths follow a string of attacks on Gaza’s Hamas-run security services. Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, internal security chief for northern Gaza, was killed with his wife and two daughters early on Wednesday, a day after Naim Abu Nahl, Gaza’s internal security director, was killed, Al Jazeera’s Nour Khaled said, reporting from Gaza City.
“What stands out is the direct targeting by Israeli forces through the assassination of security and police commanders,” Abu Amra said. Gaza’s Ministry of Interior has accused Israel of trying to spread chaos in the territory.
Near Israel’s so-called “Yellow Line” that marks areas under Israeli control, Israeli quadcopters drop bombs, and “some of them drop boxes loaded with explosives that blow the roofs off buildings,” Khaled said.
Gaza Health Ministry spokesperson Zaher al-Wahidi told Al Jazeera that more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed, including 130 this month, in Israeli attacks since the ceasefire took effect last October, with more than 6,000 wounded. “This is a systematic targeting of all the pillars of life in the Gaza Strip,” he said.
Gaza’s Health Ministry says 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since Israel launched its genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza in October 2023, in response to the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.

noticias.titulo: Why has North Korea expelled a Swiss diplomat from Pyongyang?
noticias.resumen: At the centre of the diplomatic dispute lies the Songdowon International Children’s Camp.
noticias.texto:
Why has North Korea expelled a Swiss diplomat from Pyongyang?
At the centre of the diplomatic dispute lies the Songdowon International Children’s Camp, accused of housing abducted Ukrainian children.
North Korea has expelled the head of Switzerland’s diplomatic office in its capital amid a sanctions row, only weeks after Bern reopened an office and the Swiss foreign minister discussed normalising relations.
According to North Korea’s foreign ministry on Wednesday, the decision to expel the diplomatic representative stemmed from Switzerland’s decision to impose sanctions on the Songdowon International Children’s Camp.
A day earlier, Kim Yo Jong, one of Pyongyang’s top foreign policy officials and sister to leader Kim Jong Un, described the sanctions as an “open hostile act” and an infringement of the North’s sovereignty, in a statement.
She said the camp supported “legitimate” cooperation between North Korea and Russia but didn’t directly address Western accusations that some Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces were sent there to be “re-educated”.
Here’s what we know about the spat.
What has North Korea said?
According to a statement by the foreign ministry carried by the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), the head of the Swiss diplomatic office, Sylvain Astier, was summoned and handed a memorandum calling on him to close the office.
“The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours,” the ministry said.
“Any act of violating the sovereign rights of the DPRK and the interests of its citizens can never be welcomed by us.”
What has Switzerland said?
Responding to the move, the Swiss foreign ministry said relations with Pyongyang would continue through its embassy in the Chinese capital, Beijing, and through North Korea’s embassy in Bern.
It added that it regretted the decision and was arranging for Astier to return to the Beijing embassy.
“The closure of the office does not call into question diplomatic relations between Switzerland and North Korea,” the ministry said.
Late last month, Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis travelled to Pyongyang as Bern opened the office and held talks with senior North Korean officials, including his counterpart, Choe Son Hui, on “promoting dialogue and cooperation”, KCNA said at the time.
What is the sanctioned camp?
At the centre of the diplomatic dispute lies the Songdowon International Children’s Camp, which has been accused of hosting and attempting to indoctrinate children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.
On Tuesday, Switzerland added the camp to its sanctions list over its alleged role in the transfer of these children and said it would consider closing its diplomatic office in Pyongyang.
Closely allied with Russia, North Korea has supported Moscow’s war efforts by sending thousands of troops and weapons.
Adding the camp to its list of sanctions, Swiss authorities said the facility exposes children to propaganda and activities designed to promote pro-Russia narratives.
The United Kingdom in May and the European Union in September imposed similar sanctions on the camp, freezing its assets and banning financial transactions with the facility.
What’s the status of North Korean–Swiss relations?
Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain diplomatic relations with North Korea and established relations in 1974.
Reportedly, both Kim Jong Un and Kim Yo Jong attended school in Switzerland as teenagers in the 1990s.
In 1997, the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation opened a “cooperation office” in the North Korean capital that focused on humanitarian programmes.
In 2020, amid the COVID-19 pandemic, the office shut as Pyongyang closed its borders.

noticias.titulo: Explosion occurs at oil facility in Thailand’s Bangkok
noticias.resumen: Authorities urge residents in area surrounding oil depot in eastern Bangkok to evacuate their homes.
noticias.texto:
Explosion occurs at oil facility in Thailand’s Bangkok
Authorities urge residents in area surrounding oil depot in eastern Bangkok to evacuate their homes.
An explosion has occurred at an oil facility in Bangkok, authorities said, as residents in the surrounding area were told to evacuate.
Videos posted on social media on Thursday showed flames rising high above the site in eastern Bangkok, and thick black smoke rising and sweeping across the Thai capital’s skyline.
There were no immediate reports of casualties after the blast, and the Bang Na district office did not give a cause of the explosion.
“An explosion has occurred at the Bangchak oil depot. For their own safety, members of the public in the vicinity are urged to evacuate the area immediately,” Bangna District Office said in a statement on its Facebook page.
The sprawling site in eastern Bangkok is run by Thai energy conglomerate Bangchak Corporation.

noticias.titulo: Thanksgiving and National Day of Mourning: What is the history?
noticias.resumen: Indigenous activists challenge Thanksgiving narratives and highlight ongoing struggles for sovereignty and recognition.
noticias.texto:
Thanksgiving and National Day of Mourning: What is the history?
Indigenous activists challenge Thanksgiving narratives and highlight ongoing struggles for sovereignty and recognition.
As millions of people across the United States meet with famiy and friends to celebrate Thanksgiving on Thursday, Indigenous people and their supporters will gather in Plymouth, Massachusetts, to mark the 57th annual National Day of Mourning.
For many Indigenous people, the traditional story of Thanksgiving overlooks centuries of colonisation, land dispossession and forced displacement.
But Indigenous activists say the day is also an opportunity to highlight the issues their communities continue to face, from the fight for sovereignty and the protection of their ancestral lands to the struggle to have their voices heard throughout the year.
Here is what we know:
When are Thanksgiving and the National Day of Mourning in 2026?
In the US, Thanksgiving Day is celebrated every year on the fourth Thursday of November; this year it falls on Thursday, November 26.
In 1863, during the US Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed a national day of Thanksgiving to be observed on the last Thursday of November.
In 1941, Congress officially established the fourth Thursday of November as Thanksgiving Day.
The National Day of Mourning is observed on the same day. It’s an annual Indigenous-led gathering and protest held to honour Indigenous ancestors, challenge mainstream Thanksgiving narratives and draw attention to the ongoing struggles of Indigenous peoples. It was first held in Plymouth, Massachusetts, in 1970.
Other Indigenous-led gatherings and ceremonies take place elsewhere in the US, including the Indigenous Peoples Thanksgiving Sunrise Gathering on Alcatraz Island in California.
What is the history of Thanksgiving?
The US celebration commonly goes back to the autumn of 1621, when English settlers and members of the Wampanoag came together for a three-day harvest celebration in what is now Plymouth, Massachusetts.
But the tradition of giving thanks among Indigenous peoples goes way back before the arrival of European settlers.
“It did not take colonisation to bring a concept of Thanksgiving to this continent,” Jean-Luc Pierite, president of the North American Indian Center of Boston, told Al Jazeera.
“For Indigenous peoples, we have had our ways of feasting, of expressing gratitude, of being in community,” he said.
In November 1620, a group of 102 colonists on board the Mayflower reached present-day Massachusetts. They later established a settlement known as Plymouth on the ancestral lands of the Wampanoag people, at the site of a village known as Patuxet.
Their arrival followed a series of devastating epidemics associated with European contact that had killed many Indigenous people in the region.
In March 1621, the Wampanoag leader Ousamequin, also known as Massasoit, established an alliance with the English settlers for mutual protection.
Later that year, at least 90 Wampanoag men and about 50 English settlers took part in a harvest gathering that would later become known as the “first Thanksgiving”. The moment was documented by English settler Edward Winslow.
This meeting became part of a story of friendship and cooperation between European settlers and Indigenous peoples.
But some Indigenous activists and leaders have contested that narrative, saying it ignores the broader history of colonisation, land dispossession and displacement.
It was more than two centuries after the gathering, in 1863, that Lincoln proclaimed a national day of Thanksgiving.
The proclamation came in the middle of the American Civil War and followed a years-long campaign led by Sarah Josepha Hale, a writer and editor best known as the author of Mary Had a Little Lamb.
What does the traditional Thanksgiving story leave out?
For some, the popular Thanksgiving narrative ignores centuries of violence, land dispossession and forced displacement.
“There is a sanitised version of history in which settlers and Indigenous peoples come together and share a meal,” Pierite said.
He said that this portrayal overlooks the loss of Indigenous lands and lives over the past 400 years.
As European settlements expanded, the Indigenous peoples lost enormous parts of their traditional lands through war, forced relocation and broken treaties.
In 1830, President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act, which led to the forced displacement of tens of thousands of Indigenous peoples from their homelands.
Later legislation broadened the reservation system and permitted ownership of tribal lands by non-Indigenous people. Indigenous landholdings declined from about 138 million acres (56 million hectares) in 1887 to 48 million acres (19 million hectares) in 1934.
“More than 400 years after the arrival of the Mayflower, Indigenous people are still denied basic human rights and full control of their own homelands,” Kisha James, co-leader of the United American Indians of New England (UAINE), who is Aquinnah Wampanoag and Oglala Lakota, said in a statement.
What is the National Day of Mourning, and why did it begin?
The National Day of Mourning was first held in 1970 after Wamsutta Frank James, an Aquinnah Wampanoag activist, was invited to speak at an event marking the 350th anniversary of the Pilgrims’ arrival.
After the organisers objected to his speech on the history of violence, land seizure and treatment of Indigenous peoples, James refused to deliver a different version.
Instead, Indigenous people and their supporters gathered in Plymouth on Thanksgiving Day, starting what would become an annual protest.
The gathering, organised by the United American Indians of New England (UAINE), has since become a day of remembrance, resistance and advocacy for Indigenous rights.
Today, James’s granddaughter, Kisha James, is a co-leader of UAINE.
“We are still facing many of the issues that our elders talked about in 1970 at the first National Day of Mourning,” she said in a statement ahead of this year’s gathering.
Pierite said the gathering has grown over the years, attracting both Indigenous and non-Indigenous participants.
“We’re seeing thousands of people gather with us, whether they are Indigenous or not,” he said.
How does the National Day of Mourning relate to other Indigenous struggles around the world?
Pierite said the gathering has also become a platform for expressing solidarity with Indigenous peoples and other communities around the world.
Since October 7, 2023, when a Hamas-led attack on southern Israel was followed by Israel’s war on Gaza, Palestinian speakers have been invited to participate in the National Day of Mourning and speak about their experiences, he said.
He drew parallels between the displacement of Indigenous peoples in the US and Palestinian demands for the right of return, as well as the Indigenous Land Back movement.
“We see these different causes in a very interconnected way,” he said.
“The histories that we have experienced, the suffering that we have experienced, we see that reflected in what is going on in the world today,” Pierite added.
Mahtowin Munro, co-leader of UAINE, said this year’s gathering would also express solidarity with Indigenous communities opposing mining, pipelines, resource extraction and large dams on their lands.
“From Peru to British Columbia, from Boston to the Amazon, Indigenous peoples are defending their sovereignty, calling for land back, and insisting that nothing should happen on their lands without their freely given consent,” Munro said in a statement.
“Indigenous solidarity and resistance are international.”
Why do Indigenous activists call for recognition beyond Thanksgiving?
For some, Thanksgiving also highlights a broader issue: the attention their communities receive around this time of the year and how often their struggles are not recognised during the rest of the year.
“This is a bit of a pain point for our communities because often … we get relegated to the months of October and November,” Pierite said.
He said a lot of the attention is centred around commemorations such as Indigenous Peoples’ Day and the National Day of Mourning. While these occasions help raise public awareness, he said, what’s needed is for people to be more aware of Indigenous issues all year round.
“Our issues are yearlong,” he said.
Pierite also highlighted the role of Indigenous peoples in addressing climate change and protecting the environment, saying their voices often struggle to be heard against corporate interests.
“We really need to have these types of platforms and this type of coalition building … so that everybody in the world can build a just and sustainable future,” he said.
James also called for greater recognition of Indigenous perspectives on environmental issues.
“We call on non-Native people to listen to Indigenous voices, especially about how to address the climate crisis,” she said in a statement.
How are Indigenous communities marking the day in 2026?
In Plymouth, Massachusetts, Indigenous people and their supporters are expected to gather at noon (17:00 GMT) near the statue of Massasoit on Cole’s Hill for the 57th annual National Day of Mourning.
According to UAINE, this year’s gathering will highlight issues including missing and murdered Indigenous women, girls and Two-Spirit people, federal funding cuts, Indigenous sovereignty and environmental protection.
On the West Coast, the International Indian Treaty Council (IITC) is holding its annual Indigenous Peoples Thanksgiving Sunrise Gathering on Alcatraz Island in San Francisco, California.
The gathering commemorates the Indigenous occupation of Alcatraz from 1969 to 1971, which helped galvanise the Indigenous rights movement in the US.
Organisers said the gathering honours the resistance of Indigenous ancestors and expresses gratitude for the survival of Indigenous peoples, cultures and ways of life.
Other communities mark this time of year through family gatherings, community meals and expressions of gratitude.
In Washington state, for example, elders of the Muckleshoot Tribe gathered on November 16 for an annual meal celebrating family, friendship and community.

noticias.titulo: Photos: Rallies around the world denounce violence against women
noticias.resumen: About 47,000 women and girls were intentionally killed by an intimate partner or family member last year, UN data shows.
noticias.texto:
In Pictures
Photos: Rallies around the world denounce violence against women
About 47,000 women and girls were intentionally killed by an intimate partner or family member last year, UN data shows.
Women have rallied around the world to mark the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women.
About 47,000 women and girls were intentionally killed by an intimate partner or family member last year, according to data from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and UN Women.
The figures, published on Tuesday in the 2026 Femicide Brief to coincide with the international day, show the scale of gender-based killings worldwide.
While the 47,000 figure is lower than the 2024 estimate of 50,000 victims, the UN said this change largely reflects improved country-level data rather than an actual decrease in femicides.
No region was spared, with such killings recorded across the globe. The UN found that while overall homicide rates have declined worldwide, femicide rates have fallen at a slower pace.

noticias.titulo: DR Congo Ebola cases surpass 12,000 as fighting disrupts response in east
noticias.resumen: Authorities struggle to contain country's worst Ebola outbreak, as fighting in east displaces health workers, civilians.
noticias.texto:
DR Congo Ebola cases surpass 12,000 as fighting disrupts response in east
Authorities struggle to contain country’s worst Ebola outbreak, as fighting in east displaces health workers, civilians.
The number of confirmed ‌Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has surpassed 12,000, government data shows, as escalating fighting in the east disrupts efforts to contain the country’s deadliest outbreak on record.
Ebola response workers have been forced to leave affected areas amid worsening violence in the eastern DRC, health officials and humanitarian workers said on Wednesday.
Clashes in Ituri province have intensified in recent days between the Congolese army and fighters from the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP), displacing civilians, the United Nations mission said in a statement.
Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization’s Ebola incident manager, said about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia after three days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.
“They were caught really in the crossfire, very intense fighting, and we managed to evacuate them,” Smallwood said.
The CRP is led by Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of conscripting child soldiers. The group declared a unilateral ceasefire in May, but fighting has continued.
It is one of more than 100 armed groups in the eastern DRC, where conflict has disrupted efforts to contain the country’s worst Ebola outbreak on record.
At least 12,021 infections have been confirmed, including 5,904 deaths, government data showed on Thursday.
The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of the Ebola virus, was declared in mid-May in Ituri province in the northeastern DRC. There are no approved treatments or vaccines for this species.
Delayed detection, conflict, and strained health services have accelerated the spread of infections, with cases reported in eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces.
Sandrine Buju, a humanitarian worker involved in the Ebola response, said her team came under gunfire on Monday while returning to Bunia after training community volunteers.
“We were surprised by gunfire about 15 metres (50ft) from where we were,” she told The Associated Press news agency. “I was very frightened.”
The driver immediately turned around, and the team sought protection at a UN peacekeeping base, Buju said. Peacekeepers later escorted them through two areas of fighting towards Bunia.

noticias.texto:
At least 13 dead in Indonesia gold mine flood as rescue efforts intensify
Rescue workers facing tough conditions, with narrow, deep and slippery excavation pits and minimal lighting.
At least 13 workers have died and 13 others remain missing after flooding hit an unauthorised gold mine in Indonesia’s West Java province.
Local search and rescue chief Desiana Kartika Bahari confirmed the death toll in a statement on Thursday, as rescuers battled high water, darkness and slippery, narrow terrain in search of the missing workers.
Police first received reports of trapped miners on Tuesday, about 16 hours after the flooding occurred, police said, while nearby state-owned mining company PT Antam forwarded a formal report to the Jakarta Search and Rescue Agency shortly after midnight on Wednesday, triggering a full-scale rescue operation.
Authorities said they were not immediately notified because the miners were operating illegally, and local miners and residents initially tried to pump water from the site themselves before the situation became unmanageable.
The 325 rescue personnel have been facing challenging conditions, with narrow excavation pits about 100 metres (330 feet) deep, minimal lighting and slippery terrain conditions, Desiana said.
“The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely,” Desiana explained. “All efforts are made by taking into account field conditions and prioritising the safety of personnel involved in SAR (search and rescue) operations,” she added.
Eleven miners were able to leave safely before water flooded the shafts on Monday, West Java police spokesperson Hendra Rochmawan said.
The mine is located in the Pongkor area of Bogor, a mountainous area 60km south of the capital, Jakarta, where state miner Antam runs gold-mining operations.
Small-scale and unauthorised mining often leads to accidents in resource-rich Indonesia, where mineral resources are located in remote areas in conditions difficult for authorities to regulate.
