noticias.titulo: War and drought threaten livelihoods of Sudan’s farmers
noticias.resumen: Attacks on electricity infrastructure and drought are threatening Sudan's harvests and leaving millions without water.
noticias.texto:
War and drought threaten livelihoods of Sudan’s farmers
Attacks on electricity infrastructure and drought are threatening Sudan’s harvests and leaving millions without water.
Haider Mohamed has worked as a farmer in Sudan’s Northern State for more than 40 years, growing fava beans, wheat, and a variety of seasonal crops.
But Sudan’s water crisis – a combination of lower-than-average rainfall and war-induced devastation to infrastructure – has severely affected his harvest and his income.
It’s a situation Mohamed describes as unprecedented in his 40 years of farming.
Mohamed owns a small farm covering about four hectares (about 10 acres) in al-Saleem, near the city of Dongola. He keeps part of his harvest to feed his family, and then sells the rest at local markets to cover essential living expenses, including healthcare and his children’s education.
“Our crops were destroyed last year, and this year it is difficult to generate any income because we are still facing electricity and irrigation problems,” Mohamed told Al Jazeera, referring to drone attacks on power stations that disrupted electricity supplies, and regularly stopped him from using electricity-dependent irrigation systems. “We have accumulated a lot of debt, and we fear that we will not harvest enough to feed our children, let alone have any surplus to sell in the market.”
Mohamed’s experience is far from unique. Across Northern State and other parts of Sudan, water shortages caused by declining rainfall or disruptions to irrigation are increasingly threatening agricultural production and the livelihoods of farming communities.
“Those who rely on diesel-powered pumps [for irrigation] cannot find fuel, and when it is available, it is extremely expensive,” Mohamed explained. “We also cannot afford the cost of installing solar-powered irrigation systems. At this rate, no one will be able to continue farming in this country.”
The ongoing war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in 2023, has severely disrupted fuel supplies in the country. Attacks on Sudan’s largest oil refinery, as well as fuel depots and petrol stations, have exacerbated shortages.
In just October, attacks blamed on the RSF damaged critical infrastructure across 11 states, disrupting electricity and water services and disabling several water supply sources.
Rising global energy prices have also made imports more expensive, with the United Nations reporting that the price of diesel nearly doubled between March and August this year.
Struggle to find drinking water
In Sudan’s rain-fed agricultural regions, drought has compounded the problems facing farmers.
Rainfall during this year’s June-to-September rainy season declined across most of Sudan’s agricultural areas, believed to be linked to the ongoing global El Nino phenomenon. In the southeastern states of Gedaref and Sennar, rainfall was approximately 30 percent and 20 percent compared with normal levels, respectively, according to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).
The two states normally account for about a quarter of Sudan’s sorghum production – the country’s main staple cereal.
The impact of the water crisis extends beyond the agricultural sector, affecting millions of people struggling to access drinking water and meet their basic household needs.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) says damage to water and electricity systems and other civilian infrastructure has deprived millions of people of essential services, while disruptions to water supplies have increased the risk of cholera and other waterborne diseases.
The UN children’s agency, UNICEF, estimates that more than 27 million people in Sudan are in need of water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance.
Between January and June of this year, UNICEF and its partners provided 6.6 million people with access to safe water, with approximately two-thirds of those receiving emergency assistance, including displaced people, those who had returned home and communities affected by conflict and cholera.
In the capital Khartoum, residents are still forced to stand in long queues for water, sometimes waiting for hours. Widespread disruptions to water supply networks and the shutdown of several water stations due to damage sustained during the war have left many households without a reliable water supply.
Saleh Zaki, who lives in Khartoum State’s East Nile district, said the area has suffered from water supply problems for many years, even before the outbreak of the war.
“Before the war, we repeatedly sought help from the authorities, only to be told there was no budget to address the problem,” Zaki said. “We therefore raised funds ourselves and hired a specialist to drill two wells, providing residents with limited water supply.”
“Since the conflict damaged the water networks … we urgently need more wells, repairs to the supply networks and solar-powered systems to support our neighbourhood and nearby communities,” he added.
Solar power
In August, the Sudanese government announced a series of measures designed to ease the water crisis and encourage families displaced by war to return home.
These measures include exempting solar panels imported for personal use from customs duties, taxes, and other government fees, and waiving residential water fees nationwide until the end of 2026.
However, these measures remain limited in their impact unless accompanied by broader economic policies.
“These measures should be expanded to include greater government support for the agricultural sector, incentives for farmers, and easier access to financing for solar energy systems for agricultural use,” said Mohamed Elnayer, an economist at the Sudan University of Science and Technology. “More comprehensive reforms are also needed in the housing and agricultural sectors, particularly to rehabilitate and improve water stations, expand access to reliable water supplies, and reduce the costs of essential infrastructure.”

noticias.titulo: The world must choose between nuclear abolition and nuclear catastrophe
noticias.resumen: The upcoming UN nuclear ban treaty conference offers an opportunity to challenge the dogma of nuclear deterrence.
noticias.texto:
The world must choose between nuclear abolition and nuclear catastrophe
The upcoming UN nuclear ban treaty conference offers an opportunity to challenge the dogma of nuclear deterrence.
The world is currently facing the greatest risk of deliberate or inadvertent nuclear conflict since the Cold War – or perhaps ever.
While the threat of nuclear war may have dropped out of the headlines, it did not go away with the end of the Cold War. The United States and Russia had a window of opportunity in the early 1990s to eliminate nuclear weapons when there were still only 5 nuclear powers, but they spurned it.
Fast forward to today, and these two countries that, between them, possess almost 90 percent of the world’s nuclear weapons have initiated wars with non-nuclear-armed countries: Ukraine and Iran. The aggressors’ leaders, presidents Putin and Trump, have made threats to use nuclear weapons.
It is worrying that while these threats have not gone unreported, they have quickly passed from the headlines. However, the good news is that the rest of the world is pushing back against this ongoing existential threat – not through mass protests, but through quiet, multilateral diplomacy and persistent advocacy by civil society, including my organisation, ICAN.
Putin and Trump did recently meet their Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, who commands the third-largest nuclear arsenal, for their first-ever three-way summit. They reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. But in their declaration, they did not say anything new; simply that they would discuss reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The question we face today of how we ensure our security in a world of newly competing nuclear-armed powers is, at its root, the same we have faced since the development of the atomic bomb – how do we deal with the constant threat these weapons pose to humanity?
Despite the insistence of the nuclear-armed minority that there is no alternative to their theory of nuclear deterrence, we are part of a diplomatic push offering the world a choice. Powerful countries can continue to blindly believe in deterrence dogma, a theory of human behaviour unsupported by evidence, that has led us to the brink of catastrophe more than once. Or countries can agree to the total elimination of these weapons for good.
Deterrence is based on the capability and willingness to use nuclear weapons to kill millions of innocent people. The threat is present every moment in the form of the 4,000 nuclear weapons deployed and ready to use at short notice – more than enough to end civilisation as we know it many times over. This is the current choice of a minority of countries – the nine that have nuclear weapons and their nuclear-endorsing allies, principally the members of NATO.
The alternative of abolishing nuclear weapons is growing in strength, but not talked about nearly as much. It is the choice of the majority of the world and is embodied in the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons – the United Nations’ nuclear ban treaty, or TPNW, that 101 countries have already signed or ratified.
The treaty bans nuclear weapons and all activities associated with them outright and has created a new norm of international law that makes these weapons unacceptable, alongside biological and chemical weapons.
The first review conference of the treaty will soon take place at the UN in New York under the presidency of South Africa – a country that set the example of how nuclear weapons can be eliminated by doing it. In the 1970s, Apartheid South Africa, with the help of Israel, developed a nuclear arsenal, but then voluntarily dismantled it under international supervision in the 1990s.
The conference will evaluate how the treaty has been implemented so far and identify how it can be further strengthened. Unlike the review conference of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty earlier this year that failed to reach consensus for the third consecutive time, this gathering is expected to agree on a number of significant decisions. There will be a strong political declaration stressing the importance of nuclear disarmament and the urgency of addressing the growing risk that nuclear weapons could be used again in conflict, including calling out the role of nuclear deterrence in driving this threat to all countries. There is also the prospect of more countries using the conference as an opportunity to sign or ratify the treaty.
As TPNW states have noted, deterrence does not bring security and stability; it brings chronic insecurity to the entire world. There is nothing inevitable about nuclear weapons. They are a political choice. They are created by human hands, and they can be dismantled by human hands – as South Africa demonstrated.
The remaining countries that support the treaty but still need to join it should do so now. That will highlight just how isolated the nine nuclear-armed countries are and add to the pressure on them and their allies to get on the right side of history.
The words of President Kennedy addressing the UN 65 years ago remain as relevant today: “The weapons of war must be abolished before they abolish us.”
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: Who really wants Pedro Sanchez out of power?
noticias.resumen: As Spain heads to the polls, the biggest threat to Sanchez’s international agenda comes not from Moscow, but Washington.
noticias.texto:
Who really wants Pedro Sanchez out of power?
As Spain heads to the polls, the biggest threat to Sanchez’s international agenda comes not from Moscow, but Washington.
On November 2, Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares warned that “state and non-state forces” were seeking to interfere in Spain’s November 29 parliamentary elections. Albares did not clarify whom he was referring to or what the intervention might consist of, but he did state that the far right – which hopes to enter the national government for the first time since the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975 – is the “favourite option” of these foreign actors.
Most polls predict a parliamentary majority for the conservative Popular Party (PP) together with the far-right Vox, which could form a coalition government that would expel Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez from power. Sanchez currently leads a coalition formed by the Socialist Party (PSOE) and the left-wing party Sumar.
European authorities have denounced Russian interference in various elections in recent years, aimed at supporting far-right candidates reluctant to support Ukraine. European concern began even before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, as US authorities identified “sweeping and systematic” Russian interference in the 2016 US presidential election, which brought Donald Trump to power, through the creation of thousands of social media accounts and the leaking of Democratic Party emails.
In 2024, Romania’s Constitutional Court annulled the presidential election following allegations of foreign interference and illegal campaign financing. The controversial decision led the pro-Russian Calin Georgescu, who had won the first round, and other candidates to denounce a “coup d’état”.
Spain has committed nearly four billion euros ($4.3bn) in military aid to Ukraine, so in principle it is reasonable to expect Russian interference to try to achieve a government more favourable to its interests. However, even Vox, which has an ideological affinity with Putin’s government, has “condemned Russia’s illegitimate invasion and has supported the right of the Ukrainian people to defend themselves” and supports aid to Ukraine, albeit with some reservations. Moreover, if Vox comes to power, it will do so in coalition with the PP, a pro-European party that will foreseeably maintain support for Ukraine. Putin cannot aspire to a substantial change in Spain’s position on Ukraine.
Those with the greatest interest in seeing Pedro Sanchez lose power are not Putin, but Donald Trump, Benjamin Netanyahu and their allies in Europe and Latin America.
In recent years, Sanchez has become a standard-bearer for the left on both sides of the Atlantic, thanks to his resistance to Trump’s imperialism and the genocide in Gaza.
In 2025, Sanchez rejected Trump’s demand to allocate 5 percent of GDP to defence. Spain was the only one of NATO’s 32 states to refuse, angering the Republican, who threatened trade retaliation. Moreover, Spain’s membership of the EU means that any such trade retaliation would put Washington in conflict with the entire bloc. This is an advantage that Sanchez exploited again when he denied the US military the use of its bases on Spanish territory to bomb Iran.
Sanchez’s government also broke ranks with its European partners in response to the genocide in Gaza. While the governments of Europe’s major powers wavered between inaction and open complicity, the Spanish coalition government decreed an arms embargo on Israel in September 2025, accusing it of “exterminating” and “starving” Palestinians in Gaza.
The embargo was only partial, and it was not Sanchez’s decision alone. It was a consequence of pressure from his coalition partner Sumar and massive pro-Palestine mobilisations across the country. In 2025, protesters forced the cancellation of the final stage of the Vuelta a Espana cycling race over the participation of an Israeli team. Nevertheless, the embargo’s international impact was considerable.
Sanchez is also hated by the far right in Latin America, a region with which Spain maintains close ties. The most aggressive is Argentinian President Javier Milei, known for his radical policies of social cuts, who has travelled to Spain eight times since his election in 2023. He has embraced Vox leader Santiago Abascal, been decorated by Madrid’s regional president, Isabel Diaz Ayuso of the PP, and has called Sanchez “corrupt” and a “shameful dictator”.
Although when talking about interference, European authorities usually look towards Russia, Trump’s interventions in various Latin American elections have been at least as serious.
In Argentina’s 2025 legislative elections, the US president blackmailed the electorate by stating that, if Milei’s party did not win the vote, he would withdraw the financial package promised to Argentina. His party won.
Trump did something similar regarding Honduras, when he stated that, if his preferred candidate, Nasry Asfura, did not win, “the United States will not waste its money” on aid to the country. Asfura was elected president.
Donald Trump has not openly supported any candidate in Spain, although in July he exploited the massive arrival of immigrants to Ceuta – a Spanish enclave in North Africa – to repeat his narrative about the migratory “invasion”, which benefits the Spanish far right.
Trump’s discretion surely reflects political calculation: the Republican is extremely unpopular in Spain, where 86 percent of the population had an unfavourable opinion of him, according to an August YouGov poll, and open intervention in the election campaign would strengthen the left. In fact, Sanchez has tried to mobilise a certain anti-imperialist patriotism, stating that “Spain is not governed from Washington, Tel Aviv, Moscow or Buenos Aires.”
The stakes in the November 29 elections extend well beyond Spain’s relations with the US.
First, Sanchez’s fall would deprive progressives of one of their most powerful voices in the European Union, where right-wing governments, moderate or radical, rule most countries. Moreover, a joint victory by the PP and Vox would reverse the far right’s relative electoral decline and compensate for the loss of Hungary, where Viktor Orban lost the elections last April.
On the other hand, a PP and Vox government would further dismantle the cordon sanitaire that until a few years ago prevented agreements between centre-right parties and the far right. In Italy, the far right and conservatives already govern together, as they did until recently in the Netherlands. In France, Macron’s government passed an anti-immigration law in 2023 with the support of Marine Le Pen’s party. And in the European Parliament, the European People’s Party (EPP) has agreed with the far right on important reforms such as cuts in climate policies. The Spanish coalition would be another step in this normalisation of the far right as a legitimate government partner.
As Spain heads to the polls on November 29, European concerns about foreign interference should not be limited to Russia. Trump’s interventions in Latin American elections have demonstrated that Washington, too, is willing to interfere in the democratic processes of other countries to bring ideological allies to power.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: Jannik Sinner ruled out of 2027 Australian Open after knee surgery
noticias.resumen: Sinner, a two-time champion at Melbourne Park, has not played a match since winning the 2026 Wimbledon title in July.
noticias.texto:
Jannik Sinner ruled out of 2027 Australian Open after knee surgery
Sinner, a two-time champion at Melbourne Park, has not played a match since winning the 2026 Wimbledon title in July.
World number two Jannik Sinner was on Thursday ruled out of the 2027 Australian Open in January as he recovers from right knee surgery.
The Italian, who won the season-opening Grand Slam in 2024 and 2025, announced this week that he had gone under the knife at a clinic in Finland.
He has not played a match since winning Wimbledon for the second time in July, with his appearance at Melbourne Park always in doubt.
“We’ve been in regular touch with Jannik’s team and they’ve confirmed he won’t be joining us for the AO in January following his recent surgery,” Tennis Australia chief Andrew Abdo said in a statement to AFP news agency.
“Jannik loves competing here in Melbourne and is looking forward to returning for AO 2028.
“We wish him all the very best with his recovery and look forward to seeing him back on court soon.”
Experts have speculated that Sinner’s absence could last three months.
That means the earliest he might be back in action would be during the American hard-court swing, at Indian Wells and the Miami Masters in February-March.
The 25-year-old Sinner was having a brilliant campaign before being stopped by his knee problem, with five Masters 1000 titles alongside his triumph at Wimbledon.
The Italian’s 94 percent win record in 2026 was the best of his career.
In his absence, Alexander Zverev has taken over as world number one.
“Over the past few months, together with my team, we’ve tried everything to treat my injury without surgery,” the five-time major winner said in announcing the operation on Tuesday.
“After some very encouraging progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn’t respond as we had all hoped, that’s why today I underwent a minor surgery to improve the condition of my iliotibial band.”
Spanish star Carlos Alcaraz, who, with Sinner, has become the pre-eminent force in men’s tennis, wished him well.
“Tennis misses him. I miss him,” the world number three, who has had his own injury battles, said on social media.
Sinner won his first Grand Slam in 2024 by beating Daniil Medvedev in five sets at Melbourne Park, then retained his title a year later with victory over Zverev.
He lost in the semifinals this year to Novak Djokovic, who was then beaten in the final by Alcaraz.
The Australian Open gets under way on January 17.

noticias.titulo: Gaza meningitis cases surge as collapsing infrastructure fuels health fears
noticias.resumen: Meningitis is raising alarm in Gaza, where overcrowding, damaged sanitation are putting children at risk.
noticias.texto:
Gaza meningitis cases surge as collapsing infrastructure fuels health fears
Meningitis is raising alarm in Gaza, where overcrowding, damaged sanitation and medical shortages are putting children at risk.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – For the third time in less than a month, five-year-old Omar Abu Fayed has been admitted to the isolation ward at Gaza City’s Rantisi Children’s Hospital after developing symptoms of meningitis.
Each time, his mother, Zakia Abu Fayed, thought he was recovering. But days after being discharged, his fever and pain returned.
“He doesn’t even spend a full week at home before we have to bring him back,” the 24-year-old Zakia told Al Jazeera.
Omar’s illness began with a high fever, severe headache and abdominal pain. He stopped eating, and his temperature rose above 40 degrees Celsius (104F). After five days of treatment at home with fever medication and antibiotics, his condition had not improved, so Zakia took him to hospital, where doctors diagnosed meningitis.
He was admitted for five days and discharged after responding to treatment. But about a week later, the fever returned, and he spent another 10 days in hospital.
The symptoms returned days after his second discharge, and doctors changed his treatment for a third time.
“I hope he responds this time,” she said.
The repeated admissions have left her worried not only about Omar but also about her two younger children, aged three and one. She said the hospital was crowded with children suffering from meningitis, including newborn babies.
Zakia, originally from Jabalia in northern Gaza, believes Omar may have contracted the infection at kindergarten, although its source has not been established. The family has been displaced because of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and is renting a house.
Rising cases and deaths
Zakia’s concerns come as Gaza’s Ministry of Health warns of a sharp increase in meningitis cases. On November 24, the ministry declared an epidemic alert, reporting 272 cases in October – up sharply from the usual monthly average of 30 to 50.
The ministry said 108 of October’s cases were bacterial meningitis, compared with the usual 10 to 20 a month. A further 100 bacterial cases were recorded during the first weeks of November.
It also reported 15 deaths from the disease since the beginning of 2026, including five between August and October.
Meningitis is an inflammation of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord. It can be caused by viruses or bacteria. Bacterial meningitis is particularly dangerous because it can progress rapidly and cause death or lasting complications, including hearing loss and neurological damage.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned that limited laboratory capacity is making it difficult to distinguish between viral and bacterial infections. The UN has also reported shortages of laboratory supplies and essential medicines, with about 42 percent of essential medicines at zero-stock levels in October.
These shortages are adding to the pressure on Gaza’s already weakened health system, as overcrowding and poor sanitation leave displaced families struggling to protect themselves from infection.
Hospitals under pressure
At Rantisi Children’s Hospital, paediatrician Sharif Matar said the current wave began about a month ago and was continuing, although daily admissions had fallen.
“At one stage, we were receiving more than 10 cases a day. Now we are talking about three to four cases daily. There has been a decline, but the wave has not ended,” Matar told Al Jazeera.
Meningitis cases occur seasonally in Gaza, he said, but this year’s increase has placed additional pressure on hospitals. Rantisi is one of the few remaining hospitals providing paediatric services in Gaza, he added, receiving children from across the territory.
Matar linked the spread of infections to overcrowding in displacement camps and tents, where families have limited access to water and facilities for personal hygiene.
“People are living in tents, with severe overcrowding and without sufficient means of maintaining personal hygiene,” he said.
Matar said Rantisi had not recorded any deaths directly attributed to meningitis during the current wave, to his knowledge. However, some children had developed serious complications, including hearing loss and hydrocephalus, which can require surgery to relieve pressure caused by fluid building up in the brain.
He acknowledged that some medicines were occasionally unavailable, but said the hospital had so far been able to obtain the treatments required for its meningitis patients through the Ministry of Health’s medical warehouses.
“We have not reached a point where we can say that a particular essential medicine is completely unavailable,” he said.
Fear for other children
For another mother at Rantisi, the illness has struck her six-month-old twins one after the other. Aya Salem, 29, said she had spent nearly 15 days going between hospital wards as her son Yaman and daughter Yumna became ill.
Yaman first developed a high fever about two weeks ago. After initially being kept under observation and discharged, he was brought back two days later with fever, diarrhoea and a skin rash. Doctors diagnosed meningitis, and he remained in hospital for 10 days.
As he was discharged, his twin sister’s condition worsened. Yumna was admitted with a fever that reached between 39C and 39.7C (102.2F-103.5F), accompanied by severe diarrhoea and vomiting, and was also diagnosed with meningitis. She was unable to breastfeed or take formula.
Doctors treated her with intravenous fluids, medication and zinc supplements. Her fever finally subsided the night before the interview, her mother said, but she remained unwell and had lost considerable weight.
“The doctor told me that she was among the most difficult cases. I was shocked,” Aya said.
She said she had taken precautions to protect the twins, rarely leaving their accommodation for six months except for essential errands, avoiding distribution points and not allowing visitors. But she still did not know how they had become infected.
“We live among displaced people. Every day, you do not know who your neighbour is or who might come into the area. I am extremely careful, but I do not know what happened,” she said.
She described the difficulty of maintaining hygiene in the place where the family is staying, saying there was no reliable access to clean water or adequate sanitary conditions.
Her fear is compounded by the loss of her daughters, Ayloul and Amal, who were also twins and were killed, aged three, during the war in an Israeli air strike in Gaza City on December 19, 2023.
Now, as she watches Yaman and Yumna being treated in hospital, she is pleading for action to improve the conditions in which families are living.
“Enough of what is happening to our children in Gaza. Please intervene and help improve the shattered living conditions people are facing,” she said.

noticias.titulo: How Silicon Valley became central to Israel’s war on Palestinians
noticias.resumen: From surveillance systems to AI targeting, US tech giants are deeply embedded in Israel's war machine.
noticias.texto:
How Silicon Valley became central to Israel’s war on Palestinians
From surveillance systems to AI targeting, US tech giants are deeply embedded in Israel’s war machine.
Activists have cited the Israeli military’s reported use of Amazon’s cloud infrastructure to upload millions of images of Palestinians as further evidence of the deep entrenchment of Western, and principally US, technology in Israel’s military and economic ecosystem.
According to rights groups and analysts interviewed by Al Jazeera, the trade in the technology and expertise that Israel relies on to monitor, track and kill Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza involves many of the United States’s leading technology companies, including Google, Palantir, and Microsoft. And, as Al Jazeera reported earlier this year, some of that technology has also been exported to Western governments publicly critical of Israel and its actions.
In January 2024, the US tech giant Palantir agreed to a strategic partnership with Israel’s Ministry of Defence for “war-related missions”, while Microsoft’s Azure cloud computing platform was reported to have been used to store vast archives of intercepted Palestinian phone calls that sources said helped guide deadly air strikes.
Google and Amazon, meanwhile, provide the Israeli military with advanced facial recognition and artificial intelligence capacity as part of the $1.2bn Project Nimbus.
And the US chipmaker Nvidia has become so central to the Israeli economy that economists have credited its tax payments with helping to reduce the country’s fiscal deficit.
“It’s everywhere,” said Jalal Abukhater of the digital and social rights group 7amleh, describing the surveillance Palestinians live under every day. “If you’re in East Jerusalem or Hebron, you’re being photographed. When I go to the running track, my picture is taken countless times at checkpoints or by roadside cameras.
“The 3.5 million images uploaded to Amazon are nothing. Everyone is photographed all the time, and it’s all getting fed into these systems that we don’t know about and for reasons they don’t explain.”
Silicon Valley goes to war
The rightward shift in Silicon Valley over recent years has been accompanied by more overt support for Israel.
Palantir, in particular, has been unapologetic in its support for the country throughout its genocidal war on Gaza. In July 2025, UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese found “reasonable grounds” to believe the company had provided predictive policing technology and an AI platform to Israeli forces, adding that, had proper due diligence been undertaken, technology firms such as Palantir would have divested from Israel “long ago”.
In January 2024, the Business and Human Rights Resource Centre, an international nonprofit that tracks corporate conduct, logged numerous allegations that Palantir technology had been used in Israeli attacks on Gaza. Palantir has denied abetting war crimes and denied developing the Israeli military’s Lavender and Gospel AI-assisted targeting systems.
However, Open Intel, which tracks corporate involvement in the war, has said Palantir’s software is linked to the Israeli military’s integration of intercepted communications, satellite imagery and other data to help compile military targeting lists.
Project Nimbus has also emerged as a key plank of US technology’s support for Israeli operations in the West Bank and Gaza. According to Albanese’s report, Amazon and Google stepped in when Israel’s cloud and AI infrastructure became overloaded following the beginning of its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.
And OpenAI’s models have also reportedly found their way into the Israeli military’s operations, with access provided through Microsoft’s Azure platform. Leaked documents published in January 2025 showed that the military began buying access to OpenAI’s GPT-4 in August 2023, with its use of the model increasing 20-fold following the start of the Gaza war.
In a statement to Al Jazeera, OpenAI said it “does not have any contracts with Israeli military or intelligence entities”.
“We do not control which entities Microsoft contracts with through Azure. At OpenAI, we have a rigorous process for assessing whether a proposed deployment of our technology to any national security entity aligns with our National Security Principles,” the company said in its statement.
Military intelligence to Big Tech
Analysts have also pointed to the connections between the US’s foremost tech giants and the Israeli military, specifically, members of the military’s cyberwarfare Unit 8200. In 2025, Drop Site News reported that a database of current and former members of Israeli military intelligence showed about 1,400 working at US tech firms, some 900 of them from Unit 8200, including roughly 250 at Microsoft, and others at Nvidia, Meta, Google, Intel and Apple.
The overlap in personnel raises questions about potential conflicts of interest. That is particularly relevant in the case of Microsoft, where serious concern was reported at a senior level that some employees in Israel had not been transparent about how Unit 8200 was using its technology.
The Guardian reported earlier this year that a Microsoft inquiry looked into how some Israel-based employees “had felt conflicting loyalties” to the company and the Israeli military.
Paul Biggar, one of the founders of Tech for Palestine, said that Israeli military personnel are embedded across US tech companies.
“Often, members of Unit 8200 are hired at senior levels and, as is often the case, they will hire people with similar technology and intelligence backgrounds to create a culture tied to their original unit,” Biggar said.
“You have to remember, these guys are spies,” he continued, “So the number one thing they want to do is bring in more people from Unit 8200 to increase their influence, including, for example, acquiring Israeli companies into US Big Tech”
Beyond the $1.2bn value of the Project Nimbus contract awarded to Google and Amazon, hard figures for the extent of the trade between Israel and US tech are hard to come by.
Irrespective of the sums of money, the heft of the Israeli military and US technology have combined to create one of the most surveilled populations on the planet.
“I’ve been lucky, but when people closer to me told me of having been pulled in [by the security services], they’ve been presented with a heat map of their entire lives,” Abukhater said, “Through a mixture of telephone tracking and constant surveillance, they’re shown where they’ve been and how long they spent there.
“We don’t even know half of it. When Microsoft’s role was exposed [in 2025], they revealed 200 million hours of audio recordings on a server in the Netherlands. That’s just one. Who else knows what they have and what these companies are processing?”
A Microsoft spokesperson told Al Jazeera: “Microsoft conducted an investigation into the alleged use of our technologies for the mass surveillance of civilians by the Israeli Ministry of Defence. In June, we published a final report summarising the investigation and outlining steps we are taking to strengthen our governance and oversight.
“This included establishing a process where any employee can anonymously report concerns about practices that may violate the company’s policies regarding the development and deployment of our technology through our Microsoft Integrity Portal,” the spokesperson added.
A spokesperson for Amazon Web Services told Al Jazeera: “We respect the privacy of our customers, and we do not discuss our relationship without their consent, or have visibility into their workloads. Customers regularly visit our offices for briefings and meetings with our teams, and any suggestion that these visits are anything other than routine customer engagement is wrong and unsubstantiated.”
A spokesperson for OpenAI told Al Jazeera: “OpenAI does not have any contracts with Israeli military or intelligence entities. We do not control which entities Microsoft contracts with through Azure. At OpenAI, we have a rigorous process for assessing whether a proposed deployment of our technology to any national security entity aligns with our National Security Principles.”
Palantir, Google, Nvidia, and the Israeli military did not respond to Al Jazeera’s requests for comment.

noticias.titulo: Sri Lanka mass grave revives quest for answers to forgotten Muslim massacre
noticias.resumen: As Sri Lanka's Tamil separatists fought a deadly war with the army, they also killed hundreds of Muslims.
noticias.texto:
Sri Lanka mass grave revives quest for answers to forgotten Muslim massacre
As Sri Lanka’s Tamil separatists fought a deadly war, they also killed hundreds of Muslims. Now, 36 years later, skeletal remains are offering clues to those massacres — and a path to closure.
Kattankudy, Sri Lanka — Fouzul Hinaya has lived for 36 years with the memories of two brothers who were killed in an often-forgotten chapter of Sri Lanka’s brutal civil war.
Now, the 60-year-old sees a flicker of hope. She no longer hopes for justice, but is praying that she might be able to at least bury her brothers with Muslim rituals. “I need to give [them] a dignified burial,” she said, speaking from her home in this eastern coastal city.
Tens of thousands of people, mostly civilians, were killed in the war between Tamil rebels fighting for an independent homeland and Sri Lankan forces, which began in 1983 and ended with the Tamil fighters being defeated in 2009. The Sri Lankan military has long faced accusations of war crimes committed against the country’s Tamil population.
The government and many in the nation’s Sinhala majority, meanwhile, have pointed to the bombings and assassinations carried out by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) in cities and villages across Sri Lanka. The LTTE killed then Sri Lankan President Ranasinghe Premadasa in 1993, and before that, Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi, who had previously sent Indian troops to help crush the Tamil rebels.
But the LTTE also carried out massacres of Sri Lankan Muslims in the early 1990s, starting with targeted killings in the eastern towns of Kurukkalmadam, Kattankudy and Eravur. In many cases, Muslims who were initially abducted never returned. Hundreds of bodies have never been recovered.
Then, last month, a court-appointed archaeological team found skeletal remains bearing cut marks in a Kurukkalmadam mass grave, according to Muazzam Mubarak, the lawyer who represents the victims’ families in the court.
“The priority now is to establish whose remains they are, determine what happened, and keep the families informed,” said Zacky Fouz, assistant professor in the department of political science at International Islamic University of Malaysia.
Among those waiting for a phone call is Hinaya.
The final journeys
Hinaya was one of six siblings. Fouzul Ameer and Abdur Rauff were younger brothers who helped their father, Hayath Mohamed, a logger whose income wasn’t steady, earn enough to support the family.
Ameer used to visit Akkaraipattu, a southeastern town 58km from their home town, to sell readymade garments. On a morning in July, 1990, Ameer packed his bags for that trip. “I never thought this would be his final visit”, Hinaya told Al Jazeera.
While he was returning to Kattankudy, the LTTE stopped him near Kurukkalmadam. Dozens, including Ameer, were gunned down — the death estimates vary from 60 to about 150 people.
For Sri Lanka’s Muslim population, the massacre was a turning point. Sinhalese make up 75 percent of the country’s population, while Tamils and Muslims constitute 15 and 10 percent respectively. Up until the Kurukkalmadam massacre, the LTTE had often abducted Muslims for ransom, using the money it received to fund its fighting. At its peak, the LTTE controlled almost a quarter of Sri Lanka.
Now, it was no longer Muslim money the Tamil rebels were after. They wanted blood.
In August 1990, a month later, the LTTE killed at least 300 Muslims in two mosques in the eastern towns of Kattankudy and Eravur. At the time when Ameer was killed, Abdur Rauff, another of Hinaya’s brothers, was working in a shop in the north of the country.
He returned home to join his grieving family. Days later, he set out from home with a push cart to buy provisions from the nearby town of Batticaloa.
But he was abducted by the LTTE and was never found again. He is presumed dead.
In 2016, Sri Lanka set up an Office on Missing Persons, an independent department to research the fate of missing and disappeared people. Hinaya lodged a complaint with the office, like hundreds of others from all the ethnic groups whose loved ones had been missing since the start of the civil war.
She wondered: could the mass graves that were being searched yield clues? And what’s next?
“Where the evidence supports criminal charges, the authorities should pursue them”, Fouz of the International Islamic University told Al Jazeera.
But with the mass killings, the LTTE took more than lives — it also ruptured a carefully preserved bond between Sri Lankan Tamils and Muslims.
A mass expulsion
In 1987, after Sri Lanka entered into an agreement with India, a contingent of India’s military was deployed to the country. They were officially there as peacekeepers to help implement a peace deal between Colombo and the LTTE. But they were soon the target of mistrust from both sides.
During their stint in Sri Lanka, residents of several Tamil and Muslim villages in Mullaitivu, part of the Northern Province, were forced to vacate their homes so Indian troops could set up camps there.
“This was our first displacement,” recalled Mohamed Rizni, now 59, who was ejected from his home with his family. But by early 1990, the Indian military departed from Sri Lanka. Rizni and others returned to their villages. “Tamils and Muslims were in harmony. We were like one family and we returned to our villages,” he told Al Jazeera.
That changed in October 1990. “The LTTE gathered all the Muslims in their villages in the Northern Province and informed them to leave the province within two days,” Rizni said.
Rizni was shocked. “We never posed a challenge to Tamils. We just made 5 percent of the Northern Province, while Tamils made more than 90 percent,” he said.
In October 1990, the LTTE forcibly expelled the entire Muslim population of the Northern Province, estimated between 75,000 and 100,000. They were not allowed to take anything with them except clothes. They moved to other parts of the country as refugees. Decades later, Rizni still remembers what the family lost to the LTTE: The rebels took 99 buffaloes, 42 cows, a four-acre coconut estate, an eight-acre paddy field, a house and a grocery shop.
Pursuing justice
Fouz said the LTTE’s attacks on Muslims showed the exclusionary character of its vision of a Tamil homeland.
“The movement claimed the north and east as a Tamil homeland, yet these provinces were also home to long-established Muslim communities with their own political aspirations and claims to land and belonging,” Fouz told Al Jazeera.
He pointed to the contradiction in the LTTE’s claim to be fighting against Sinhala majoritarianism by reproducing “that same logic of exclusion in its treatment of Muslims”.
In 2009, Sri Lanka crushed the LTTE, bringing the three-decade-old civil war to an end. According to United Nations estimates, nearly 40,000 civilians were killed in the final stage of the war in the Northern Province.
After the war, many Muslim refugees resettled in their villages in the north.
Yet Fouz, the academic, and Rizni, the survivor of two rounds of displacement, said that Sri Lanka had not yet carried out any comprehensive resettlement.
Riyas Farook, a parliamentarian from the ruling National People’s Power alliance, described the killing and the forced expulsion of Muslims in 1990 as serious crimes against humanity.
“No political struggle or ethnic demand can justify killing innocent people or forcing families to leave their homes,” Farook told Al Jazeera.
Farook said he expected authorities would conduct a proper and independent investigation, identify the victims and establish the facts unearthed from the Kurukkalmadam mass grave.
“We fully understand the difficulties faced by northern Muslim families who were forced to leave their homes,” he told Al Jazeera. “Our responsibility is not only to help them return, but also to ensure that they can rebuild their lives with dignity.”
Ultimately, Rizni said, he hoped that the traditional harmony that once marked Muslim-Tamil ties could be revived. “Tamils and Muslims will always have a good relationship. Muslims will not forget the expulsion.”
But for what the LTTE did to Muslims, “we will not blame the Tamils,” he told Al Jazeera.
The Kurukkalmadam mass grave excavation offers one pathway to that closure, Fouz suggested. “How the authorities follow through at Kurukkalmadam,” he said, “will determine whether Sri Lankan Muslims can finally get what they’ve long waited for: answers.”

noticias.titulo: ICC judge Kimberly Prost tries war crimes. She’s a target of US sanctions
noticias.resumen: Apps not working. Bank transfers not going through. And a court fighting for international law must skirt US firms.
noticias.texto:
ICC judge Kimberly Prost tries war crimes. She’s a target of US sanctions
Apps not working. Bank transfers not going through. And a court fighting for international law must skirt US firms.
Kimberly Prost was walking down a London street when she realised she needed help with directions. So, she did what millions of people around the world do and tried to open Google Maps on her phone.
But the app would not load. The map was unavailable.
Connectivity was not the problem. Prost was experiencing the effects of United States sanctions imposed on her and fellow judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC).
In February 2025, soon after returning to power, US President Donald Trump issued an executive order authorising his administration to institute financial penalties, asset freezes and visa restrictions on those helping the ICC with its investigations.
Over the course of the rest of the year and through 2026, the Trump administration has issued sanctions aimed at ICC judges, including Prost, and individuals such as the United Nations Special Rapporteur for the Occupied Palestinian Territories, Francesca Albanese. The sanctions also target the institution of the ICC.
The sanctions are widely seen as an attempt to weaken the ICC in response to the court’s attempts to hold US soldiers to account for alleged war crimes, and to seek the prosecution of the leaders of Israel – a close US ally – for crimes committed in Gaza during its genocidal war. Last week, Trump stepped up his campaign against the ICC, using an unprecedented trilateral meeting with the presidents of China and Russia to seek their collective clout in punishing the international court. He has described the ICC as a “rogue globalist organisation”.
But the sanctions against the court and its judges are threatening the very functioning of the institution, directly impacting the lives of judges like Prost, as well as the ICC’s ability to serve as one of the UN’s pre-eminent judicial pillars of international law.
“There’s constant pressure on your daily life,” Prost said, in an interview with Al Jazeera.
From the Rome Statute to battling the US
Prost, a Canadian jurist, was in the room when the Rome Statute, which established the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2002, was being drafted. She has since worked as one of the judges on the court that has tried dozens of individuals for war crimes, genocide, and crimes against humanity.
However, the ICC’s recent investigations into the US and Israel’s alleged war crimes have sparked accusations from those two countries that the court has breached its brief: Neither the US nor Israel is a signatory to the Rome Statute, and they argue that the court therefore has no jurisdiction over them.
“The ICC is politicised and falsely claims unfettered discretion to investigate, charge, and prosecute nationals of the United States and our allies. This dangerous assertion and abuse of power infringes upon the sovereignty and national security of the United States and our allies, including Israel,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement last year.
However, the US has been quiet about the fact that ICC investigations it has objected to pertain to alleged crimes committed in states that are party to the Rome Statute, including Palestine and Afghanistan.
Prost said that questions of jurisdiction were very much part of the negotiations that led to the framing of the Rome Statute. In all, 125 states are parties to the treaty, and so are expected to abide by the ICC’s rulings.
The statute, which set the rules on how the court functions, represents “the will of those who participated in negotiations” that led to the formation of the ICC, she added.
But while a majority of UN member states are parties to the Rome Statute, many of the world’s most powerful nations — including the US, China, Russia, India and Israel — are not.
Until recently, these countries would object to the ICC’s functioning, refuse to cooperate, reject its findings, and claim immunity from its actions.
However, in Trump’s second term, the US has publicly expanded its fight against the ICC. Washington is no longer ignoring or even just punishing the ICC.
In July, Rubio stated the Trump administration’s new goal: “We will dismantle the ICC—brick by brick, if necessary,” he said.
Navigating life and courtrooms under sanctions
While US sanctions against the ICC and its judges have been widely criticised by many governments and human rights organisations, they have fundamentally changed the way the institution needs to function to stay afloat — and how its judges now must navigate everyday life.
“Every time I go to transfer some funds, I have to consider, will it work? Or how do I do it without a credit card?” Prost explained. In the UK, for instance, she has had funds frozen during transactions, in what she describes as over-compliance by Western companies and organisations.
“I tried to transfer money to a young couple as a wedding gift … Money sent from here in The Netherlands in euros to the United Kingdom in pounds had been blocked on the basis of the order of the President of the United States,” she said. “I have said this to the UK authorities: ‘I don’t understand. The sovereign state of the United Kingdom can do nothing about it?’”
Operating an international courtroom, while under sanctions, is a whole other challenge.
The US has allowed the court a six-month grace period before some sanctions are implemented, after which it faces the prospect of its assets being frozen, travel bans on its members, properties belonging to the ICC being blocked, and telecommunications and enterprise software suspended, among other issues. The court has already begun transitioning away from US-based banking and technology systems.
“But the problem is there are certain limitations,” Prost admitted, pointing to over-compliance by governments as well as private companies that do not wish to risk the ire of the US in its campaign against the ICC.
Governments that claim to support the ICC, she said, could activate their own sanctions-blocking mechanisms, in effect demanding that companies and institutions in their countries do not comply with the US measures.
“Because if you are implementing these sanctions when you are not obligated by law, you are complicit in threatening judges and the International Criminal Court,” Prost said.
Afghanistan war crimes trial
The specific sanctions against Prost came after her ruling to authorise the ICC’s investigation into US personnel in Afghanistan. In 2020, the court had initially authorised its prosecutor to start a probe into alleged crimes in Afghanistan, encompassing all armed conflict within the country.
After a brief pause, following a request from the previous Afghan government, the investigation was resumed in 2022, focusing on alleged crimes by the Taliban and the local branch of ISIL (ISIS), while allegations against the US military and Afghan soldiers were deprioritised. The investigations led to arrest warrants against four Taliban leaders. But little progress was made concerning the other allegations.
However, Prost, who was part of the 2020 decision to investigate the conduct of US military personnel in Afghanistan, was eventually sanctioned by the US State Department, in August 2025. Prost remains unapologetic. “I was sanctioned on the basis of my participation in an appeals chamber decision which I would make again today on the basis of the evidence,” she said.
Earlier this month, in a blow to the Afghanistan investigation, an ICC bench issued a decision to halt investigations into war crimes allegations against the US military, citing a lack of confidence in the prosecution’s ability to pursue the case.
While the prosecutor’s office has appealed the decision, the move has raised concerns among human rights groups and Afghan survivors about whether the move was in response to political pressure on the ICC. Prost also has questions about the ruling. “I sit basically in the same shoes as everyone does,” she said, without elaborating.
‘The court must carry on’
The court, and its judges, are no strangers to threats, Prost said. But the rather unusual adversary in this case has prompted an equally unusual reaction.
“Sitting judges are speaking out,” she said. “We don’t normally do that. But this is such a blatant attack … that’s very apparent from the statements that have been made by the Secretary of State … they want to tear down the institution.”
“This is being done in order to try and get us not to do our jobs, not to issue decisions, or to do so in the way the United States administration would like.”
Despite the mounting pressures, Prost says the court remains steadfast in its commitment to the victims who have approached the ICC.
“The most important thing we can do right now in the face of these intimidation tactics, we must continue to do our work. We must continue to hear cases. The court must carry on,” she said. “It’s too important. The victims are too important.”

noticias.titulo: South Korea’s central bank hikes interest rates amid AI chip boom
noticias.resumen: Bank of Korea raises key rate by 0.25 percent amid booming exports of semiconductors.
noticias.texto:
South Korea’s central bank hikes interest rates amid AI chip boom
Bank of Korea raises key rate by 0.25 percent amid booming exports of semiconductors.
South Korea’s central bank has hiked interest rates as red-hot chip demand drives one of the Asian economy’s fastest expansions in more than a decade.
The Bank of Korea (BOK) on Thursday raised its key rate by 0.25 percent to 3.25 percent, citing strong domestic growth and above-target inflation.
Despite tensions in the Middle East, the global economy is expected to maintain a favourable growth trend due to “robust AI investment”, the BOK said in a statement.
Meanwhile, inflation is projected to “stay elevated for some time” amid the fallout of higher energy prices, the BOK said.
“Looking ahead, the global economy and financial markets will be affected by the AI investment outlook, by changes in monetary and fiscal policies in major economies, and by developments in the Middle East,” the central bank said.
South Korea’s inflation rate stood at 2.8 percent in October, above the BOK’s 2 percent target.
Citing expectations of sustained growth in exports and investment, the BOK raised its gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 to 3.9 percent and 4.1 percent, respectively.
The BOK in August forecast that growth would reach 3.3 percent this year and 2.9 percent in 2027.
South Korea, which is home to top memory chip makers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, has been a major beneficiary of the multi-trillion-dollar AI investment boom.
South Korea’s exports rose 94 percent year-on-year in October to reach $115.3bn, following an all-time monthly record of $120.9bn in September.
Semiconductors accounted for nearly half of total exports, led by SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, which together control about 80 percent of the global market for high-bandwidth memory and 60 percent of the market for dynamic random-access memory, according to Counterpoint Research.
GDP increased 3.4 percent year-on-year in the July-September quarter, far outpacing forecasts.
Excluding the outlier years of the COVID-19 pandemic, Asia’s fourth-largest economy is on track for its strongest performance since 2010, when GDP expanded 6.2 percent.
After a tech-led sell-off the previous day, South Korea’s stock market rose on Thursday alongside a rebound in equities across the region.
Seoul’s Kospi closed up 0.3 percent, while the Nikkei 225 in Tokyo and the Taiex in Taipei finished 0.9 percent and 2.5 percent higher, respectively.

noticias.titulo: Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court cancels major power contract
noticias.resumen: The court's five-to-four ruling ends Luma Energy's operations after a contentious legal battle.
noticias.texto:
Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court cancels major power contract
The court’s five-to-four ruling ends Luma Energy’s operations after a contentious legal battle.
In a tight vote, Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has ruled in favour of ending the government’s contract with Luma Energy following a controversial legal battle with the private power company.
The five-to-four ruling made public on Wednesday envisions a one-year transition period.
Power outages have continued to dog the Caribbean island since Hurricane Maria inflicted vast damage to power infrastructure in 2017, leading to years of bitter recriminations over financial and policy autonomy in the US territory.
The San Juan government sued Luma nearly a year ago, following up on a campaign promise made by Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez to cancel the contract.
Luma has faced protests for years from Puerto Ricans, who raised concerns about the cost and quality of its services.
Gonzalez said her administration would seek a new company within the year awarded by the court. She assured that transmission and distribution operations would not revert to Puerto Rico’s Electric Power Authority, from which Luma had initially taken over in 2021.
She blamed Luma for “constant interruptions” and “unnecessary outages”, asserting they have enough funds to provide proper service, as she accused the company of driving the cost of electricity in the territory to record highs.
Meanwhile, a federal control board that oversees the island’s finances issued a statement saying its immediate concern is the continuity of power services.
“The Puerto Rican government’s decision to terminate the contract creates enormous uncertainty at a time when the people and businesses of Puerto Rico look for stability,” the board said, noting that there is no “clear plan or successor company in place”.
But Gonzalez rejected those concerns, bluntly saying, “There will be no chaos.”
Tensions in court
With the narrow ruling came allegations that judges had been pressured to vote in favour of cancellation.
Judge Angel Colon Pérez, who voted against the cancellation, asserted that the final ruling stemmed from “an excessive eagerness to satisfy a capricious request from the leader currently in power”, in an apparent reference to the governor.
However, Judge Roberto Feliberti Cintron, who was part of the majority vote, sharply denied the allegations.
“We do not bow to external pressures, we do not yield to intimidation, nor do we allow smear campaigns to influence the exercise of our judicial function,” Cintron wrote. “Our obligation is to the Law, Justice, the People, and our conscience.”
Luma also commented on the allegations.
“In light of the serious allegations that have been raised publicly regarding attempts to influence the Court, we reiterate our call for an immediate, rigorous, and transparent investigation,” it said.
The company said in a statement on Wednesday that it disagrees with the court’s decision but will respect the judicial process and is “carefully evaluating all available legal alternatives”.

noticias.titulo: Six killed, including children, in plane crash off Mississippi coast
noticias.resumen: US authorities are investigating the reason behind the crash that killed members of the Stokes and Knox families.
noticias.texto:
Six killed, including children, in plane crash off Mississippi coast
US authorities are investigating the reason behind the crash that killed members of the Stokes and Knox families.
First responders have found the bodies of six members of two families, including three children, killed in a small plane crash off the coast of Mississippi, United States.
Authorities are investigating the cause of the crash on Tuesday. Relatives said they were on their way home from a fishing trip.
The passengers were members of two families returning home to Fort Myers, Florida, from New Orleans Lakefront airport, Louisiana.
The plane’s pilot, Brent Stokes, 50, was president of a marine contracting company based in Fort Myers, according to Jackson County Coroner Bruce Lynd Jr. Stokes’s company’s website described him as an “avid fisherman and life time boater”.
The other victims were Stokes’s 16-year-old son, Hunter; Stokes’s sister, Arlyn Knox, 43; her husband, Michael Knox, 43; and their two sons, 12-year-old Charles Holden Knox and 10-year-old Truett Knox.
Lynd said autopsies are being performed on Brent Stokes and Michael Knox, who was also a licensed pilot.
Responders searched for hours and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane’s cabin floating on the water, according to coastguard spokesperson Juan Ros.
Divers found their bodies in the fuselage part of the plane after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands National Seashore.
The Knox and Stokes families confirmed their deaths in an emailed statement provided to The Associated Press news agency.
“They died doing what they loved: celebrating the start of a wonderful holiday season with a fishing trip together, before heading home to be with the rest of our family,” the statement said.
Weather’s potential impact
The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile, Alabama, reported at about 3:45pm (21:45 GMT) on Tuesday that it had lost contact with the aircraft, according to the coastguard.
Shortly before losing contact with the plane, an air traffic controller at Gulfport–Biloxi International airport advised the pilot of precipitation and adverse weather in the area.
The plane had been flying at about 9,000 feet (2,743 metres), above the bottom of the cloud layers when it began descending rapidly in a right-hand turn, according to FlightAware tracking data analysed by Steven Arroyo, a retired airline captain with 50 years of flying experience.
“It’s highly, highly irregular,” Arroyo told AP. “I think it’s safe to say this aircraft had some serious problems.”
Todd Curtis, an aviation expert and former Boeing safety engineer, said that nothing appeared out of the ordinary based on the publicly available audio recordings.
But he noted that precipitation in below-freezing temperatures can cause dangerous icing, potentially leading to inaccurate instrument readings or loss of lift. It is unclear whether the plane had a de-icing system.

noticias.titulo: Brazil blasts ‘unacceptable’ new US tariff proposals
noticias.resumen: President Lula’s office says Brazil will not yield to threats and aims for a negotiated resolution.
noticias.texto:
Brazil blasts ‘unacceptable’ new US tariff proposals
President Lula’s office says Brazil will not yield to threats and aims for a negotiated resolution.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has voiced outrage over new tariffs proposed by US President Donald Trump’s administration on Brazilian aircraft and sugar.
Brazil was not ruling out “reciprocal measures”, Lula’s office said in a statement on Wednesday after the US proposed a 10 percent tariff on finished aircraft made by Brazilian planemaker Embraer.
“The unilateral decision by the USTR [Office of the United States Trade Representative] is an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the statement continued.
Washington also plans to raise duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas to rectify what it calls “unreasonable” trade practices.
The new tariff rate would ensure that sugar from Brazil could not be shipped through third countries into the United States, the USTR’s office said.
The move is part of a broader wave of proposed tariffs targeting 14 major trading partners, including China and the European Union.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said his office was proposing changes to tariffs imposed in July after Brazil made “no meaningful progress” on the issues.
Greer said Washington remains open to talks.
Brasilia said it had been negotiating “in good faith” with Washington for more than a year and that the two sides had agreed to establish a working group on trade issues in August.
The president’s office said Brazil would continue to seek “a negotiated solution” without indicating whether the country would exercise its right to challenge the proposed tariffs before the World Trade Organization.
The tariffs, which could take effect as early as January, could raise the price US carriers pay for Embraer jets at a time when they are already grappling with a surge in jet fuel prices due to the US war on Iran.
