noticias.titulo: Watch: Alaskan flying team airdrops Thanksgiving turkeys to remote communities
noticias.resumen: For the last few years, the "turkey bombers" have taken to the skies for the benefit of residents in off-grid communities.
noticias.texto:
Alaskan flying team airdrops Thanksgiving turkeys to remote communities
For the last few years, "turkey bombers" Esther Keim and Heidi Hastings have taken to the skies to airdrop Thanksgiving turkeys to residents in off-grid communities in south-central Alaska.
Hastings pilots the plane while her best friend Keim drops the turkeys out the plane window, delivering to families who may not otherwise get one of the birds, since they are cut off by snow and ice.

noticias.titulo: Deadly fire erupts near Cairo killing dozens of people
noticias.resumen: At least 31 people have died in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo, after a fuel tanker overturned, says Egypt's health ministry.
noticias.texto:
Deadly fire erupts near Cairo killing dozens of people
Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured after a large fire broke out on a busy highway in Cairo.
Footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.
The fire occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, north of the old city centre. Egypt's health ministry said the injured were being treated at hospitals nearby.
Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported that a high-voltage cable fell in front of a fuel tanker, causing the driver to lose control and the tanker to overturn, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.

noticias.titulo: Andalusia offers a glimpse of Spain’s future as the far right gains ground
noticias.resumen: Ahead of Sunday's election, Andalusia signals Vox’s rise as immigration and right-wing alliances reshape politics.
noticias.texto:
Andalusia offers a glimpse of Spain’s future as the far right gains ground
Ahead of Sunday’s election, Andalusia signals Vox’s rise as immigration and right-wing alliances reshape Spain’s politics.
Andalusia, Spain – Surrounded by shelves heaving with canned goods and cured meats, the owners of a family-run grocery store are locked in a debate about Spain’s upcoming elections.
All politicians are “liars”, proclaims 32-year-old Antonio Cerezo, announcing he will cast a blank ballot. His cousin, Patricia Nicolas Cerezo, 43, is less certain, riddled with doubt about who to support.
As for her 18-year-old son, first-time voter Alfonso Duque, the only choice is the far-right Vox party: “It can’t get worse than this”.
The one thing that the family in the small village of Rioja seems to agree on is that Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s socialists must go.
A former socialist bastion, the southern region’s political landscape has changed. Since May’s regional election, it has been governed by a coalition of the conservative People’s Party (PP) and Vox, once a fringe party that has drawn support by championing migrant deportations and tapping into a wider wave of far-right, anti-establishment support across Europe.
Ahead of Sunday’s snap vote, observers say Andalusia’s political dynamics could offer a glimpse of what might come next nationally.
That arrangement could soon be tested at the national level.
Opinion polls put the PP first, followed by Sanchez’s Socialists (PSOE), with Vox third.
The PP is projected to fall short of an outright majority, but together the two right-wing parties are expected to have enough seats to govern.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo has indicated that he would prefer to lead a minority government with Vox’s backing in parliament, while leaving open the possibility of a coalition like the one in Andalusia.
Tucked away between rows of greenhouses and arid mountains in the southern region of Andalusia, Rioja is home to about 1,600 people.
Overlooking the plains framing the quaint village is a giant silhouette of a bull. For much of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship, this area remained poor and largely agricultural.
As machines took over more of the work in the fields, many Andalusians left for jobs in industrial centres such as Barcelona and Madrid. In the mid-seventies, the Socialists found fertile ground in a society that had long felt marginalised and neglected.
In 1982, the PSOE won an absolute majority in Andalusia’s first regional election, beginning a stretch in power that lasted more than three decades.
‘The PP opened the door to the far-right’
But by 2018, the Socialists’ hold on the southern region was starting to crack.
A series of corruption scandals tarnished the party’s image, benefitting the PP. The PSOE still came first in that year’s regional election, but the conservatives took power with the backing of the liberal Ciudadanos and Vox.
It was a turning point.
“For the first time, the PP opened the door to the far-right to be able to govern – that created a precedent for everything that happens today nationwide,” said Bosco Govantes, political science associate professor at Sevilla’s Universidad Pablo de Olavide. “Before, there was a red line, a stigma, over collaborating with the far right. But that move in Andalusia kicked off the normalisation of Vox’s narrative.”
The party was founded in 2013 when a group of ultraconservatives, led by Santiago Abascal, broke up with the conservatives they accused of being too indulgent towards Catalan separatists.
Vox at first struggled to get into the political mainstream, but entered Andalusia’s regional parliament in 2018.
Once the Catalan issue faded from the national debate, the party shifted its focus to migration.
Abascal accuses Sanchez of enabling what he calls “a migrant invasion” to “replace the Spanish people” as the Socialist government adopted an open-door policy and legalised undocumented migrants who had worked in Spain for years.
Since the start of Sanchez’s rule to last year, the number of foreign-born residents in Spain rose from 6.3 million to 10.4 million, official figures show. He takes pride in the policy, as Spain’s GDP grew under his tenure.
Vox, the likely kingmaker that is expected to increase its vote share more than any other party compared with the 2023 elections, wants to reverse those policies.
Some observers say the conservative party has had to harden its discourse, such as calling for stricter measures against migrants, to stop haemorrhaging voters to its right.
Polling by Ipsos suggested up to 20 percent of Spaniards who voted for the PP in the 2023 elections intended to vote for Vox on Sunday.
Sanchez has pitched the election as a battle between progress and regression, warning that PP and Vox “only agree when it comes to cutting back rights”.
But that argument falls flat in parts of Andalusia, where some do not fear a Vox-PP deal.
“I don’t mind if Vox is in government,” said Rosaria, a 69-year-old retired housewife, while adjusting her white scarf with a red floral pattern. “The PP will keep them in check. It’s a party with vision and structure”.
Sanchez warns that Vox wants to roll back women’s rights.
The issue of gender violence divides the two parties.
Last year, the PP backed the renewal of Spain’s cross-party pact on gender-based violence.
Vox wants to repeal the 2004 gender-based violence law, which protects women from abuse by current or former partners. The party argues that the law discriminates against men and wants to replace it with legislation covering domestic violence regardless of the victim’s sex.
At an event against gender-based violence, Rioja’s PP mayor Olga Maria Gonzalez Jurado was asked how the two parties were getting on in government in Andalusia.
“I think it’s going well,” she said, but she deflected questions on whether the PP had hardened its stance on immigration to keep up with Vox.
In Andalusia, the two parties have been pushing for stricter housing rules for non-Spanish applicants.
Councils can already give people who live or work locally priority for subsidised housing, regardless of nationality. Last month, the two parties backed a non-binding motion urging Madrid to give Spanish citizens priority for subsidised housing and housing aid. Their regional coalition deal also pledges to give people with longstanding ties to Andalusia or Spain priority for public benefits and social housing.
In other regions, the two parties’ cooperation has reached classrooms and places of worship. Aragon dropped a school programme teaching Arabic and Moroccan culture this year and Andalusia is due to follow in 2027.
In the Murcia town of Jumilla, Muslims held Eid al-Fitr prayers in a car park after PP and Vox backed restrictions on the use of municipal sports facilities. The restrictions have drawn criticism over their impact on Muslim religious gatherings.
In Valencia, the parties backed a rule requiring meat served in school canteens to come from animals stunned before slaughter, which still allows halal meals that meet the requirement. In the Balearic Islands, they voted to send Spain’s Congress a bill to ban the burqa [full-face veils sometimes worn by Muslim women that hide the entire face, including eyes] and niqab [similar, but the eyes are visible] in public spaces.
Vox has called for the deportation of foreigners it says, among other grounds, also live on public benefits. This measure – to remove someone with a valid right to stay – has no equivalent in Europe.
The party’s policies have left migrants on edge.
Yudy Ramirez is from Colombia and entered Spain four years ago. For years, took care of her child while juggling two jobs as an in-house caregiver and fruit picker at a greenhouse in Almeria for five euros per hour.
In June, the 49-year-old finally received legal papers.
“Many of us are scared, because returning is not in the plans at the moment,” she said.
Still, not all migrants are targeted in the same way.
Vox’s rhetoric has an ethno-racial undertone which looks at Spanish-speaking foreigners coming from Latin America in more favourable terms as they belong to an Iberosphere which connects far-right movements in the Latin world whose centre is occupied by Vox.
Andalusia heavily relies on foreign workers for its greenhouses.
According to Govantes, the issue is not with migrants working in Spain but with them being recognised for their rights. The PSOE’s regularisation, he said, forced owners to make legal contracts, pay social security and provide benefits.
“Migrants’ work has always been tolerated as long as it was invisible and illegal. As they became visible and legal, they were accused of robbing Spanish people of jobs,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Why is Italy angry with Ukraine for striking Russian ships off Libya?
noticias.resumen: Analysts say Rome fears instability in Libya could hurt its energy interests and efforts to curb irregular migration.
noticias.texto:
Why is Italy angry with Ukraine for striking Russian ships off Libya?
Analysts say Rome fears instability in Libya could hurt its energy interests and efforts to curb irregular migration.
Italy has denounced Ukraine for carrying out attacks against Russian vessels in Libyan waters, saying it was wrong to “violate Libya’s sovereignty”.
Rome’s rebuke marks a crack in its relationship with Ukraine, which Italy has largely supported since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, including with military assistance.
It coincides with growing concern about the involvement of foreign powers in a divided Libya, as well as the risk of other nations being drawn into the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
So why has Italy weighed in now, and what makes Libya so strategically important to Rome?
Why did Ukraine carry out an attack in Libyan waters?
Kyiv claimed it sank a Russian warship and struck a cargo vessel transporting military equipment off Libya’s coast on Sunday night. The attack on the warship at Benghazi port in eastern Libya killed two naval officers of the self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), according to Libya’s eastern-based forces.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the vessels as legitimate targets, arguing Kyiv had the legal right to defend itself against “Russian aggression”.
He stressed that Ukraine’s actions were “not intended to harm Libya or its people” and that Kyiv respects Libya’s territorial integrity.
“Ukraine is not ‘dragging’ anyone into the war or ‘transferring’ the war anywhere,” Sybiha said in a statement on Telegram.
How did Libya react?
Musa Al-Koni, the vice president of Libya’s Tripoli-based Presidential Council, called the attack “a declaration of war against the Libyan state”.
Libyan authorities “hold the Ukrainian side fully responsible for these terrorist acts”, he added.
The LNA, a rival power that controls eastern and southern parts of Libya and maintains close relations with Russia, promised to retaliate against the Ukrainian attack “at the appropriate time and place, and by the appropriate means”.
Libya is divided between the UN-recognised government in Tripoli and a parallel administration based in Benghazi, backed by the LNA and its renegade commander, Khalifa Haftar.
How did Italy react?
Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said it was a mistake for Ukraine to “violate Libya’s sovereignty” and that Rome, which has a small military presence in Libya, had received no prior notice of the operation.
“Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv’s intentions to strike in Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port,” Tajani told Italy’s Corriere della Sera newspaper.
Italy’s far-right League party, which is a member of the coalition government, also criticised the attack, saying it risked sowing instability inside Libya.
The comments expose a rare rift with Ukraine, which Italy has largely supported in the war against Russia. Italy has provided Ukraine with more than 3 billion euros ($3.29bn) worth of military aid, according to data from the Kiel Institute think tank, while also backing sweeping sanctions against Russia.
However, there has been division within Italy’s government over further aid to Ukraine, with Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, who heads the League party, opposing more weapons shipments or funding.
Matteo Villa, a senior research fellow at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI), told Al Jazeera that Ukraine’s recent attack off Libya is likely to deepen these domestic tensions.
It “gives Salvini an opportunity to strengthen his case, questioning whether Western military assistance risks enabling Ukraine to pursue objectives that run counter to Italy’s own national interests”, said Villa.
What relationship does Italy have with Libya?
Italy, whose southern islands lie 300km (186 miles) across the Mediterranean from the Libyan coast, has spent years building ties with rival factions in western and eastern Libya.
“Over the past few years, Rome has shifted from almost complete support for the UN-backed Western government in Libya towards building working relationships with the Haftar-controlled East as well,” said Villa.
Italy has also for years helped provide funding, equipment and training for Libya’s maritime authorities, despite reports of migrants being abused and tortured in Libyan custody.
The aim has been to curb irregular migration from Libya to Italy, one of the most perilous and contested Europe-bound routes.
Alessia Melcangi, a nonresident senior fellow with the North Africa Program at the Atlantic Council’s Rafik Hariri Center and Middle East Programs, said Italy’s condemnation of Ukraine partly serves as a form of “damage control” to help Rome balance its competing geopolitical interests.
“Rome needs to demonstrate that its relationships with Kyiv, Tripoli and Benghazi give it meaningful influence over developments affecting its security,” Melcangi told Al Jazeera. “Otherwise, perceptions of exclusion or ambiguity could cause lasting diplomatic damage.”
Why is Italy concerned about conflict spilling into Libya?
Villa said Rome’s concerns are fuelled by its geographical proximity to Libya, as well as its economic and strategic interests there, specifically in terms of energy and “migration control”.
“Last year, Libya accounted for roughly a quarter of Italy’s crude oil imports, making it its largest supplier, and the country is by far the main departure point for migrants reaching Italy by sea,” said Villa.
Aldo Liga, a research fellow at the Middle East and North Africa Centre at ISPI, told Al Jazeera that potential escalation that further destabilises Libya would “threaten the security of trade routes and energy flows”, creating a volatile security situation in the Strait of Sicily.
“Instability in Libya is perceived as a direct threat to Italy’s national interests,” he said.
In his interview with Corriere della Sera, Foreign Minister Tajani cited the presence of the Italian military and Italian petroleum company Eni in Libya as being among his concerns about the Ukrainian intervention.
“What happened is worrying,” Tajani said, referring to the Ukrainian attack. “The war between Russia and Ukraine must be prevented from widening, avoiding new outbreaks from occurring.”

noticias.titulo: UN ruling disputes Israeli allegations used to dismiss UNRWA Gaza staff
noticias.resumen: Tribunal raises questions about the credibility of UNRWA's decision to dismiss its staff without substantiated evidence.
noticias.texto:
UN ruling disputes Israeli allegations used to dismiss UNRWA Gaza staff
Tribunal raises questions about the credibility of UNRWA’s decision to dismiss its staff without substantiated evidence.
A United Nations tribunal has cast doubt on evidence used by UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, to dismiss staff in 2024, finding that the decision was based almost entirely on unsubstantiated allegations by the Israeli government.
UNRWA dismissed nine Palestinian employees in January 2024 after allegations by Israel that they had participated in the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.
The UNRWA Dispute Tribunal, an impartial tribunal within the UN, noted that the UN’s internal investigation did not include testimonies from the 19 staff members whom Israel accused of involvement in the attacks, according to the judgement seen by Al Jazeera on Thursday.
The judgement said “safety and security concerns” meant that the UN Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS) “was not able to interview the 19 staff members and afford them usual due process to respond to the allegations”.
The tribunal also said the allegations against the workers were “based almost entirely on information in Israel’s possession”.
“That information has remained in the custody of Israeli authorities and they alone have remained privy as to exactly how it was collected, by whom, when, and where,” it said.
The tribunal also expressed doubts over telephone conversations and messages that Israel claimed to have intercepted and presented as evidence of the staff members’ involvement in the attacks, including with someone “identified by Israeli officials as a Hamas operative”.
“OIOS did not confirm in the investigation report that it was satisfied that the caller was a Hamas operative or that the ‘user’ of the receiving phone was the Applicant,” the judgement said.
It added that one of the Israeli claims of an alleged intercepted phone call between a Hamas operative and a UNRWA staff member was with a duplicated SIM card, which is common in Gaza. “It was determined that the comments made in intercepted calls related to that SIM card were not made by the UNRWA staff member as initially alleged,” the judgement said.
The tribunal’s ruling, dated November 11, found that UNRWA had failed to produce evidence supporting its decision to dismiss one of the nine employees, identified as Abu Awad.
The tribunal described Israeli evidence as unsupported and of “limited evidentiary value and reliability” and awarded Awad a year’s pay and $5,000 in compensation for “moral damages”.
The ruling raises questions about the credibility of the decision by UNRWA, the main humanitarian organisation operating in Gaza, to dismiss its Palestinian staff on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the attacks committed by Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups.
In January 2024 after consulting UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, former UNRWA Commissioner General Philippe Lazzarini decided that the agency would terminate the contracts of nine staff members.
Their termination letters informed them that the allegations against them were “very serious and credible”.
The dismissal decisions were confirmed after a UN investigation that concluded they were likely to have been involved in the October 7 attacks.
Reports have suggested that Lazzarini and Guterres likely made this decision in the hopes that appeasing Israel and its allies would allow humanitarian work in Gaza to continue.
But UNRWA still experienced critical funding cuts from donors. About 600 of its staff members were laid off, salaries in Gaza were cut by 20 percent and aid access remained blocked by Israel amid a worsening humanitarian crisis in the enclave.

noticias.titulo: Can Trump continue with Iran war despite funding restrictions?
noticias.resumen: A Congress budget bill could serve as a pressure tactic on Trump to end the war but could also trigger a shutdown.
noticias.texto:
Can Trump continue with Iran war despite funding restrictions?
A Congress budget bill could serve as a pressure tactic on Trump to end the war but could also cause a government shutdown.
As US Democrats prepare to assume control of both houses of Congress in January following victory in the midterm elections, the issue of ending the war on Iran is back in sharp focus.
Until now, efforts by the Democrats to end the nine-month war that has led to soaring food and fuel prices have failed. Now, they fear that as Iran and the US remain deadlocked in the Strait of Hormuz, President Donald Trump could opt to restart strikes on Iran, triggering likely retaliatory attacks across the Gulf.
A new budget bill is in the works and could serve as a pressure tactic on Trump if it limits funding for the war. So what are Trump’s options now?
Here’s what we know:
Can Democrats use the funding bill to end the war on Iran?
With federal funding set to expire on December 11 , Republican and Democratic legislators are negotiating to reach a bipartisan agreement for the next round of funding. This must be agreed to avoid a government shutdown and ensure federal agencies, services and military operations during the Iran war can continue.
Last week, Congress representatives Yassamin Ansari and Ro Khanna called on Democratic colleagues to use the deadline to pressure the White House to end the war.
“Ahead of the December 11 government funding deadline, Congress faces the task of approving a funding package to maintain government operations,” their statement read.
“Congress must use its constitutional power of the purse to ensure that not another cent of taxpayer money goes towards prolonging this war. We will oppose any funding package that does not explicitly prohibit funds from being used for offensive operations in Iran. Passing such a measure would defy the demands of Americans who want this war to end – now.”
According to the most recent polling from Reuters/Ipsos, 71 percent of Americans say they want the new Congress to end the Iran war.
Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King’s College London, said the bill is “potentially the first serious institutional constraint on Trump’s freedom to wage war against Iran”.
“Until now, Washington’s military strategy has been largely insulated from congressional opposition. The Democrats are trying to change that by making continued offensive operations conditional on congressional authorisation,” Krieg told Al Jazeera.
What is the main obstacle?
Politicians are divided about whether bringing an end to the war now is worth the risk of a government shutdown. Last year, the US government shut down for 43 days from 1 October to 12 November, because Congress failed to pass funding for 2026.
“The American people don’t need another government shutdown,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters this week. “I think that would be a colossal mistake and a real disservice to the people of this country.”
Senator Peter Welch, a Vermont Democrat, told Reuters that the “big obstacle is that we don’t want to fund the war, we don’t want to shut down, how do you solve that?”
A new bipartisan funding package would require 60 votes in the 100-seat Senate, which until January has 53 Republicans and 45 Democrats. When the new class of senators is sworn in during January, this will flip to 44 Republicans and 54 Democrats.
Another issue is that it may not be that easy to end the war, regardless of the funding issue.
Krieg said: “Restricting offensive spending does not end the war. The American blockade remains in place, Iran continues challenging maritime navigation, and neither side has resolved the fundamental disputes over nuclear inspections, sanctions and Hormuz. The legislation is still a proposal, and its effectiveness will depend on the final wording and whether Trump signs it,” he added.
Could Trump veto a bill that cuts all military spending?
Yes.
While the Democrats won big in the midterms, Trump still retains executive authority enshrined in the Constitution, which states that the president can reject legislation passed by Congress.
A presidential veto can only be overturned by a two-thirds majority in both houses of Congress, something the Democrats do not have the numbers to muster without significant Republican support.
Trump’s presidential veto could be a double-edged sword when it comes to military funding. If he uses it to block a bill denying him funding for the war, paycheques for military personnel would also be blocked as a result of a government shutdown.
Another scenario is that the military retains funding for defensive purposes, which could ultimately continue the war and the ongoing naval blockade of Iran’s ports.
What happens if a Democrat bill isn’t vetoed? Would that end the war?
According to Krieg, even if a new finance bill were to block more funding for the Iran war, Trump could continue military operations with existing resources for “some time”.
“The Pentagon has considerable operational capacity in theatre and the absence of additional funding does not immediately prevent the president from ordering another round of strikes.”
He explained that there is, however, an important difference between having the military capability to escalate a conflict and “having the financial resources to sustain another prolonged campaign”.
“American expenditure is already approaching $50bn, while shortages of precision munitions and air-defence interceptors are becoming an increasingly serious concern. The decisive question is whether Congress simply refuses additional funding or explicitly prohibits offensive operations using money already appropriated,” he said.
Is there a precedent for Congress using funding to end wars?
Yes.
During the Vietnam War, Congress passed a resolution in 1964 that granted then-President Lyndon B Johnson the authority to send troops to Southeast Asia without declaring war. However, as the war dragged on and troop morale tanked, the war grew increasingly unpopular.
In 1973, Congress repealed the resolution and ordered forces to withdraw.
Less successfully, in 2007, the Democrats tried repeatedly to end the Iraq War and linked a troop withdrawal timetable to a funding bill.
However, then-President George Bush vetoed the bill, which led to Democrats and Republicans going back and forth over it.
Eventually, the Democrats backed down and withdrew the troop withdrawal condition from the bill.
According to Krieg, the strongest tool the Democrats have in ending the Iran war now is their ability to withhold funding.
“The 11 December funding deadline gives Democrats leverage to negotiate restrictions before they assume control of Congress in January. The emerging discussion about replenishing US munitions stockpiles in exchange for restrictions on offensive operations is particularly important,” he said.
“However, Trump retains his veto, so Democratic majorities alone cannot guarantee that new restrictions become law. Ultimately, I think the greatest consequence of congressional intervention could be to accelerate the search for a negotiated settlement.”

noticias.titulo: How an oil feud is deepening rift between Baghdad and Iraq’s Kurdish region
noticias.resumen: Prime Minister al-Zaidi's move to take control of border crossings and oilfields has drawn a sharp response from Erbil.
noticias.texto:
How an oil feud is deepening rift between Baghdad and Iraq’s Kurdish region
Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s move to take control of border crossings and oilfields has drawn a sharp response from Erbil.
Iraq’s federal government and the semi-autonomous Kurdish region are locked in their sharpest confrontation in years over who controls the country’s oil, its border crossings and the revenues that flow from them.
The crisis escalated this week. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered federal authorities to take over all border crossings in the northern Kurdish region, close unofficial crossings used for smuggling, and seize control of oilfields in disputed provinces held by Kurdish security forces. Within 24 hours, Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court had issued a ruling backing Baghdad’s powers.
The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) has called the measures a violation of the constitution and accused Baghdad of trying to return Iraq to centralisation. On Wednesday, as reports spread that army units were heading north, the government in Baghdad insisted it had no plans to send troops into the region.
Here is what we know about the dispute, and where it could be headed.
What are the tensions about?
On the surface, the dispute is about oil smuggling.
On Tuesday, al-Zaidi ordered the Border Ports Authority to take over all crossings into the Kurdish region and directed the closure of all unofficial crossings. He told the energy police to secure all oilfields. He also ordered the federal Oil Ministry to take over the management of fields in Kirkuk, Nineveh, Salahuddin and Diyala provinces.
Those provinces lie in a belt of territory that both Baghdad and Erbil claim. The 2005 constitution set out a process under Article 140 to settle their status, but it was never completed.
Kirkuk, home to some of Iraq’s largest oilfields, has been the most bitterly contested. Kurdish forces took control of the city in 2014 after the Iraqi army withdrew from conflict with ISIL (ISIS). Federal forces retook it in October 2017, after the Kurdish region held an independence referendum which Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court later declared unconstitutional and void.
Al Jazeera correspondent Suhaib al-Asa has reported that the oil sites named in this week’s order are, in practice, outside the semi-autonomous Kurdish region but still under the control of its security forces.
The court ruling raised the stakes further. In an interpretive decision, the Federal Supreme Court affirmed the federal government’s authority to secure Iraq’s international borders and deploy the armed forces across all Iraqi territory. The court said federal authorities could supervise border crossings, including those in the Kurdish region. It also confirmed Baghdad’s power to oversee the production and export of oil and gas, as well as oil and non-oil revenues.
Both sides have framed the dispute as a constitutional battle, said Tallha Abdulrazaq, an independent international security and defence consultant based in the United Kingdom. Baghdad cites federal authority over national wealth and borders under Articles 110 and 112, while Erbil invokes shared customs administration and regional autonomy under Article 114.
“Paradoxically, both sides are right,” Abdulrazaq told Al Jazeera. “Since its adoption in 2005, Iraq’s constitution has contained contradictory and ambiguous provisions on oil and border management, making it a recurring recipe for political chaos.”
What has the Iraqi government said?
Baghdad presents its measures as a campaign against corruption and smuggling, not a move against the Kurds.
“National sovereignty is indivisible,” said al-Zaidi, who is also commander-in-chief of the armed forces. He described protecting Iraq’s wealth as “a battle for existence” in which the state would put an end to all forms of smuggling.
The orders follow an investigation into smuggling at the state-run North Oil Company. Al-Zaidi also dismissed eight security and administrative officials, including the head of the Border Ports Authority, Kirkuk’s operations commander and the province’s police chief.
Government spokesperson Haidar al-Aboudi told state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya on Wednesday that there was “no truth” to reports of troops moving towards the region. He said al-Zaidi was committed to “protecting the people of the region, not threatening them”. He added that the salaries of the Kurdish region’s public employees would be secured in the 2027 budget.
Baghdad is framing the measures as part of a wider drive to secure state security. Earlier this month, Iraqi forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad, a longtime stronghold of the Iran-aligned armed group Kataib Hezbollah. According to Reuters, the group allowed the forces in under a settlement brokered by politicians.
Abdulrazaq said al-Zaidi was justified “on the narrow facts”. “Oil smuggling across unofficial crossings is real and well-documented. However, smuggling is the pretext,” he said.
The security and defence consultant described the escalation as “largely a calculated domestic manoeuvre”. In Jurf al-Sakhar, al-Zaidi faces steep hurdles, he said. Rebuilding the town, returning Sunni Arab residents displaced for 12 years and fully expelling Kataib Hezbollah all risk triggering an intra-Shia clash.
“A controlled dispute with the Kurdistan Regional Government carries far lower political costs for Baghdad than an armed confrontation among Shia factions,” he said.
Al-Zaidi also needs to show his Shia coalition partners and armed factions that “he is decisive with everyone, not just selectively targeting some Shia militias”, Abdulrazaq added. He suggested a hard line towards the Kurds “may even have been an explicit demand from those factions” at the height of the Jurf al-Sakhar standoff.
Why are oil revenues so important?
Oil is the backbone of Iraq’s economy. It accounts for the overwhelming majority of state revenue and pays the salaries of millions of public employees, including those in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
Baghdad claims smuggling is draining that wealth on a large scale. Al-Aboudi said tens of billions had gone into “private pockets and accounts” without benefiting the region’s residents. According to Al Jazeera’s al-Asa, the government estimates that 200,000 to 230,000 barrels of oil per day (bpd) are smuggled, worth about $200m a month.
Al-Asa has reported that oil is moved from the disputed provinces to other parts of Iraq and then abroad, or sent directly from Sulaimaniyah, Kirkuk and Erbil towards Iran. Most of the region’s unofficial crossings are on the Iranian border, he said.
The Iraqi News Agency has published excerpts from a government intelligence report which traces smuggling routes from Kirkuk and Sulaimaniyah to Iran and on to Afghanistan. The report also describes operations to disguise Iranian oil products so they can be passed off as Iraqi.
For Erbil, control of oil has been central to its autonomous status. In February 2022, the Federal Supreme Court ruled the region’s oil and gas law unconstitutional. The Kurdish region, which has enjoyed broad autonomy from Baghdad since the 1990s, has in the past ignored rulings by the federal court, and did so with that one.
The region’s independent exports suffered a major blow in March 2023 when the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline was halted after the International Chamber of Commerce in Paris ordered Turkiye to pay Iraq $1.5bn in damages over unauthorised crude oil exports from Iraq’s Kurdish region transported without Baghdad’s approval. Exports resumed in September 2025 under an interim deal between Iraq’s federal government, the KRG and foreign oil producers.
Revenue from border crossings matters, too. Salim Zakhour, a researcher in constitutional law and political systems who is based in Qatar, told Al Jazeera: “One of the key points of debate in the court’s decision is that it gave federal authorities oversight of revenues from non-oil fees and taxes, and I think this is one of the issues that could be contested in the court’s rulings.”
What has the Kurdistan Regional Government said?
The KRG has rejected Baghdad’s measures, calling them “a violation of the constitution and an infringement on the region’s rights”, and said it rejected “the language of threats” and a military approach to the dispute.
After a meeting on Wednesday, chaired by Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, the KRG’s Council of Ministers said it rejected “any attempt to return Iraq to a centralised system”. Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani said addressing the region in “military language” did “not solve any problem”.
Erbil has said it supports efforts to fight corruption and smuggling. It has called for the dispute to be settled through dialogue and full implementation of the constitution.
Opposition to Baghdad’s measures has spilled onto the streets. On Thursday, thousands of demonstrators gathered in Erbil, the capital of the semi-autonomous Kurdish region, protesting against the federal government’s move to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities. Erbil-based broadcaster Kurdistan24 reported that tens of thousands of people joined and that protesters were calling for Kurdish political unity.
The Kurdish news agency Rudaw reported that the region’s two main political parties, the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), issued a joint statement that Baghdad’s decisions were “unexpected and deeply surprising”, warning that undermining the power of the Kurdish political entity is a “red line”.
But Abdulrazaq called the show of solidarity “a defensive reflex” driven by each party’s interests. A threat from Baghdad to one party is a threat to both, he said, and both risk losing the lucrative positions and budgets they have gained since the 2003 US-led invasion.
“It is therefore a pragmatic unity that will rapidly dissolve once the immediate threat recedes,” he said.
Where is this dispute headed?
For now, Baghdad appears eager to avoid any sort of military showdown. Abdulrazaq noted that the government has denied deploying troops to the region. It has also sent Popular Mobilisation Forces chief Faleh al-Fayyad to press Kurdish authorities for cooperation.
The legal ground has shifted in Baghdad’s favour. “The court’s decision is final and decisive,” the legal researcher Zakhour said. “But the issue is not only constitutional and legal. There is a political problem.” He said Erbil had been counting on challenging the measures in court, but al-Zaidi had “pre-empted this step”.
Outside support for Erbil also looks thin. Abdulrazaq said Washington is “heavily focused on supporting Zaidi”, particularly his agenda to consolidate state authority and rein in Iran-backed Shia armed groups.
“The Kurds should not expect American backing in this dispute; if anything, Erbil is more likely to face quiet US pressure to accommodate Baghdad’s demands,” he said.
Tehran, he said, is also clearly satisfied with the pressure on Erbil. Iran is angered by the presence of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in the region and has carried out drone strikes on their camps. Abdulrazaq stressed, however, that there is “no hard evidence” that Baghdad’s timing is part of a direct quid-pro-quo with Iran over Jurf al-Sakhar.
Ankara’s calculus is more pragmatic, he said, anchored in trade, energy and border security. Turkiye has little interest in an armed crisis on its southern border that could send more refugees across, and is likely to avoid overt intervention, he said. Instead, it will quietly favour an arrangement that keeps commerce stable and curbs smuggling.
What happens next?
In an effort to defuse the crisis, Iraq’s four presidencies have agreed to a proposal by Supreme Judicial Council head Faiq Zaidan to hold a national dialogue on December 1. The four presidencies are those of the republic, the government, parliament and the judiciary.
Abdulrazaq said the dialogue offered “a face-saving opportunity rather than a permanent fix”. He said it could lead to a temporary compromise, such as a joint oversight mechanism that polices official crossings while closing down unofficial ones.
“Long-term, however, the underlying tensions will remain in play,” he said. “The constitution is contradictory and Iraq doesn’t have a federal law that clearly delineates who is responsible for what in the oil and gas sector. These issues will simply resurface at a later date, even if both parties want to kick the can down the road.”

noticias.titulo: Inside Liberland, the crypto ‘country’ few have heard of
noticias.resumen: Al Jazeera's Antoine Allen reports on a group of people trying to build a tax-free nation.
noticias.texto:
Inside Liberland, the crypto ‘country’ few have heard of
Al Jazeera’s Antoine Allen reports on a group of people trying to build a tax-free nation.
“Police, there’s a police boat!” I say.
I had been followed by the police before but never imagined I would be tracked by a Croatian police boat along the European Union’s longest river, the Danube, on my way to a so-called crypto bro tax-free paradise.
They did not approach us. They did not shout. They used cameras to film us while we filmed them.
Croatia says it is protecting its border from people trying to claim this disputed territory as their own country: Liberland.
The boat chase was just one of many surprises my investigation into Liberland led me to.
I secured access to Vit Jedlicka, a Czech politician and YouTuber who says he spent years trying to change his own country. He decided it could not be done, so instead he searched for a country of his own. How?
“We were looking for no-man’s land and we just googled for it,” he told me.
He found a 7sq km (2.7sq mile) forested peninsula on the west bank of the Danube, left unsettled by a border dispute between Croatia and Serbia. In 2015 he declared it the Free Republic of Liberland. Its number one rule is no taxation.
Vit is not shy about his backers. “We have lots of billionaires that signed up for citizenship,” he said. The concept of Liberland has even had long-standing support from Javier Milei, now Argentina’s president.
But Vit has been chasing this dream since 2015. What made my experience different was the people I met at Liberpulco.
Because entering Liberland risks arrest, its supporters gather at a festival up the river in Serbia. It merges the Liberland gathering with Anarchapulco, the anarcho-capitalist conference founded by Jeff Berwick.
The aspiring citizens know exactly how their views are seen from the outside. Jeff said what I was thinking.
“Most people haven’t heard about Liberland, but if they have heard of it, they usually think it’s crazy conspiracy theorists, crazy anarchists.”
He wasn’t apologising. “Anarchy is a Greek word, without rulers. We just believe that the best way for humans to coexist is without being slaves to a ruler.”
On taxes, Vit set the tone. “Taxes are just fines for being productive.”
On the state, he went further. “The state would put you in jail if you start a Ponzi scheme. But if they run a pension system, which is a Ponzi scheme, they don’t save any money.”
The conference had a series of speakers. One said: “I didn’t like the vaccines, I didn’t like the mandates. So I spoke out against that. I got into trouble.”
Another told the crowd we are living in a matrix. “Words are a spell,” he said. “That’s why we call it spelling.”
Each speaker offered advice on how to gain freedom. The fear of an overbearing government seemed to be the main thing uniting the attendees.
Vit and Jeff gave me free rein. Over the week I joined a meditation class and watched a knife defence class led by an instructor who taught himself from YouTube.
But the session on how to stop your government watching you was the one we were told not to film.
Headlines brand Liberland a playground for billionaires. So I went on a journey to track them down at the conference.
“Are you a billionaire?”
“Not yet.”
“No.”
“No, no. I have a small farm, I have a few horses.”
I found none.
But I discovered that the movement to set up free and self-governing communities is growing around the world. Liberland sits at one end of a spectrum that runs from homesteading to private cities such as Prospera in Honduras.
Tim Allen of the Free Cities Foundation was clear about Liberland’s biggest problem. “Your territory is only as good as you can defend it.”
Croatia rejects Liberland outright. In a statement to Al Jazeera, its Foreign Ministry called it a provocative action with no basis in law. In 2023, Croatian authorities demolished the settlement Liberlanders had built on the land.
On my last evening, I boarded Vit’s yacht in the middle of the Danube as he handed out medals and passports, with a Croatian police boat a few hundred metres away.
Two thoughts kept running through my head. The first: Am I in a James Bond film?
The second: If I am, who is the villain?
Is Liberland a scam, selling passports for a country nobody can enter without fear of arrest? Or is it simply wealthy people trying to hold on to their money, without a care for how taxes often help those in need?
The banquet auction gave me part of an answer. It wasn’t exactly a billion-dollar bidding war.
Whether they had lots of money or lived off the land, they were united by one belief: They don’t like big government, or even mainstream media.
But I kept thinking about who Liberland would leave out. When I asked Vit who could become a citizen, he was direct. “We also don’t accept people that are insolvent.”
A country with limited government also has limited safety mechanisms for people of more modest means when they fall into trouble.
Vit hopes Liberland will become a state within 15 to 20 years. “We are not teenagers yet,” he told me.
The land is real. But Liberland is still a far-off dream, with a passport you can’t use.
So I’m left with one question: Does the world need another country, especially one with freedoms only for the rich?

noticias.titulo: Haftar meets Erdogan: Can Turkiye reunify Libya as it courts rival sides?
noticias.resumen: Maritime agreement pivotal for Turkiye's Eastern Mediterranean gas claims as Libya's unification process faces hurdles.
noticias.texto:
Haftar meets Erdogan: Can Turkiye reunify Libya as it courts rival sides?
Analysts say a unified Libya best protects Turkiye’s economic and maritime interests, but instability and divisions remain major hurdles.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan hosted eastern Libyan military commander Khalifa Haftar in Ankara on Wednesday, days after the Tripoli-based prime minister from the rival administration held talks with the Turkish foreign minister in Istanbul.
Haftar’s first trip to Ankara comes nearly seven years after Turkiye helped the internationally recognised Government of National Accord (GNA) repel a military offensive led by his self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA).
But following the 2020 United Nations-brokered ceasefire, Turkiye has pivoted towards a pragmatic approach, working to bring the rival administrations towards a unified government and military as it seeks to safeguard its maritime interests in the Mediterranean Sea.
The meetings come ahead of an expected visit by Erdogan to Libya, his first in 15 years, as Ankara seeks to reconcile the country’s rival administrations.
So what are Ankara’s interests in forging closer ties with Haftar, and what are the challenges ahead as Ankara seeks to reunify Libya?
Why did Turkiye invite both leaders?
Turkiye’s 2019-20 military intervention in support of the Tripoli-based government turned the tide of the Libyan civil war, forcing Khalifa Haftar’s forces to retreat from western Libya. But after the ceasefire later that year, Ankara began establishing contacts with the eastern authorities.
This rapprochement accelerated in 2025, after the United States launched efforts to reconcile Libya’s rival governments. A concurrent UN track produced the 4+4 agreement this past August, a political roadmap for a unified government and nationwide presidential and parliamentary elections within two years.
Turkiye was among the states to welcome and encourage the reconciliation process, while deepening its diplomatic and military ties with the east. In July, Ankara reached agreements with Haftar’s LNA on military infrastructure and training.
Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst, told Al Jazeera that Turkiye’s military strength and staying power have granted it prestige across Libya.
“Today, no Libyan leader of consequence can afford to spurn Ankara,” he said.
Of particular importance to Ankara’s relations with Libya is a maritime boundary agreement that it signed with the Tripoli-based government in 2019, but which was only adopted by the east last month.
The deal is a political flashpoint for several countries in the Eastern Mediterranean, opposed by Greece and Israel, and has been criticised by Egypt, which argued that it violated its own maritime rights.
But Ankara has defended the agreement as lawful.
What steps has Turkiye taken to unify Libya?
Turkiye has sought to bring Libya’s rival military leaderships together. In May, Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler met Abdulsalam al-Zoubi, the deputy defence minister in Tripoli, and Saddam Haftar, Khalifa Haftar’s son and a senior LNA commander. Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin later met Saddam Haftar in the eastern city of Benghazi.
In October, Ankara hosted further talks on military reunification, including discussions on establishing a joint military command in the central city of Sirte. However, disagreements over who would exercise political authority over a unified military remain unresolved.
On the economic front, Turkiye was among 10 countries that welcomed Libya’s adoption of its first unified national budget in more than a decade.
Ankara has also coordinated its diplomatic efforts with other countries involved in the reconciliation process. In June, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan held talks in Cairo with his Egyptian and Saudi counterparts and with Massad Boulos, a senior adviser to US President Donald Trump.
In August, Fidan travelled to Tripoli and Benghazi for separate meetings with Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah and Khalifa Haftar respectively.
Ankara has, however, not publicly endorsed a specific power-sharing arrangement. US mediators have backed a contentious proposal to make Saddam Haftar chairman of the Presidency Council, the three-member body that serves as Libya’s head of state.
It is unclear whether Erdogan’s December visit will bring Dbeibah and Khalifa Haftar together for direct negotiations. No such meeting has been confirmed.
Why does Turkiye want a united Libya?
For Turkiye, much is at stake in Libyan reconciliation. Ankara has military and economic interests in both parts of the country, as well as the maritime boundary agreement that underpins its claims to potentially gas-rich waters in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Bringing Libya under a single government would allow Ankara to pursue its defence, energy and reconstruction agreements within a unified institutional framework.
“Turkiye has gone from backing one side to engaging both because a stable, unified Libya best protects its economic and maritime interests,” said Sansom Milton, a senior research fellow at the Center for Conflict and Humanitarian Studies.
Saban Kardas, a research professor at Qatar University, told Al Jazeera that the effort was also in line with Turkiye’s historic approach to diplomacy with a divided state.
“The idea is to push for a national unity of some form. To make engagement sustainable, you need to see some measure of national unity,” he said.
What challenges remain ahead for Turkiye?
Although Ankara is currently well-positioned with Tripoli and Benghazi, analysts told Al Jazeera that instability and diverging visions of who will lead a reconciled Libya present major hurdles.
“Despite the assets and advantages Turkiye has accumulated in Libya, the country remains volatile,” Harchaoui said.
Libya is grappling with a deepening economic crisis, a weakening dinar, rising living costs, fuel and cash shortages and deteriorating public services. All of these have led to an increase in protests and strikes over the past year, casting a shadow over efforts for political stability.
While Saddam Haftar’s proposed appointment as chairman of the Presidency Council has the backing of US mediators, it faces opposition from powerful armed and political factions in western Libya, particularly in Misrata.
The city, a stronghold of the 2011 uprising that toppled Muammar Gaddafi, also helped defeat Khalifa Haftar’s offensive in 2020.
“A further difficulty is that western Libya has no single chain of command, so leaders in Tripoli cannot guarantee that the armed groups around them will accept a deal reached in their name,” said Milton, of the Center for Conflict and Humanitarian Studies.
“The main challenge is that division remains profitable for elites and armed groups on each side, who control separate revenues and institutions and have little incentive to merge them,” he added.
Kardas said, “It comes down to the local parties to put aside their differences and work through their deadlocks and divisions.”

noticias.titulo: Jordan Parliament debates ‘antiterror’ law after deadly Karak church attack
noticias.resumen: House votes to refer draft amendments to the 2006 Anti-Terrorism Law to its Legal Committee for review.
noticias.texto:
Jordan Parliament debates ‘antiterror’ law after deadly Karak church attack
House votes to refer draft amendments to the 2006 Anti-Terrorism Law to its Legal Committee for review.
Jordan’s Parliament is reviewing proposed amendments to its “antiterrorism” law that would double minimum prison sentences for “terrorism”-related offences after an attack at a church in Karak last month that killed nine people.
House of Representatives Speaker Ibrahim Tarawneh said the chamber had pledged to review legislation and consider amendments after the attack at the church in southern Jordan and the killing of a police officer in the capital, Amman.
The House voted to refer draft amendments to the 2006 Anti-Terrorism Law on Wednesday to its Legal Committee for review. The legislation will return to the chamber for debate and a vote before proceeding to the Senate and, if approved, royal ratification.
On October 23, gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud in a rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority. Authorities said 34 people were wounded.
Last week, Jordan’s State Security Court sentenced three men to death for the attack.
On Wednesday, the court sentenced another man to death for killing the police officer in Amman. The officer was stabbed while on guard duty near the Sri Lankan embassy on November 5.
The government-backed amendments would raise minimum prison terms to 10 years and up to 15 years in certain cases while retaining the death penalty for the most serious offences, the state-run Jordan News Agency reported.
The proposed amendments drew criticism from First Deputy Speaker Ayatollah Freihat, who said legislation should not be based on knee-jerk reactions to events, FactJo, a Jordanian news agency, reported.
He raised concerns that the amendments could also harm freedom of expression in Jordan.
Freihat called on the government to withdraw the draft amendments and form a committee of legal experts to review the state’s criminal policy, criticising the use of “vague” formulations in defining “terrorism”, including “disrupting public order” and “harming the public interest”.
Earlier, King Abdullah II had said the kingdom would not be shaken by the attack on the church. Opening the new session of parliament this month, Abdullah said “the treacherous hand of terrorism” had reached out “to test the resilience of our state and the resolve of our people”.

noticias.titulo: Is UBI the solution to mass unemployment in an AI economy?
noticias.resumen: AI's rapid advance has led to calls for universal payments to prevent poverty and wealth inequality.
noticias.texto:
Is UBI the solution to mass unemployment in an AI economy?
AI’s rapid advance has fueled calls for universal payments to prevent poverty and wealth inequality.
As rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) raise fears of mass job losses, calls for the rollout of universal basic income (UBI) are gaining traction.
UBI is a regular cash payment made to every citizen regardless of employment status, income or wealth.
Proponents of UBI in the United States argue that governments should look to UBI to offset AI’s expected impact on the labour market and prevent extreme poverty and wealth inequality.
Here is what we know:
When did the concept of UBI begin?
The idea of universal payments is not new.
In 1797, Thomas Paine, one of the key thinkers of the American Revolution, proposed an early version of UBI in a pamphlet titled Agrarian Justice. He argued that land was originally common property, shared by all of humanity. Those with no land, he said, were owed compensation as a basic human right.
Under Paine’s proposal, each person would have received a lump sum of 15 pounds when they turned 21, followed by an annual payment of 10 pounds from age 50, paid for by a tax on inherited property.
The idea resurfaced in the 1960s from opposing ends of the ideological spectrum.
US economist Milton Friedman proposed a “negative income tax”, under which the government would top up the earnings of anyone falling below a set threshold. Friedman, a champion of free-market policies, argued that his proposal would be cheaper than existing welfare programmes.
US civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr, in his 1967 book Where Do We Go from Here, called for a guaranteed income as a way to end poverty.
King Jr’s vision came close to being enshrined in law in 1969, when President Richard Nixon proposed the Family Assistance Plan, a minimum income for families with children. Nixon’s proposal passed the House of Representatives but stalled in the Senate, and the plan was eventually abandoned.
After falling out of fashion in subsequent decades, proposals for universal payments have re-entered the mainstream in recent years amid the rise of automation and AI.
Who is backing UBI?
Some of the loudest proponents of UBI are the people developing AI.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has been pushing the idea for years.
In a 2024 interview with the All-In Podcast, Altman proposed a twist on UBI that would give everyone a stake in the productive gains of AI.
“I wonder if the future looks something like more like universal basic compute than universal basic income and everybody gets like a slice of GPT 7’s compute and they can use it, they can resell it, they can donate it to somebody to use for cancer research,” Altman said, suggesting that citizens could “own part of the productivity” generated by AI instead of receiving cash.
In April, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk said in an X post that a government-distributed “Universal High Income” would be the best way to deal with large-scale unemployment caused by AI.
Musk said AI and robotics would produce an abundance of goods and services far in excess of the increase in the money supply in future, so there would not be inflation.
Some observers have questioned the motivations of such proposals from billionaire tech executives.
Jonathan Portes, a professor of economics and public policy at King’s College, London, said tech leaders promoting UBI are acting out of “perceived self-interest”. In his view, a basic income could make job losses easier to accept as people are more likely to tolerate AI replacing their work if they are being paid.
“Partly it’s just another cool sounding idea,” Portes told Al Jazeera. “We should not take these people seriously on public policy issues at all.”
Who would pay for UBI, and how is it different from social welfare?
Most UBI proposals envision a system paid for by taxes, much in the same way as existing welfare programmes, though some pilot schemes have been funded by private donations.
Unlike traditional social welfare, which typically requires applicants to demonstrate financial hardship, UBI is paid to every member of a population without conditions.
Portes said UBI high enough to support acceptable living standards is not likely to be economically or politically viable in the near future.
While “a realistic UBI could help provide a better level of protection, increase individual autonomy and increase labour market flexibility, getting there would be complex”, he added.
“Many of the claims for it and fears are grossly exaggerated,” Portes said.
So who would benefit from UBI?
While everyone would get some financial benefit, some economists and technologists argue that the biggest beneficiary could be the economy.
In a scenario where AI leads to mass layoffs, people will have less money to spend. From this perspective, UBI would function less as a form of charity than as a way to keep consumer spending going.
That is the case made by Martin Ford, a futurist and the author of Rise of the Robots.
Ford argues that jobs are how purchasing power reaches common consumers, viewing UBI as a way to repair the link between production and spending rather than redistributing wealth for its own sake.
“Jobs are that mechanism that gets purchasing power to consumers so they can then drive the economy,” Ford said in a 2017 TED Talk.
“If, in fact, that mechanism begins to erode in the future, then we’re going to need to replace it with something else, or we’re going to face the risk that our whole system simply may not be sustainable.”
What are the arguments against UBI?
The most common objection is that unconditional cash discourages work. The evidence suggests the effect is real but modest.
In the biggest US trial of its kind, about 1,000 low-income participants were given $1,000 a month for three years.
OpenResearch’s Unconditional Cash Study, backed by OpenAI’s Altman, found that participants worked only 1.3-1.4 hours less each week compared with the control group.
More than half of recipients’ increased spending went on basic necessities such as food, housing and transport.
The study found no significant effect on physical health, and gains in wellbeing faded after the first year.
Another objection is cost.
In the US, paying each family of four a universal payment of $30,000 – slightly below the official poverty line – would cost approximately $8.5 trillion each year, according to the Tax Project Institute.
That would dwarf current levels of spending on welfare.
The US government spent $1.7 trillion on some 90 welfare programmes in 2025, according to the conservative Heritage Foundation.

noticias.texto:
FIFA says personal and business information stolen in cyberattack
No files from the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project were accessed, according to media reports.
FIFA said it had been the victim of a criminal cyberattack that gave unauthorised access to personal and business information, although no files from the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project were accessed, according to media reports.
FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information,” a FIFA spokesperson told Al Jazeera.
FIFA strongly condemned the “unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data,” adding that such actions were “a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy”.
It also said that :”FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement.”
FIFA did not say how many people or organisations were affected, when the attack took place or what the business information included. Its reference to publication did not say whether any data had appeared online, or where.
Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot on X of what it claimed were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the hack when responding to a post that said more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been leaked.
The person with knowledge of the matter told the Reuters news agency that less than 0.1 percent of the total data held by world football’s governing body was affected.
A FIFA source told The Athletic that the person – or group – responsible for carrying out the cyberattack gained access by impersonating staff rather than a systems or technical failure.
FIFA President Gianni Infantino said in July that his organisation had scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors following a widespread backlash.
The plan ‌involved raising up to $4.2bn by selling a 20 percent stake in a new unit that would run FIFA tournaments, including the World Cup.

noticias.titulo: ‘Symbolic’: Why did UK sanction Yemen’s Houthis amid attacks on Saudi?
noticias.resumen: UK sanctions Iran-backed group and its leaders, accusing them of undermining stability in the Middle East.
noticias.texto:
‘Symbolic’: Why did UK sanction Yemen’s Houthis amid attacks on Saudi?
UK sanctions Iran-backed group and its leaders, accusing them of undermining stability in the Middle East.
London, United Kingdom – The United Kingdom has slapped sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis and four of their senior leaders after accusing the Iran-backed group of renewed “aggression” inside Yemen and attacks targeting civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting the financial district in Riyadh this week, as they engage in a civil war with Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
Fighting has escalated since July as a 2022 United Nations-brokered ceasefire collapsed. Since then, the Houthis have captured the Red Sea port of Mocha and the island of Mayyun, extending control over the Red Sea in a setback to the Saudi-backed government.
The war erupted after the Houthis captured the capital, Sanaa, in late 2014, forcing President Abd Rabbu Mansour Hadi to flee. Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the Hadi government as it saw the Iran-backed group’s rise in neighbouring Yemen as a security threat.
The UK government announced its sanctions on Tuesday, accusing the Houthis of undermining peace and security in Yemen and the region. It froze assets and placed travel bans on the group and its leaders, including Interior Minister Abdulkarim Amir al-Din Hussein al-Houthi and Security and Intelligence chief Abdul Hakim Hashem Ali al-Khaiwani.
Chief prosecutor Sarim al-Din Mufadal, who has been accused of perpetrating “sexual violence, including rape and torture”, also faces an asset freeze and travel ban.
UK’s interests in the Middle East
“The Houthis’ renewed aggression targeting our partners and innocent civilians is unacceptable, and they must be held to account,” said UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who linked the sanctions to attacks on shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb strait in the Red Sea, one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world.
“Today’s measures send a clear message to the Houthis – we will always act in support of British values and interests,” he said in a statement.
The British move comes nearly a month after it decided to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia, a close ally going back decades that has increasingly come under missile and drone attacks in recent weeks.
Britain also sent Tornado fighters to Saudi Arabia in the wake of the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait in 1990, according to the Royal Air Force Museum.
The Houthis have also targeted oil installations and a major pipeline that helped Saudi Arabia export its oil while Iran essentially blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint. Tehran said it has blocked the vital waterway, through which most of the Gulf oil and natural gas passes, in response to the US-Israel war on Iran.
The UK has naval and logistics bases in the neighbouring Gulf nations of Bahrain and Oman. In May, it agreed a free trade deal with the six Gulf Cooperation Council states.
‘To turn the screw on the Houthis’
Thomas Juneau, an associate fellow with Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, said the sanctions were imposed during a diplomatic push by Riyadh.
“Saudi Arabia has been asking other countries to list the Houthis as a terrorist entity, to turn the screw on the Houthis and to help in its campaign against the group,” he told Al Jazeera.
The sanctions, Ahmed Nagi from the International Crisis Group (ICG) said, are “intended to send a political message about where the UK stands on the current escalation and the Houthi actions”.
In January 2024, the UK and the United States jointly sanctioned four Houthi figures, including the group’s defence minister and naval commander, over attacks on Red Sea shipping, and a month later, a second package targeted the Quds Force, the overseas unit of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The same month, the UK joined the US in carrying out air strikes on Houthi positions over attacks on ships in the Red Sea, which had disrupted maritime trade. The Houthis had imposed a ban on ships linked to Israel from passing through the waterway in response to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
The Houthis are already under a UN arms embargo, and London is now “going further”, Nagi, who is a senior Yemen analyst at the ICG, said.
This month, the UN Security Council renewed its Yemen sanctions regime until November 2027 through a UK-led resolution.
Raiman al-Hamdani, a Yemeni researcher and analyst, said the UK, as the Security Council’s lead on Yemen, had helped shape that regime and “this latest step continues a longstanding policy rather than breaking from it.”
‘Largely symbolic’
But Nagi called the UK move “largely symbolic”.
“The four Houthi leaders targeted by the sanctions are unlikely to travel to the UK or hold assets there, so the practical impact will probably be limited.”
Al-Hamdani said the group’s income comes “largely from the black market, smuggling, taxation of local businesses and control of ports and customs, none of which a UK asset freeze touches”.
“The missile and drone programme hasn’t slowed despite years of UN, US, EU and UK listings,” he added.
Juneau from Chatham House agreed the sanctions would not change Houthi behaviour soon but said that while sanctions by individual countries other than the US have little effect alone, they can matter collectively, which is why Saudi Arabia is pressing as many countries as possible to act.
He also pointed to the Houthis’ growing influence in the Red Sea, which has concerned Saudi Arabia as well as its Western allies.
The British foreign secretary on Tuesday pointed out how Houthi actions in the Red Sea were “driving up the cost of living for the British people” and “undermining the stability of the Middle East”.
Analysts pointed out that the UK government statement is silent on the other parties to the war – the Yemeni government forces and Saudi Arabia – even as it said the Houthis’ “reckless aggression is responsible for this conflict”.
Nagi said the omission reflected how London sees the war.
“From London’s perspective, the Houthis are the ones attacking Saudi Arabia and escalating the conflict, rather than the other way around,” he said.
Juneau was blunter. “Sanctions are always political. You sanction your opponents. You don’t sanction your partners or friends,” he said.
Humanitarian concerns
Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, expressed concerns that the sanctions would impact aid organisations engaged in humanitarian work in Houthi-held areas.
“As Yemen relies heavily on imports, curbs affecting commercial goods could also push up food prices,” she told Al Jazeera.
“The sanctions really can have quite devastating impacts for the populations living in territories under Houthi control, even if that’s not what the UK intends by the sanctions,” she warned.
This is the case even though the UK’s sanctions already include a humanitarian exception covering aid and other activities that meet basic human needs, she said.
Moreover, the UK has not proscribed the Houthis under “antiterrorism” laws despite its other Western allies – the US, Canada and Australia – designating the Iran-backed group as a “terrorist” organisation.
Juneau called the aid agencies’ fear that proscription could hamper humanitarian deliveries “a valid concern” although some people argued the Houthis’ diversion of aid has already made such work extremely difficult.
The Houthis have repeatedly denied that they have diverted humanitarian aid.
Al-Hamdani said sanctions have not forced the Houthis to change their tactics. They do not “appear to respond to human rights criticism or listings”, he said, adding that the group “tends to treat detainees and abuses as bargaining chips to strengthen its negotiating position and demands”.
Rather, he said, sanctions “risk deepening polarisation and closing off the political settlement the war needs”.

noticias.titulo: James ‘Fergie’ Chambers: US trying to cast ‘antiwar ideas as extremist’
noticias.resumen: Recently bailed activist denies accusations of supporting Hamas, claiming he is being punished for supporting Palestine.
noticias.texto:
James ‘Fergie’ Chambers: US trying to cast ‘antiwar ideas as extremist’
The recently bailed activist denies US accusations of supporting Hamas, claiming he is being targeted for supporting Palestine.
Madrid, Spain – James “Fergie” Chambers, a pro-Palestine philanthropist who is the subject of an ongoing extradition request by the United States government, said he believed the US is targeting supporters of the people of Gaza worldwide.
The US government’s case centres on Chambers’s alleged laundering of $7.5m, which he is said to have wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, allegedly using the cash to support Hamas.
He is not charged with any “terrorism” offences and denies any wrongdoing.
Chambers, a self-proclaimed Marxist-Leninist and the heir to the Cox Enterprises media fortune, believes supporters of the Palestinian cause are being targeted around the globe.
“I think that when the neocolonial system starts to break apart economically, militarily, which I believe is happening, it becomes desperate. And when it becomes desperate, it becomes more violent and more violent,” he told Al Jazeera.
“And all these things sort of converge around the occupation of Palestine because we understand the occupation of Palestine as basically nothing more than an expression of US military and business interest. So that is the focal point of repression.”
He added: “In relation to the Palestinian cause and other causes, I think there is a kind of effort certainly in the US to designate [expressing] antiwar ideas as extremist and terrorist.”
‘They haven’t accused me of sending money to Hamas’
Chambers, who was released from prison in Madrid on bail last week after serving four months on remand, said he was being targeted by the US because of his support for the Palestinian cause.
“I’m not even accused of sending money anywhere illegal. I’m accused of wanting to, which is sort of a crazy distinction to me. They haven’t accused me of sending money to Hamas, no. They’ve accused me of wanting to send money to Hamas,” he said.
A keen football fan, he said he transferred the money to Club Africain, a Tunisian football team, which he sponsors.
He said he had met someone from the Iranian embassy in Tunisia at an international book fair in 2023.
“[They] tied in a narrative which says that … I allegedly visited the Iranian diplomats, which is not true. I met someone from the Iranian embassy at an international book fair, who told me that US citizens are allowed to have tourist visas. I never met an official at the embassy. I never went into the offices at the embassy.”
The 41-year-old said a forensic accountant had presented Club Africain’s accounts to the Madrid court.
As part of a deal in which his family cut ties with him at the time, he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m in mid-2023.
“I’m assuming the implication is that I would have met with these people and then transferred money to Tunisia to a football club with the intention of then laundering it to Hamas.”
The US Department of Justice said it did not want to comment when contacted by Al Jazeera.
Chambers said he was “very publicly” affiliated with the club, which won the Tunisian championship this year, and he made a four-year sponsorship deal.
“They had millions of euros worth of debt, which is why they contacted me to get involved. And the money was used to pay off debts, to revamp the team facilities, training facilities, youth programmes, pay overdue salaries. And then in return I had some involvement in management,” he said.
Chambers also said Tunisia was a “closed economy”.
“When you move money into Tunisia, you’re not allowed to move it out,” he said, adding that one of his “most constant emotions in all of this is just downright confusion”.
Chambers, who has given financial aid to 100 projects in 20 countries, including some in Palestine, said he was always careful to obey the law.
“There is no smoking gun. There’s no unloaded gun. There’s nowhere that I said I wanted to support any illegal groups,” he said.
Chambers said he was a target for supporting the Palestinian cause.
“I think the combination of an overall effort by the US authorities to criminalise basically the Palestinian cause in any capacity … this is a part of that,” he said. “You know the fact that I happen to have a lot of resources. And I speak out unapologetically and freely about my positions on US imperialism. These things just combined to make me a target and an example.”
Prison staff ‘saw me as being somebody who shouldn’t be there’
The father-of-four, who has been reunited with his family after being released on bail, is awaiting the court’s decision. His case has also drawn attention to concerns about the implications of the US extradition request.
During his time in jail, he said he received letters of support from many strangers as well as political parties from all sides.
“Even within the prison staff, there was a kind of consensus that people saw me as being somebody who shouldn’t be there,” he said.
However, he said he faces an uncertain future.
“I still don’t know … whether I am going to face decades of my life in a federal penitentiary in the US,” he said.
The High Court said it had decided to release Chambers after US authorities acknowledged what they described as substantial and unintentional errors in the Spanish translation of an FBI agent’s sworn statement, submitted in support of the extradition request. The proceedings have been the subject of further reporting on the extradition case in Spain.
Chambers was arrested on an Interpol Red Notice in Ibiza in July, but has since applied for asylum in Spain.
He cannot be extradited until the asylum claim is resolved, and if it is successful, he cannot be extradited from Spain to the US at all.
