noticias.titulo: LeBron James becomes oldest NBA player to post triple-double as 76ers win
noticias.resumen: James posted 25 points, 12 assists and 10 rebounds as Philadelphia snapped Miami's seven-game winning streak.
noticias.texto:
LeBron James becomes oldest NBA player to post triple-double as 76ers win
James posted 25 points, 12 assists and 10 rebounds as Philadelphia snapped Miami’s seven-game winning streak.
LeBron James became the oldest player in NBA history to produce a triple-double, leading Philadelphia to a 114-104 victory over the Miami Heat in the NBA Cup on Wednesday.
Four-time NBA Most Valuable Player James, who turns 42 on December 30, scored a season-high 25 points, passed off a season-high 12 assists and pulled down 10 rebounds to break his own triple-double age mark.
“Father Time always wins, but right now he’s giving Father Time hell,” Heat coach Erik Spoelstra said.
Miami grabbed a 32-29 lead after the first quarter, but James scored 14 consecutive Sixers points in a second-quarter run for a 62-53 half-time lead, and the hosts never lost the edge in the second half.
“We wanted to get back to our defensive identity,” James said. “We didn’t do that in the first quarter, but for the next 36 minutes I thought we got back to that.”
The 76ers improved the best record in the Eastern Conference to 15-4 while snapping a seven-game win streak for Miami (10-7).
Both clubs are 2-1 atop Cup East Group B, but with a win, Miami would have clinched the group and advanced to the knockout stage of the in-season tournament.
With Joel Embiid out due to illness and Jaylen Brown out after early left hamstring tightness, it fell to James to score and set up his teammates.
“That’s my favourite aspect of my game besides my IQ,” James said.
“To be able to go out there and just play like a quarterback role and watch these guys run the right routes, and it’s my job to put it on time and on target, it was fun.”
Tyrese Maxey led the 76ers with 30 points while VJ Edgecombe added 18.
“These are my young bulls right here,” James said. “They keep me going. They keep me energised.”
Giannis Antetokounmpo led Miami with 32 points and 14 rebounds.
James left the Los Angeles Lakers in the off-season and selected the 76ers from several clubs in hopes of capturing a fifth NBA crown.
Mavericks win group
The idle Dallas Mavericks became the first team to reach the Cup knockout round, clinching the West Group A title when the Phoenix Suns lost 116-104 at Houston.
Alperen Sengun had a triple-double with 23 points, 11 rebounds and 11 assists for Houston, while Kevin Durant added 20 points and Devin Booker led Phoenix with 25.
At Portland, Deni Avdija scored 33 points, and Damian Lillard added 29 to lead the host Trail Blazers over San Antonio 116-111, leaving West Group C deadlocked with the Spurs, Lakers, Portland and Golden State atop it at 2-1.
“It showed our maturity,” Lillard said. “We won a tough one.”
French star Victor Wembanyama scored 44 points and grabbed 16 rebounds to lead the Spurs, who fell to 15-4 after their first road loss of the season.
Jalen Brunson and Mikal Bridges each scored 19 points as the defending NBA and NBA Cup champion New York Knicks beat visiting Cleveland 121-102 for their sixth consecutive victory.
Karl-Anthony Towns had 12 points and 10 rebounds, and Jose Alvarado scored 21 off the bench for New York. Donovan Mitchell scored 30 points, and James Harden added 28 for the Cavaliers.
Minnesota’s Jaden McDaniels scored 32 points and grabbed 10 rebounds to lead the Timberwolves in a 113-106 victory at Oklahoma City.
Minnesota’s LaMelo Ball had 19 points, eight assists and seven rebounds but left the game late with a left ankle injury.
Two-time NBA MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander led Oklahoma City with 32 points.
Julius Randle scored 28 points to lead Brooklyn’s 104-97 victory at Milwaukee, the Nets snapping a five-game losing skid.
Jaylen Wells scored 19 points to lead Memphis’ 115-97 home victory over the Los Angeles Clippers.
Golden State’s De’Anthony Melton scored 24 points to lead the Warriors over visiting Sacramento 129-110.
Matas Buzelis scored 24 points to lead Chicago over host Charlotte 107-105 as the Hornets’ losing skid reached six games.

noticias.titulo: Iraq denies reports of troop movements towards Kurdish region
noticias.resumen: Government says there is 'no truth' to media reports that Iraqi army units were moving towards the Kurdistan region.
noticias.texto:
Iraq denies reports of troop movements towards Kurdish region
Government says there is ‘no truth’ to media reports that Iraqi army units were moving towards the Kurdistan region.
Iraq’s government has denied local media reports that army units were moving towards the Kurdistan region, as a top court backed Baghdad’s authority over the region’s border crossings and oil in a deepening dispute with Erbil.
Government spokesperson Haidar al-Aboudi told state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya on Wednesday that there was “no truth” to the media reports. He said oil smugglers were diverting “tens of billions” into “private pockets and accounts”, and that the salaries of Kurdistan’s public employees were not part of the dispute.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said “national sovereignty is indivisible” and that protecting Iraq’s wealth was “a battle for existence” in which the state would end all forms of smuggling.
Al-Zaidi has ordered the Border Ports Authority to take over all crossings in the Kurdistan region and to close unofficial crossings. He has also ordered federal authorities to take over oil fields in Kirkuk, Nineveh, Salahuddin and Diyala that are under Kurdish security control.
Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court has issued an interpretive ruling affirming federal powers to secure international borders and deploy armed forces across all Iraqi territory. It also affirmed Baghdad’s right to oversee border crossings, including those in Kurdistan, the production and export of oil and gas, and both oil and non-oil revenues.
Border Forces Commander Mohammed Abdul Wahab Sukkar al-Saidi told the state-run Iraqi News Agency on Thursday that the command had “begun implementing the directive of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces to close all unofficial crossings” with neighbouring countries.
He did not say how many crossings would be affected.
The Kurdistan Regional Government’s council of ministers, chaired by Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, said it rejected “any attempt to return Iraq to a centralised system”. Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani rejected addressing the region in “military language”, saying this “does not solve any problem”.
Thousands of people gathered in Erbil, the capital of the Kurdish region, on Thursday to protest against the government’s plan to take over border crossings and oil operations.
Reporting from Erbil, Al Jazeera’s Mahmoud Abdel Wahed said the protesters claim the government’s plan “touches on their sovereignty and their territorial integrity, and that this undermines the constitutional rights of the Kurdish people”.
“The question now is whether or not the government of Baghdad will be able to solve this peacefully without triggering a new chapter of conflict, a new political and economic confrontation with the Kurdish region.”
Baghdad says some 200,000 to 230,000 barrels of oil a day are being smuggled, worth about $200m a month, Al Jazeera correspondent Suhaib al-Asa said.
Salim Zakhour, a researcher in constitutional law and political systems, told Al Jazeera that the ruling, issued within 24 hours at al-Zaidi’s request, gave Baghdad a legal basis to act. “The court’s decision is final and decisive,” he said. “But the issue is not only constitutional and legal. There is a political problem.”
The country’s four presidencies have agreed to hold a national dialogue on December 1 to resolve the crisis.
The orders followed an investigation into smuggling at the state-run North Oil Company, after which al-Zaidi dismissed eight officials, including Kirkuk’s police chief and operations commander.

noticias.titulo: Highway explosion in Giza: How deadly are Egypt’s roads and railways?
noticias.resumen: Egypt has suffered another tragedy as a deadly road explosion kills 31 and injures dozens.
noticias.texto:
Highway explosion in Giza: How deadly are Egypt’s roads and railways?
Egypt has suffered another tragedy as a deadly road explosion kills 31 and injures dozens.
An explosion rocked a highway in Cairo when a fuel truck overturned and caught fire, killing at least 31 people on Wednesday.
Egypt’s public prosecutor has announced an investigation into the crash, and the Ministry of Health said it will continue to monitor the situation.
But Egypt is no stranger to deadly accidents on its roads, despite spending billions of dollars on its transportation systems.
So what exactly caused the explosion and how unsafe are Egypt’s roads?
Here is what we know.
What happened?
On Wednesday evening, a fuel tanker travelling on a busy ring road in Giza’s Imbabah district, a highly populated, working-class part of the Greater Cairo area, crashed and exploded, causing a fire that killed at least 31 people and injured 21 others.
Local media have reported that the explosion happened after the truck driver swerved to avoid a high-voltage cable which fell in front of the vehicle.
Twenty-seven vehicles were caught up and burned in the accident, according to Egypt’s judicial office.
Thirty-nine ambulances were dispatched to the scene, taking the injured to nearby hospitals for treatment, the Health Ministry said.
Egypt’s public prosecutor announced that there will be an investigation into the crash and ordered DNA samples from victims.
How unsafe are Egypt’s roads?
Egypt, which has a population of around 120m, is known for its dangerous roads. It clocked up a total of 44,940 road deaths and 476,126 injuries between 2019 and 2025, according to the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS).
Last year, more than 5,800 road deaths and 84,000 road injuries were recorded by the agency, with pedestrians making up more than one-third of those killed.
Children under the age of 15 made up 1,580 of the deaths and 29,101 of the injured.
A World Bank report in 2020 found that the incidents occur because 97 percent of Cairo’s streets lack traffic lights and 78 percent of them have no clear pedestrian footpaths.
What is Egypt’s train system like?
In 2025, there were 170 train incidents recorded, resulting in the deaths of 44 people and injuries to 215.
Earlier this month, at least seven people were killed and more than 125 others injured when a train backed into another, also in Giza, triggering calls for political accountability.
Egypt’s Ministry of Transport said that approximately $37bn was spent on transport investment between 2014 and 2024, but recurring incidents have raised questions about the effectiveness of this project.
The leader of the centrist Reform and Development Party’s parliamentary bloc, Irene Saeed, called for full financial transparency on how the Ministry of Transport spent its funding and loans in 2016.
A member of the Egyptian Parliament and leader of the Justice Party, Abdel Moneim Imam, told Al Jazeera earlier this month that the continued “turning of a blind eye to the shortcomings and the recurrence of accidents without genuine accountability leads to the continuation of the crisis”.

noticias.titulo: ‘Proscribing free speech’: Why a Jewish group is challenging UK’s Hamas ban
noticias.resumen: The Jewish Network for Palestine says the complete ban on Hamas was being used to stifle free speech.
noticias.texto:
‘Proscribing free speech’: Why a Jewish group is challenging UK’s Hamas ban
The Jewish Network for Palestine says the complete ban on Hamas was being used to stifle free speech and to target its members.
London, United Kingdom – The Jewish Network for Palestine (JNP) has filed an application to reverse the proscription of Hamas under Britain’s Terrorism Act, arguing that the ban is being used against its members and is hampering freedom of speech in the United Kingdom.
The JNP filed a formal de-proscription application on Thursday under Section 4 of the Terrorism Act, which oversees applications to remove a group from the UK’s list of banned organisations.
This follows the arrest of the 80-year-old son of Auschwitz survivors and the prosecution of a 72-year-old Jewish writer – both members of the JNP’s Steering Group – for pro-Palestinian and anti-Zionist speech.
The JNP was founded in 2018 by British members of the United States organisation Jewish Voice for Peace, a group which aims to bring together Jews and non-Jews who support Palestine. It is one of 11 Jewish and Jewish-led organisations that form the UK’s Jewish bloc for Palestine, which is frequently present at protests against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and pogroms in the West Bank.
According to the chair of the JNP, David Cannon, proscription of Hamas has made it near-impossible to openly discuss the events of October 7, 2023, when Hamas led an attack on villages and army outposts in southern Israel. In particular, the JNP says, it has been unable to talk publicly about false narratives that followed for fear of contravening the act.
“Now, all of these things needed to be discussed, but the UK government’s proscription of the political wing of Hamas has made referring to such evidence [of false reporting] risk the accusation of supporting Hamas, which is not what we’re saying. We’re saying that we want to discuss these issues,” he said.
In the days following October 7, when more than 1,000 people were killed, many stories about babies being killed by Hamas fighters and mass rapes were circulated in international media. There has been no evidence of these.
Cannon added that one of the group’s active members had resigned, fearing that what she could say would affect her immigration status if found to violate the act.
According to the application, the JNP has about 600 members and supporters.
‘Disproportionate interference’
The JNP’s application was filed five years to the day after the British government proscribed the whole of Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
Hamas’s armed wing had been banned in 2001, but in 2021 the then-Home Secretary Priti Patel extended the ban to cover the whole political group, describing the organisation as “fundamentally and rabidly anti-Semitic” and arguing that the proscription was required to protect the Jewish community.
The government did not, however, explain how the proscription of Hamas would protect the Jewish community in the UK. Instead, the JNP argues that the designation has now been used against the Jewish community it was supposed to protect.
The group also argues that the continued proscription of Hamas in its entirety was a “disproportionate interference with the rights of JNP and its members” under the European Convention on Human Rights Articles 9, 10 and 11 on freedom of thought, expression and assembly, with the burden of the proscription falling on people in Britain.
Finally, they argue, Hamas has “no presence in the UK and has not been shown to pose a specific threat to it”.
“The less intrusive position that applied before November 2021 shows that proscription of the whole organisation is not necessary. On a proper application of the policy, and with the impact on JNP weighed, continued proscription is not justified,” the application stated.
Following the JNP’s application, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmoud has 90 days to consider it beginning the day after it is received. If it is refused, the group can appeal the decision.
‘Chilling free speech’
Tony Greenstein, 72, an anti-Zionist writer and blogger and prominent member of the JNP, was prosecuted for publishing a blog on October 7, 2023, titled “Full Support for the Gaza Ghetto Uprising”, in which he evoked the Jewish Warsaw Ghetto Uprising in 1943.
While his post only mentioned Hamas in passing, in November 2024 Greenstein was charged under section 12 of the British Terrorism Act with inviting support for Hamas on the basis of one sentence in that blog and for writing “please share” on social media, promoting the piece.
After nearly three years and appearances in different courts, Greenstein was acquitted in August this year.
“If you can’t actually say what you think about an organisation without watching over your shoulder in case you’re contravening some law, then that’s chilling free speech, and that is the real issue,” Greenstein told Al Jazeera.
“That’s been made time and time again about the Terrorism Act. It’s really about clamping down on free speech,” he added.
During the criminal proceedings against him, five banks and building societies closed his accounts.
In Greenstein’s view, arresting Jews is not the best way to protect the Jewish community in the UK.
“It’s a very good way of protecting Zionism and the Zionists, and that is the difference,” he said. “The way they dress up their foreign policy choices is by saying they’re protecting a particular community. The reality is, of course, banning or proscribing Hamas has nothing at all to do with racist attacks against Jews, they’re completely separate phenomena.”
He added: “Hamas doesn’t operate in Britain. It never has operated in Britain …So how can we be at risk of being attacked by a group that doesn’t even exist here? It was about stopping people expressing an opinion on what’s happening in Gaza and in the occupied territories. That’s a very different thing.”
The right to oppose a genocide
One of the founders of the JNP is Haim Bresheeth-Zabner, an 80-year-old Jewish-Israeli anti-Zionist filmmaker and film studies professor at the School of African and Oriental Studies (SOAS).
He was arrested and held for 13 hours in November 2024 immediately after he made a speech at a protest in Swiss Cottage, north London. It was part of wider protests held weekly by the International Jewish Anti-Zionist Network with the JNP’s involvement against the Israeli ambassador and the actions of the Israeli government in Gaza. In his speech, Bresheeth-Zabner said that the Israeli army “cannot fight the resistance” and “cannot win against Hamas … against Hezbollah …[or] against the Houthis”.
“They [the police] refused to discuss with me what I said that is considered applicable under the Terrorism Act. It took many hours of waiting in a very cold car park … I’m 80 … I have heart failure and cancer. So I wasn’t feeling all that well, but that didn’t make a difference. I also told them that I need to take my medications in the early evening, and they disregarded that,” Bresheeth-Zabner told Al Jazeera.
While he was not charged following his arrest, he said the ban has been used against people who want to speak up against the genocide in Gaza, making it impossible to criticise the Israeli army.
“This is a really odd situation where Britain, as a society, as a politicised society, as a country, as a regime, if you want, is not acting to uphold international law, and is proscribing our ability to speak against the genocide, to speak against Zionism, to speak against Israel. When we do that, we are arrested. We are charged,” he said.
“We’re [the JNP] supporting human rights, and human rights include the right to oppose a genocide, not just our right to oppose a genocide, but of course the rights of the victims of the genocide to resist it.”

noticias.titulo: Are Trump’s tariffs aimed at securing US-friendly trade deals?
noticias.resumen: New US policy threatens further tariff hikes on China, India, Vietnam if trade negotiations fall through.
noticias.texto:
Are Trump’s tariffs aimed at securing US-friendly trade deals?
New policy threatens further tariff hikes on China, India, Vietnam if trade negotiations fall through.
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has proposed a new slate of trade tariffs against 14 of the US’s key trading partners, including China, India and the European Union.
The tariffs, which would go into effect next year, will hit China the hardest, potentially subjecting its products to a 40 percent import tax.
Washington says the tariffs, announced by the US Trade Representative (USTR) on Wednesday, are a response to unfair trading practices which harm US manufacturing, including “excess industrial capacity” – subsidies and policies that enable manufacturers to overproduce and undercut the US.
But Trump has long used tariffs as leverage in trade negotiations.
So, is the latest tariff announcement an effort to win concessions in upcoming trade deals? Here’s what we know:
Which economies do the tariffs target, and when would they start?
The tariffs would be imposed on products from China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam, according to the USTR. The maximum rates facing each country range from 20 percent to 40 percent.
It is unclear when exactly the tariffs would take effect, but a senior US official told the AFP news agency they would likely start in January at the earliest.
Why is the US imposing trade tariffs?
Trump has launched several rounds of trade tariffs against other countries and economies during his second term in office, with his administration citing various laws and justifications for the policies each time.
In April 2025, Trump imposed a sweeping raft of import taxes against almost all US trade partners, known as the “Liberation Day” tariffs. He said the measures were retaliation for unfair trade practices, including high tariffs, against the US that hurt local manufacturing. Trump imposed those tariffs under an emergency powers law, but the Supreme Court struck them down in February this year.
Then, in July, Washington cited a different law – section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 – to impose more tariffs on more than 80 countries. This time, Trump’s administration claimed the targeted countries had failed to adequately restrict imported goods made with forced labour.
The latest tariff announcement also cites section 301 of the same trade act, which allows Washington to penalise countries it determines are treating US businesses unfairly. It follows an eight-month investigation into what Washington calls “structural excess capacity”, by which governments give their industries unfair advantages with subsidies, suppressed wages and other policies.
Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners were using “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base”.
Inga Fechner, a senior economist at ING THINK, wrote that “while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind.”
Is this really about clinching better trade deals for the US?
For several targeted countries, that appears to be a big factor.
The tariff announcement comes as the US negotiates trade agreements with several of the targeted countries, including China, India, Vietnam and Singapore, with some of the proposed tariff rates explicitly linked to the outcome of those talks.
China’s tariffs are due to rise by 20 percent, respecting a cap under a current US-China trade truce. But if talks to secure a new trade deal fail by January 10, when that truce is due to expire, the rate could double to up to 40 percent, according to USTR.
Vietnam would also be subject to a capped tariff rate of 20 percent if it makes a trade deal with Washington, which it is actively negotiating. But if those negotiations fall through, its rate would jump to 35 percent.
India would face a 17 percent tariff rate if a trade agreement is reached with Washington, but a 25 percent rate if not.
Singapore faces a 10 percent tariff if it reaches a trade deal with the US, but a 20 percent rate if not.
Madeline Chalecki, assistant director at the Atlantic Council’s GeoEconomics Center, said the US is also exercising leverage over Mexico, which Trump recently said the US is close to concluding a trade deal with. Mexico was among the countries included in the USTR’s excess capacity investigation, but has not yet been hit with new tariffs.
“The threat of additional tariffs may be a better negotiating chip than the duties themselves,” the Atlantic Council quoted Chalecki as saying.
Mona Paulsen, an assistant professor at the London School of Economics and Political Science Law School, told Al Jazeera that beyond tariffs, the bigger worry regarding US trade negotiations is whether they are “from the beginning, an asymmetrical exercise more calibrated to US economic growth, and less one about two (or more) partners cooperating”.
How have targeted countries responded?
Some of the targeted countries or blocs have criticised the US’s new tariffs, while others have pledged to step up efforts to pursue trade deals with the US.
China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun accused the US of engaging in “political manipulation”, saying the “so-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false issue”. Commerce Ministry spokesman He Yadong called on the US to “correct its erroneous practices” and said Beijing reserves the right to “take necessary measures” in response.
Singapore also called on the US to reevaluate the policy, which it expressed disappointment over.
India said any trade concerns between it and the US should be resolved in ongoing trade negotiations.
Vietnam said it was working to conclude a trade pact with the US and promised to address the “overcapacity” issue and to improve forced labour regulations.
The EU’s trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, said he strongly opposed the US tariff move, adding that Washington must abide by the 15 percent tariff limit it has already agreed for goods imported from the bloc.
Why else might Trump be imposing new tariffs now?
Several analysts say Trump is trying to set up a long-term tariff infrastructure, despite the Supreme Court striking down his “Liberation Day” tariffs earlier this year.
Josh Lipsky, vice president and chair of international economics at the Atlantic Council, said the Trump administration’s latest announcement appears to be an attempt to set up a “tariff web – one meant to stick past this administration”.
Gregory Shaffer, professor of international law at the Georgetown University Law Center, told Al Jazeera that Trump is trying to “set tariffs globally” without having to deal with Congress.
US Senator Ron Wyden, a Democrat who is expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee in next year’s Congress, called the tariff move “a blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs”.
“Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution,” said Wyden.

noticias.titulo: Thanksgiving dinner costs rise, putting pressure on US households
noticias.resumen: Turkeys see a 26-percent price rise, forcing families to reconsider hosting and opt for potluck-style celebrations.
noticias.texto:
Thanksgiving dinner costs rise, putting pressure on US households
Turkeys see a 26-percent price rise, forcing families to reconsider hosting and opt for potluck-style celebrations.
Across the United States, kitchens will fill with the smell of roasting turkey as Americans gather to celebrate the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday.
Every family has its own traditions. Some swear by sweet potatoes topped with marshmallows. Others have carefully guarded family recipes for gravy, and there is always the perennial debate over pumpkin or pecan pie – and whether it should be served with a dollop of whipped cream or a scoop of ice cream.
But regardless of what makes it onto the Thanksgiving table this year, many Americans have something less appetising in common: a heftier grocery bill. The cost of a typical Thanksgiving meal is up 11 percent from last year, according to a new analysis by the think tank The Century Foundation.
Grocery prices jump
The prices of many typical side dishes are up by double-digit percentages. Green beans are up 36.7 percent in price for a 1.5-pound bag, from $2.99 to $4.08 in a year’s time. Russet potatoes are up 6.8 percent for a five-pound bag, and Granny Smith apples, which are typically used in apple pie, are up 10.2 percent for a three-pound bag.
The centrepiece of the Thanksgiving table, the turkey, is also up by 26 percent compared with this time last year.
“Thanksgiving is supposed to be about gathering around the table, but this year many families are deciding how many people they can afford to feed,” Kyle Moore, chief economist at The Century Foundation, said in a statement.
Measuring just by the number of guests, the American Farm Bureau forecasts a rise of 6 percent for a 10-person meal, marking the first increase in price since 2022, when prices hit a record high, according to the report.
Some grocers are doing what they can to keep prices lower for consumers, including Baris Avci, who runs Green Valley, a small neighbourhood grocery store in the Bushwick neighbourhood of Brooklyn, New York.
“Some very important things like eggs, milk, sugar, we sell almost at cost. We don’t make much money, but we also have a certain percentage to [sustain] the business. Like how the people struggle, we struggle too,” Avci told Al Jazeera.
Higher prices mean that some shoppers are having to rethink their traditions. Sam Braverman, who was shopping at Green Valley, told Al Jazeera that in past years, his mother hosted Thanksgiving and took care of all the costs, but given price increases, his family is taking a different approach.
“Well, my ma is more open to kind of a potluck vibe this year, of people sort of bringing a few things,” Braverman told Al Jazeera.
“To make that same meal is going to be 130-150 percent of what it was last year, so you might as well accept some offerings.”
Heightened costs can stem from bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has led to a rise in the cost of both fuel and fertiliser needed in the food production supply chain.
During the spring planting season, prices for urea, which is used in fertilisers, jumped by as much as 50 percent when the war began, meaning that farmers needed to pay more for fertiliser. Those costs were ultimately passed down along the supply chain from farmers to warehouses and then onto supermarket shelves.
Tariff-driven pressures have also led to heightened costs. For example, tariffs on steel used in cans have caused prices to increase on canned goods for consumers. In September, Campbell’s Soup said it would raise prices by 4 to 5 percent on 60 percent of its products.
Some big-box retailers like Walmart, however, are using their economies of scale to cut prices for consumers. Every year, the Bentonville, Arkansas-based chain offers a holiday meal package that consumers can buy, which includes a complete holiday meal for 10 people. It will cost shoppers 12 percent less than the same deal last year.
Financial strain
For those bearing the brunt of the costs, that means more people are finding ways to borrow or at least scale back. A third of Americans who are planning on hosting this year say that doing so is putting them under financial strain, according to a report from LendingTree, an online loan marketplace.
As a result, nearly 62 percent of hosts say they’re going to borrow money to host this year – 18 percent of whom say they’re using what are called buy now, pay later (BNPL) loans, which are deferred payment plans for expenses.
Usage has jumped significantly in recent years, with 16 percent of Americans using BNPL loans, which are offered by fintech companies like Affirm and Klarna, marking a six-percentage-point jump since 2021, according to an August report from the US Federal Reserve.
It found that those with lower credit scores and lower incomes, as well as younger people and both Black and Hispanic adults, are more likely to use these services than the general population.
Travel slump
There are slightly fewer people travelling for Thanksgiving this year, too. The American Automobile Association (AAA) forecasts that more than 81.6 million Americans will travel, marking a slight decline of 121,000 travellers, including those travelling by plane, car, bus and train. The decline marks a reversal of the trend, as the number of travellers climbed over the last three years.
“After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower, partly because of higher travel costs this year,” Stacey Barber, vice president of AAA Travel, said in a news release announcing the data.
Seven in 10 Americans are planning not to travel this holiday season at all, according to a report from the financial services company BNO, marking a 10-percent drop from this time last year.
While the average price for a gallon of petrol (3.78 litres) is down from last month – $3.61 on Tuesday versus $4.29 a month ago for regular fuel – it is still higher than this time last year, when it was $3.06, according to AAA’s daily fuel price tracker.
For those hitting the skies, domestic airfares rose 31 percent for Thanksgiving travel, averaging $402, according to a report released in September by the travel website Hopper, which tracks holiday travel trends, marking this Thanksgiving as the most expensive holiday travel season in a decade.

noticias.titulo: Palestine coach says team represents suffering but also offers hope
noticias.resumen: Despite navigating personal hardships, Ihab Abu Jazar calls it a 'badge of honour' to coach the Palestine football team.
noticias.texto:
Palestine coach says team represents suffering but also offers hope
Despite navigating personal hardships, Ihab Abu Jazar calls it a ‘badge of honour’ to coach the Palestine football team.
For Ihab Abu Jazar, being the coach of Palestine’s national football team comes with burdens far heavier than sporting responsibilities.
His mind constantly returns to his family in Gaza, now displaced and living in tents amid Israel’s genocidal war on the Palestinian territory.
“Truthfully, it is difficult to carry out your professional responsibilities while your family and your people are living through such circumstances,” he told Al Jazeera earlier this month while in Doha.
“For me to coach the Palestinian national team, a team that represents this suffering, and to try to make it a source of joy, bring a smile to people’s faces or give the Palestinian people hope, means a great deal to me personally.”
The 46-year-old former footballer said it was a “badge of honour” to coach the national team, which he led to 2027 AFC Asian Cup qualification after taking the reins in 2024.
The team were drawn in Group A against Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Oman, with the tournament rescheduled from January to December 2027 due to the ongoing conflict in the region.
Palestine have enjoyed considerable success in recent international friendlies, including a 2-2 draw with New Zealand, defeating Tajikistan 4-2, and thrashing China 5-0.
But the victories are bittersweet, given what’s happening at home.
He was in Algeria for a training camp with the national team when he received news that his house had been destroyed. His entire family now lives in al-Mawasi, a coastal area where more than 900,000 displaced people are sheltering in southern Gaza.
“The Palestinian people are suffering wherever they are,” Abu Jazar said.
He recounted an ordeal he went through before a qualifying match against Kuwait. Israel had issued a forced evacuation order for the area where his family lived, but his brother, Khalil, refused to leave.
“He had reached a point where he was simply saying, ‘Where am I supposed to go? Where can I possibly go?’” Abu Jazar recalled.
He made a last-ditch attempt to convince his brother to flee before boarding the team bus headed to the stadium for the match.
“I kept trying to call, but I could not get through. At that point, I had to trust that, God willing, my brother had listened to what I told him,” Abu Jazar said.
“We also had a match to play in the name of Palestine. We had to concentrate and do our job.”
Abu Jazar was able to breathe a sigh of relief after the match when he eventually got through to his brother, who assured him that they had all managed to leave safely.
A passion for sport is shared throughout Abu Jazar’s family. His mother, Huda, played volleyball at school and even offers her son tactical advice over the phone.
“Sometimes we talk about football and sports; she evaluates the players and discusses their performances after a match,” he said. “To be honest, she understands football very well in general.”
Abu Jazar’s message to the world is: “We are a people who simply want to live. We are a people with ambitions and hopes, a people with creative minds, thinkers, and scientists.
“And sport is also part of the culture and identity of any society. We, too, are sporting people; we are football-loving people.
“So, we ask the whole world to grant us our rights.”

noticias.titulo: Kenya gov’t violated constitution with Ebola quarantine site, court says
noticias.resumen: Kenya's High Court orders halt to ⁠further works at quarantine facility until details of deal with US are disclosed.
noticias.texto:
Kenya gov’t violated constitution with Ebola quarantine site, court says
Kenya’s High Court orders a halt to further works at the quarantine facility until the government discloses details of agreement with the US.
A court in Kenya has ruled that the government breached the constitution in allowing the construction of a United States-backed Ebola quarantine facility at a military airbase in the country.
High Court Judge Patricia Nyaundi said on Thursday that the government should have disclosed the details of the agreement with the US and sought public input before signing the deal on the facility near the town of Nanyuki in central Kenya.
The court ordered that any further works at the quarantine facility be stopped until the government meets these conditions.
“Put differently, the petitioners, the people of Kenya and more significantly, the residents of Laikipia County have been left with the position of persons standing outside the sealed wooden window, straining to discern what is taking place on the other side,” Nyaundi said in her ruling.
“They are aware that the decisions affecting their community are being made and implemented, yet they have been denied any meaningful opportunity to know, interrogate or participate in those decisions.”
The 50-bed facility, located inside Laikipia airbase near Nanyuki, was intended to quarantine people exposed to Ebola, including US citizens. Seven American aid workers who had been ‌in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to help tackle the Ebola outbreak quarantined at the facility in July.
Kenyans have staged angry protests against the facility, as residents accuse the US of offloading Ebola risks onto Kenyans. In June, at least one person was killed after Kenyan police opened fire at demonstrators protesting against the facility.
The week before, hundreds took to the streets in Nanyuki amid growing frustration among residents as Kenyan and US authorities publicly reaffirmed their commitment to the plan despite court orders. At the time, the demonstration also turned violent, with at least two people killed and one wounded.
Kenya’s High Court had temporarily suspended the facility’s construction in late May, but it found that Health Minister Aden Duale failed to comply with the orders. Duale later told the court he had ordered an immediate halt to construction and related activity at the site.
Kenya reported its first imported case of the Bundibugyo Ebola ‌strain in early October in a traveller who had arrived from the DRC via Uganda. As of mid-November, Kenya had recorded two deaths and seven other cases, all of whom have recovered. No new cases ‌have been reported in Kenya since October 19.
There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo strain responsible for the outbreak, which the World Health Organization declared an international public health emergency on May 17.
The government has not yet commented on Thursday’s court ruling.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine drone attack kills five in Russian-occupied Zaporizhia
noticias.resumen: Russian forces launch ballistic missile attack on Ukrainian capital Kyiv, hitting a shopping centre and other buildings.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine drone attack kills five in Russian-occupied Zaporizhia
Russian forces launch ballistic missile attack on Ukrainian capital Kyiv, hitting a shopping centre and other buildings.
At least five people have been killed and three others were wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russian-occupied Zaporizhia, a Russian-installed official said, as Russian forces hit Ukraine’s capital Kyiv in a ballistic missile assault.
“Following an enemy drone attack on a parking lot, five people were killed and three others wounded in the locality of Vesioloye,” Moscow-installed governor Yevgeny Balitsky wrote on Telegram on Thursday.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces hit a major Russian military base east of Moscow, damaging five aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Russian authorities also reported repelling drone attacks in the Tuymazinsky district in the Bashkortostan region and in the city of Nevinnomyssk in the Stavropol region.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and fighting has continued despite a renewed US-backed push to end Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.
Russia has claimed the annexation of the southern region of Zaporizhia, which it partially controls, since September 2022.
The Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, was targeted with ballistic missiles late on Wednesday, striking a shopping centre and two other buildings on the east side of the Dnipro River bisecting the city, with warnings for residents to remain in shelters still in place, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Thursday its forces had carried out a massive overnight strike on Ukraine, hitting military-industrial facilities in Kyiv, the Interfax news agency reported.
The Defence Ministry also said Russian forces had struck a dry cargo vessel southeast of Odesa in the Black Sea overnight, according to the news agency. The ministry alleged the ship was carrying military equipment and dual-use goods to Ukraine.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said the residents heard loud ballistic missile impact sounds late on Wednesday, which injured at least seven people.
“People who live in certain areas of the city that come under frequent attack, they go and spend their nights in the shelter, even before air raid sirens raise alarm,” she said. “Coming into this winter, Russia has really heightened its attacks, especially on energy facilities.”
Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said Russia “is putting pressure on Kyiv’s military infrastructure, straining its air defences, and everything that can support military supply chains”.
“Russia has also been hitting power plants ahead of cold weather. The aim is to wear down morale and inflict economic damage, in addition to all these military effects,” she added.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, MacAlpine said Ukraine’s energy capacity is below 40 percent of pre-war levels, as a number of the combined heating and power plants in Kyiv and the region have repeatedly gone offline due to attacks.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte urged Russia not to “expand the war” in Ukraine, in a joint statement issued on Wednesday after meeting in Florida.
“We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible,” the statement added.
The joint appeal by Trump and Rutte comes after the US leader described Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” during a meeting in China last week.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has taken issue with Trump’s comments on Putin.
“For us, he is a killer,” Zelenskyy told CNN.

noticias.titulo: Is authoritarian Vietnam ready to phase out the death penalty?
noticias.resumen: Vietnam has voted to abolish the death penalty for six more crimes, continuing a decades-long trend of restricting capital punishment.
noticias.texto:
Is authoritarian Vietnam ready to phase out the death penalty?
November 26, 2026
Vietnam, a country once considered one of the world's most prolific executioners, is steadily reducing the number of crimes punishable by death.
On November 20, the country's National Assembly approved a revised Penal Code that abolishes capital punishment for six offenses, including drug trafficking, rape of a person under the age of 16 and crimes against humanity.
When the legislation takes effect next March, just four offences — treason, murder, terrorism and illegal drug production — will remain punishable by death, down from 44 in 1997.
Although Hanoi has given little indication that it intends to do away with capital punishment entirely, few countries that still regularly execute prisoners have narrowed its legal application so considerably.
Authoritarian Vietnam's crime reforms
The reforms are particularly striking given that they come as Vietnam's ruling Communist Party has intensified its crackdown on political dissent and independent civil society.
Minister of Public Security General Luong Tam Quang said the changes reflect humanitarian considerations, the need for more proportionate sentencing and Vietnam's international integration, while maintaining a tough approach to crime, according to the state-run Vietnam News Agency.
Vietnam's gradual reduction in the number of offenses punishable by death reflects an evolution in its criminal justice philosophy, said Tran Dai Lam, a lawyer at the ANVI law firm in Hanoi.
"There is a growing recognition that the effectiveness of criminal law depends not necessarily on the severity of punishment, but on the certainty that criminal offenses are detected, prosecuted and punished," he told DW.
Moving towards abolishing the death penalty?
Vietnam's latest reforms come barely a year after the National Assembly abolished the death penalty for eight other offences, including embezzlement, bribery, espionage and the illegal transportation of drugs.
The removal of capital punishment for drug trafficking is particularly significant given the prominence of narcotics-related offences in Vietnam's criminal justice system and the country's proximity to the Golden Triangle, one of the world's largest illicit drug-producing regions.
The new legislation also provides for existing death sentences to be commuted to life imprisonment for offences that will no longer carry the death penalty.
Hai Luong, a lecturer in criminology at Griffith University in Australia, told DW that Vietnam has been taking a "retentionist-but-reductionist" approach.
"Vietnam is reforming the death penalty rather than abolishing it," he said. "The trend is towards a more limited and selective use of capital punishment, but not yet towards its complete removal."
According to Luong, the gradual reduction in capital offences reflects Hanoi's efforts to modernize its legal system without relinquishing its authority to severely punish what it considers the most serious crimes.
Vietnam's integration into international norms
Growing international recognition that capital punishment has little additional deterrent effect is also informing Vietnam's approach, he explained.
Decades of harsh penalties for drug-related offences have done little to stem the international narcotics trade, while the continued expansion of drug trafficking networks in Southeast Asia has raised questions about the effectiveness of executions as a crime prevention measure.
Vietnam's growing integration into the international community, including its participation in international drug control conventions and closer diplomatic ties with Western countries, has also given Hanoi greater incentives to align its criminal justice system with international standards, Luong added.
Vietnam's gradual retreat from capital punishment could also bring it closer to the European Union on human rights.
Brussels has repeatedly called on Hanoi to abolish capital punishment, a subject regularly raised during bilateral human rights discussions.
The EU, one of the world's most vocal advocates of abolition, has long opposed capital punishment as part of its foreign policy.
An EU spokesperson told DW that Brussels welcomes "Vietnam's latest reduction in crimes punishable by capital punishment. This is a positive step and shows a disposition to consider gradual reform, leading towards a moratorium first and finally to the abolition of the death penalty."
"Any concrete step towards this ultimate goal would be very much welcomed by the EU," they added.
However, Vietnam's reforms still fall short of international human rights standards, particularly since the death penalty remains available for drug-related offences that do not involve intentional killing.
Nor is there much evidence that progress on capital punishment is accompanied by improvements in other areas of Vietnam's human rights record, notably freedom of expression and association.
How often is the death penalty used in Vietnam?
It is also difficult to establish whether Vietnam's legislative reforms have resulted in fewer executions.
The authorities classify execution statistics as state secrets. Amnesty International believes Vietnam continues to make extensive use of capital punishment, but it cannot provide reliable annual figures.
Vietnam's capital punishment reform allows the state to continue executing people to fulfil its political and public security goals, "while also managing, or massaging, its international reputation through highly publicized 'reductionist' reforms," Daniel Pascoe, an associate professor of law at the City University of Hong Kong and an expert on capital punishment, told DW
For example, he added, although the recent abolition of the death penalty for drug trafficking is welcome, "it doesn't tell us whether the Vietnamese authorities will now simply charge a higher number of suspects with the drug production offence, which remains death-eligible."
Southeast Asia shifts away from capital punishment
Vietnam's reforms are part of a broader, if uneven, shift away from capital punishment in Southeast Asia.
Cambodia, the Philippines and Timor-Leste have abolished the death penalty altogether. Malaysia abolished mandatory death sentences in 2023, while Indonesia's new Penal Code, which took effect this year, allows for death sentences to be commuted under certain conditions following a 10-year probationary period.
However, Singapore has increased its use of capital punishment in recent years, particularly for drug-related offences, while Myanmar's military authorities resumed executions in 2022 after a hiatus of more than three decades.
Pascoe told DW that although the impact of Vietnam's reforms on execution numbers remains unclear, there is symbolic significance in one of Southeast Asia's most authoritarian governments visibly restricting the death penalty.
"If a one-party state like Vietnam can reduce the scope of capital punishment, why shouldn't Singapore,Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Laos, Brunei and Myanmar also do so?" Pascoe added.
The number of countries actively executing people is close to being at an all-time low, but those that are actively executing, such as Iran and Singapore, seem to be increasing their use, Sara Kowal, co-director of Eleos Justice, a research and advocacy initiative against the death penalty at Australia's Monash University, told DW.
"Vietnam's dramatic reduction of death-eligible offences is another really positive sign that the global trend towards abolishing the death penalty is continuing,” Kowal said.
"It would be great to see Vietnam take the next step to establish an official moratorium on all executions," she added.

noticias.titulo: Iranian drone attack kills 2 Italians in Kuwait
noticias.resumen: The Italians were employed as technicians for the Italian branch of German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall. One Kuwaiti and one Pakistani national were also injured in the attack.
noticias.texto:
Iranian drone attack kills 2 Italians in Kuwait
November 26, 2026
An Iranian drone strike on Kuwait left two Italians dead on Thursday, the Italian Foreign Ministry said.
What do we know so far?
The Italians were working for the Italian branch of German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall.
"An explosion caused by a drone attack... occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working," the statement from the Foreign Ministry said.
Kuwait's Defense Ministry said a Kuwaiti and Pakistani national were injured in the "criminal attack" on a "vital site" and taken to the hospital.
Meloni extends 'heartfelt condolences' to victims of families
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she learned of the "tragic" deaths of two Italian citizens in Kuwait during a European Council meeting.
"On behalf of myself and the government, I express my deepest sorrow and extend my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families," Meloni posted on X. "My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also said she was "saddened" by the news.
"We must step up pressure on Iran to put an end to these unacceptable attacks against its neighbors and our partners in the Gulf," von der Leyen said. "Today's events are yet another reminder that security in the Gulf is a matter of security for us all."
Kuwait, a US ally in the Middle East, has been frequently targeted by Iranian attacks since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran in February.

noticias.titulo: Africa: Opposition voices face growing pressure
noticias.resumen: Opposition politicians and government critics say arrests, prosecutions and restrictions on public activity are making it harder to challenge those in power. Is a broader pattern emerging?
noticias.texto:
Africa: Opposition voices face growing pressure
November 26, 2026
From Cameroon and Tanzania to Mozambique, Nigeria and Zambia, opposition leaders have accused authorities of limiting political freedoms through legal action and restrictions on public activity.
In each case, officials say the measures are justified under national laws and security provisions.
"Cameroon is very sensitive, and it is important that we know when to criticize the government and when not to criticize the government openly," said Ngam Glory Ani Mbom, a citizen of the Central African country.
She says fear of arrest and violence discourages political participation. "You cannot talk about democracy when opposition supporters cannot freely express their minds to the public," she told DW.
For Nda Grimbald, deputy secretary-general of Cameroon's opposition Social Democratic Front, one of the biggest obstacles is organizing public meetings.
"The first major challenge we face as members of the opposition is the non-authorization of public rallies, public meetings," he told DW, noting that opposition proposals receive little attention in parliament. "Private members' bills are not even listened to."
Cameroonian law guarantees freedom of assembly but allows authorities to restrict gatherings on grounds of public order or national security. Organizers are also required to notify officials in advance.
Tanzania: Trial and prison
In Tanzania, opposition leader Tundu Lissu was arrested in April 2025 and charged with treason. In November 2026, the High Court acquitted him of treason but convicted him of incitement and sentenced him to four years in prison.
Prosecutors argued that Tundu Lissu's remarks were intended to disrupt Tanzania's 2025 general election. In its ruling, the court said it was satisfied that his statements were intended to "disrupt elections and instigate violence."
Lissu rejected the verdict, calling the case "political persecution." He told the judges: "I was not charged with incitement but you judges are convicting me with it just to impress the person who gives you the titles." He added: "Excuses were created to imprison me."
Gerson Msigwa, Tanzania's chief government spokesperson, directly rejected allegations of political repression and human rights violations.
"Concerns of diminishing civic space and restrictions on political parties to engage in political processes in the lead up to the general election are unfounded and misleading," Msigwa said in response to Amnesty International's accusations of a "wave of terror" sweeping Tanzania ahead of the 2025 vote.
Mozambique: Charges disputed
In Mozambique, opposition figure Venancio Mondlane faces five charges linked to protests after the disputed 2024 election, including incitement to terrorism and public advocacy of crime. Prosecutors accuse him of encouraging violence and civil disobedience. Mondlane denies the allegations.
"I have more than enough evidence. There's plenty to go around. Many of my statements were precisely in the opposite direction," he told DW, adding that the protests were intended to prevent violence.
Pedro Sinai Nhatitima, a judge counselor and spokesperson for Mozambique's Supreme Court, defended the court's decision not to allow live broadcasts of Mondlane's trial. He denied that the proceedings are politically influenced, saying the court will decide the case according to the law.
Nigeria: Policing dissent?
In Nigeria, police in Borno State arrested five men wearing T-shirts bearing the slogan "Tinubu Must Go!" The police say the men were not arrested for their political views, but were found with suspected drugs and other items and face allegations including public disturbance and thuggery.
In Kano, police blocked access to a venue for a planned meeting, citing public safety concerns.
Zambia: Courts and controversy
In Zambia, opposition leader Brian Mundubile has criticized what he describes as a retreat from democratic rights. The courts were closed on August 24, the final day for filing a presidential election petition. The judiciary cited security reasons, while police said intelligence-led security assessments were under way at several government institutions.
State House presidential aide Clayson Hamasaka denied that President Hakainde Hichilema had ordered the closure to prevent an election challenge.
The same month, former opposition lawmaker and cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot dead during a security operation at Mundubile's residence. Authorities said the operation followed intelligence about individuals considered a national security threat, and that officers came under gunfire and returned fire.
Mundubile, who faces treason and sedition charges with other opposition figures, has called for fairness in the proceedings. "We expect an open court process. We are innocent of all the charges against us," he said.
Zambian constitutional lawyer Linda Kasonde has warned: "As you can see, our public institutions are on trial. Democracy in Zambia is on trial."
Cameroonian political analyst Kenang Derek Fay says that despite the setbacks, democratic development across the continent remains a work in progress.
"We are far from getting to the best level," he said. "It is a democracy still struggling to find its way."
DW correspondent Moki Edwin Kindzeka contributed reporting.

noticias.titulo: Freigang banned — Germany star to miss 2027 World Cup
noticias.resumen: Germany forward Laura Freigang has been suspended until October 2027 after missing three doping tests, ruling her out of next year's Women's World Cup in Brazil. Freigang denies any intention to evade controls.
noticias.texto:
Freigang banned — Germany star to miss 2027 World Cup
November 26, 2026
Laura Freigang is set to miss next year's women's World Cup in Brazil after being suspended for missing doping tests, the German Football Association (DFB) said in a statement on Thursday.
Freigang, who has played 45 matches for Germany and scored 17 goals, will be suspended until October 7, 2027 after reaching a settlement with the DFB, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and Germany's National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA). The suspension is for the next 16-months as it began retroactively on June 8, 2026, when she was notified by the DFB, and prohibts Freigang from playing for club or country.
"It's important to me to emphasize once again that I was never suspected of doping," Freigang said in a statement on Instagram.
"My agreement to a settlement does not mean that I share all the assessments of my case. The past few months have been extremely difficult for me. Another legal process would have entailed significant financial, mental, and emotional strain. This is why I decided to take this path, in the hope of finding some peace, clarity and perspective for myself," she added.
"It was never my intention to let it get this far. Sports have defined my life since I was little. It breaks my heart that, for now, I won't be able to step onto the field, help my team, or live the daily life that I love so much."
End of an ongoing process for Freigang
This brings to a close a case that has been ongoing for months. The 28-year-old had been accused of not being where she said she would be for a doping control on three occasions between March 2025 and February 2026.
In June of this year, Freigang explained missing the tests "were not deliberately avoided appointments but inconsistencies or misunderstandings in the comprehensive details that have to be updated daily and which we as national team players have to update in the system on a daily and hourly basis."
The ban ends her World Cup hopes, something the DFB has also acknowledged.
"We are simply so sorry for Laura on a personal level because of this situation. The past few weeks have been very stressful for her," said DFB Sporting Director Nia Künzer. "We hold her in high regard both as a player and as a person, and — as we have done in recent weeks — we will continue to stay in touch with her and support her as best we can."
The situation also puts her future at her club, Eintracht Frankfurt, into question. Freigang's contract runs until June next year.
"The agreement that has now been reached provides clarity and planning certainty through a process that is unique to Eintracht Frankfurt — for us as a club, but above all for Laura," Katharina Kiel, Frankfurt's director of women's football, said.
The club and Freigang, who has played 180 Bundesliga games in her career, are now set to enter talks to determine the shape of her contract moving forward.

noticias.titulo: FIFA says a cyberattack against it targeted a 'limited set of personal and business information'
noticias.resumen: World football's governing body says the cyberattack targeted personal and business information. They struck at a sensitive time for the under-fire organization and its president, Gianni Infantino.
noticias.texto:
FIFA says cyberattack against it accessed a 'limited' set of data
November 26, 2026
FIFA told news agencies on Thursday that it had been targeted by a person or group seeking access to its data.
"FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorized access to a limited set of personal and business information," a FIFA spokesperson told the Reuters news agency, issuing similar comments to other outlets.
Reuters cited a person "with direct knowledge of the matter" as saying that less than 0.1% of FIFA's total data had been compromised.
This person also said that no files from the controversial, abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project that looked to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors had been accessed.
What else did FIFA say about the cyberattack?
FIFA said that it was working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement, in the aftermath of the event.
It did not say when the attack took place, list the precise nature of the compromised data or specify how unauthorized access to FIFA data had been sought, amid reports of people having posed as FIFA officials rather than actually hacking the organization or otherwise compromising its cybersecurity systems.
"FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data," the Zurich-based organization said. "Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned."
Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot of what it said were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the cyberattack when responding to a post saying that more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been posted.
FIFA did not explicitly state whether it was talking about the same supposed incident.
The breach comes at a sensitive time for the organization. Still reeling from the scandalfollowing this summer's World Cup of its now-aborted plans to sell off World Cup commercial rights shares, it's now trying to secure another term for its embattled president, Gianni Infantino.
Infantino is the favorite for an election on March 18, when he is expected toface challenges from Kohzo Tashima of Japan and Philippe Diallo of France. But until the turbulence of the last six months, it seemed most likely he would simply stand unopposed and extend his 11-year tenure without a fight.

noticias.titulo: EU-Indonesia trade deal opens new markets, but challenges remain
noticias.resumen: The agreement offers new export and investment opportunities for Jakarta and Brussels. But can Indonesia turn Europe's growing interest in its markets and critical minerals into sustainable gains at home?
noticias.texto:
EU-Indonesia trade deal opens new markets, but challenges remain
November 26, 2026
As the European Union seeks to deepen its presence in Asia and diversify its trade relationships, Indonesia is emerging as an increasingly important partner.
At a signing ceremony in Brussels last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the bloc's trade agreement with Jakarta as one of its "most ambitious deals" in the region, linking markets of 730 million people.
The deal, the culmination of nearly a decade of negotiations, reflects the EU's efforts to diversify its trade partnerships, secure access to critical raw materials and reduce strategic dependencies on China.
For Indonesia, it offers opportunities to attract investment, expand exports and strengthen its position in global supply chains.
The agreement will gradually scrap tariffs on more than 98% of product categories, covering almost the entire value of bilateral trade over 15 years.
Indonesia's strategic importance to Europe
For the EU, gaining better access to critical raw materials, particularly nickel, and diversifying its supply chains are central to its strategic partnership with Indonesia, said Philip Schleifer, an associate professor of political science at the University of Amsterdam.
"The main strategic interests are opening up a large and growing market for European companies, diversifying and deepening its economic partnerships, reducing strategic dependencies on China, and securing access to critical raw materials," Schleifer told DW.
Indonesia's mineral resources are particularly important for Europe's green and digital transitions. Nickel, for instance, is a key material for batteries and electric vehicles.
The agreement also creates opportunities for European investment in strategic sectors, including electric vehicles, electronics and pharmaceuticals.
But Indonesia has its own industrial ambitions. The government wants to move beyond exporting raw materials by developing domestic processing industries and retaining more value from its natural resources.
"The challenge for the EU is to reconcile its own interest in securing raw material supply with Indonesia's industrial development objectives," said Eline Blot, a senior policy analyst at the Institute for European Environmental Policy (IEEP).
Export opportunities and challenges for Indonesia
Yose Rizal Damuri, an economist at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said his institution's study estimates Indonesian exports could increase by around 60% in the coming years.
"Not only can Indonesia increase exports to Europe, but it can also become more strongly integrated into the global supply chains of European companies," Yose told DW.
Potential beneficiaries include labor-intensive manufacturing sectors such as textiles, garments, footwear and furniture, alongside other Indonesian commodities and manufactured products.
The agreement could also encourage European investment and create employment opportunities. However, Yose stressed that access to the European market does not automatically translate into higher exports.
He identified three priorities for Indonesia: raising awareness of the agreement among domestic businesses, strengthening production capacity and improving the country's business climate.
"Various trade agreements signed by Indonesia have relatively low utilization rates. The value of exports using these facilities remains limited compared with overall export values," he said, emphasizing the need for better information and outreach to producers.
Syafruddin Karimi, an economist at Andalas University, also highlighted the opportunity to diversify Indonesia's export markets and reduce dependence on major trading partners such as China, the United States and regional Asian economies.
However, he warned that Indonesian producers must improve their compliance with European standards.
"Products must be traceable, including whether their production involves environmental damage or labor practices that undermine human dignity," Karimi said.
Environmental costs of economic integration
The expansion of trade and investment could also increase environmental pressures, particularly in nickel mining, palm oil production and manufacturing.
IEEP analyst Blot warned that increased production without stronger environmental safeguards could worsen pollution, ecosystem degradation and industrial emissions. "Nickel mining and processing can contribute to pollution and ecosystem degradation, while palm oil remains closely associated with deforestation," she said.
The EU's Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) presents another challenge for Indonesian producers, particularly small-scale farmers who may lack the resources, technical capacity and documentation needed to demonstrate compliance.
Blot acknowledged that these requirements could create disproportionate costs for smaller producers and potentially favor larger companies.
However, she cautioned against using smallholders' livelihoods as an argument to weaken environmental regulations.
"Rather than weakening environmental requirements, the priority should be to ensure that smallholders receive adequate financial and technical support to meet them," she said.
Professor Schleifer at the University of Amsterdam also warned that growing global demand for Indonesian natural resources could create environmental and social problems previously associated with commodities such as timber, palm oil and coal.
While Indonesia has considerable bargaining power because of its mineral wealth, the challenge is ensuring that increased demand translates into domestic industrial development rather than simply expanding resource extraction.
Can Indonesia turn market access into sustainable growth?
The agreement includes a dedicated Trade and Sustainable Development chapter covering climate change, biodiversity conservation, sustainable forest management and labor rights. It also provides mechanisms for cooperation and civil society participation.
However, there is no guarantee these commitments will be implemented. "Experience with other EU trade agreements suggests that there is often a big gap between sustainability commitments on paper and outcomes on the ground," Schleifer said.
For Indonesia, the challenge also lies in preparing domestic industries to compete. Karimi stressed that the government, both at national and regional levels, must work with businesses to improve production standards, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises.
Yose also emphasized the importance of a predictable business environment, warning that frequent policy changes and regulatory uncertainty could discourage investors.
"Without improvements in the domestic business climate, this will not become a reality. Everything will remain good on paper but will not turn into real momentum for change," he said.
Ultimately, the trade agreement offers Indonesia an opportunity to strengthen its position in international trade and attract investment from Europe.
But whether the agreement delivers broader economic benefits will depend on the country's ability to develop competitive industries, move into higher-value production, and ensure that environmental protection and workers' rights are not overlooked.
DW's Muhammad Athif Aiman contributed to this article.

noticias.titulo: Joshua Kimmich critcizes Bayern bosses over Musiala health comments
noticias.resumen: Joshua Kimmich has slammed Bayern Munich's leadership over comments about Jamal Musiala's health issues. The bosses have questioned whether the player can return to previous form – and is still worth his high salary.
noticias.texto:
Kimmich critcizes Bayern bosses over Musiala health comments
November 26, 2026
Bayern Munich's disappointing 2-1 Champions League defeat at Lille on Wednesday night – in which Jamal Musiala came on for the last quarter of an hour – was overshadowed by comments the club's captain made afterwards.
"It must never happen that something like this is played out at a player's expense. Of course, the club always comes first and is bigger than the player, but it's not bigger than the person," Kimmich told reporters in the mixed zone.
"That's an absolute no-go and not Bayern-like," he added.
Kimmich was responding to recent comments made by Bayern supervisory board members Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge.
"If he (Musiala) doesn't return to being the Jamal of old, then we need to have a conversation with his family, with the player, and, above all, with his agency – because, frankly, the current financial figures would no longer be justifiable," Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told Sky on Friday.
Honorary President Uli Hoeness has described the situation as a "dilemma" for the club, while CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen raised the prospect of talks with Musiala's management and family.
Neurological condition
While theGermany player has struggled with a number of injuries over the past couple of seasons, his health came into sharper focus in August, after he collapsed on the pitch in a couple of preseason matches. He subsequently revealed that he had been diagnosed with a neurological condition which causes him to suffer from occasional "absence seizures."
Kimmich added that criticism of a players' performances was legitimate, but that concerns about Musiala's situation should have been dealt with behind closed doors.
"That's something you should sort out internally, around a table, rather than trying to resolve it publicly," he said.
"It's not that he has problems because he's unprofessional. He's there every day trying to get the maximum out of himself."
Talks between two sides ongoing
Meanwhile, Bayern bosses met with Musiala's agents on Tuesday, and clarified the timeline of events, dismissing speculation that the player could have concealed the condition when he signed his last contract extension.
Bayern said the two sides agreed that he was first examined for seizure symptoms in April 2025, two months after he had signed his contract extension, which makes him one of the club's top earners and is to keep him in Munich until 2030. Discussions between Bayern management and Musiala's representatives are reportedly ongoing.

noticias.titulo: Crew member dies after diesel tanker sinks off Ibiza coast
noticias.resumen: Authorities rescued 17 crew members but one later died in hospital after a diesel tanker sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza. A contingency plan against possible pollution damage is now in place.
noticias.texto:
Crew member dies after diesel tanker sinks off Ibiza coast
November 26, 2026
A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities said on Thursday.
The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, said in a statement.
According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue vessel.
The chemical tanker was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona when it sank about 30 nautical miles (56 kilometers) off Ibiza's northwestern coast.
The nationalities of the crew or the cause of the sinking was not immediately clear.
Authorities monitor pollution risk
The Transport Ministry said the maritime rescue vessel Guardamar Talia had reported no wreckage, floating debris or signs of pollution at the site as of Thursday morning. It added that another rescue ship was heading to the area to continue monitoring the situation.
Spain's maritime rescue service deployed an aircraft and the Clara Campoamor, a vessel equipped to respond to oil spills, to inspect the area.
Spain's merchant marine authority has activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest.
The Balearic regional government said it was assessing the incident and its potential impact, including the risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.
The importance of Ibiza for biodiversity
The waters surrounding Ibiza are a critical zone for biodiversity as they host sea turtles, dolphins and the ‌Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds.
The area also hosts vast Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, which are essential for maintaining marine biodiversity.
Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the area affected was "particularly vulnerable."
But he said the Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood."
"It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment," he said.
Spain's worst maritime environmental disaster happened in 2022, when the tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region. It spilled tens of thousands of heavy fuel oil and polluted beaches across Spain and France.

noticias.titulo: What is the US permitting bill and would it actually help the climate?
noticias.resumen: Sweeping US legislation to speed up energy projects has found rare bipartisan support. Supporters say it would unlock clean energy and lower energy bills, but critics say it's a gift to fossil fuels.
noticias.texto:
Could the US energy permitting bill cut emissions and costs?
November 26, 2026
