noticias.titulo: Powerful storms disrupt holiday travel, as Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed
noticias.resumen: Extreme weather that has unleashed strong winds, high tides, heavy rain and floods is expected to impact travel plans of an estimated 81.5 million people as they travel across the United States.
noticias.texto:
Powerful storms disrupt holiday travel, as Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed
Tens of millions of people are bracing for delays at airports and highways across the country on Thursday, as powerful storms across the United States threatened to disrupt travel for the Thanksgiving holiday.
On the West Coast, high tides have flooded streets along California's shorelines and knocked off a part of Pacifica Pier. The floods have also prompted evacuation warnings. On the East Coast, authorities are preparing to weather the impact of a storm making its way up into New England from the southeast with strong winds and heavy rain. Snow was also forecast in parts of the Midwest.
Some 81.5 million people in the U.S. are expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA.
Hundreds of flights had already been cancelled or delayed by early morning Thursday, particularly on the East Coast, where authorities have warned people to stay home as the storm barrels through. The majority of people are expected to travel by car for the holidays, and the winter weather could affect their plans due to visibility issues on the road.
Richard Bann, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center, told NPR that the East Coast storm remained the main concern, calling it a "multi-hazard" storm.
"It's going to be getting better organized as we go through the day, and it'll be spreading a considerable amount of wind, heavy rain. The real concern with this thing is going to be coastal flooding," Bann said.
Meteorologist Matthew Cappucci with The Washington Post and MyRadar told NPR the storm's magnitude at this time of the year was "unusual."
"We would expect this in deep winter," Cappucci said.
The storm in the East Coast, however, is expected to mostly clear out by Saturday, easing weekend travel for those returning from Thanksgiving gatherings.
Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City delayed
Beyond travel, several Thanksgiving parades have also been affected by severe weather.
The incoming storm is expected to cause high winds in New York City, prompting Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Wednesday to delay the city's famous Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade. Organizers were already inflating the iconic giant balloons for the parade on Wednesday when officials announced the decision.
The parade, which is now expected to take place on Saturday, will be the city's 100th, and while it was cancelled before during World War II, this is the first time that it's been postponed in the last century.
The parade's organizers said it took two years to prepare the elaborate celebration, which includes over 11,000 participants and volunteers, thousands of high school marching band musicians from across the country and hundreds of balloon handlers. In previous years, up to 2 million spectators have attended the parade.
"Safety is and will always remain our top priority, and this will be a heavy storm," Mamdani told reporters.
He urged the city's residents to prepare for extreme weather conditions. He said the city expected sustained winds between 30 and 40 mph and possible gusts as high as 65 mph, with resulting floods and flash floods.
"Generation after generation has watched Spongebob and Spiderman soar down our streets and has taken in Garfield floating down 6th Avenue. And I know this change of plans will cause inconveniences," Mamdani said. "Yet safety has to come first."
Philadelphia also grounded all balloons for its parade this year due to winds.
Steve Kastenbaum contributed reporting for this story.

noticias.titulo: Anthropic chief denies wanting humans to 'surrender' free will to AI
noticias.resumen: Dario Amodei's comments come amid a growing debate over how to maintain human autonomy in the face of superintelligent AI systems.
noticias.texto:
Dario Amodei's comments come amid a growing debate over how to maintain human autonomy in the face of superintelligent AI systems.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Wednesday denied wanting humanity to cede its free will to artificial intelligence, amid recent veiled criticism from fellow tech executives.
Several rival AI leaders, including from Meta, have highlighted the importance of defending human agency as AI evolves. Amodei’s comments followed an Axios report this week that suggested Anthropic’s leadership takes the view that humanity should “surrender” some decision-making power to superintelligent AI systems.
"No, I do not believe that we should 'surrender human free will' to AI systems, and it's absurd to suggest that I do," Amodei wrote in a lengthy post on X. "We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security," he added.
The debate over human agency comes after Anthropic said last week that its Claude AI model had helped solve what’s widely thought to be the “biggest maths problem of all time”.
The news prompted Meta’s top AI executive, Alexandr Wang, to warn on X on Sunday that the mathematical achievement marked “the beginning of a significant change” in how humans interact with the technology. He added: "We should not be okay with a 'handover' of society to AI.”
Fears that AI tools could slip out of human control have haunted Silicon Valley since a string of incidents this summer, including the hacking of Hugging Face by autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI.
Anthropic’s Amodei has previously made comments suggesting humans should be willing to relinquish some autonomy to AI. In February, he told The New York Times that in "life-critical, safety-critical cases, we really want to turn it over" to AI. And in late 2024, he predicted that AI systems "will be the leaders, and they'll be ordering humans or other AI systems around."
Anthropic’s initial public offering last week was the largest on record, with the company’s value at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value, despite concern over an AI bubble and growing fears the technology threatens lives and livelihoods.

noticias.titulo: Iraq sentences eight French nationals to life for joining Islamic State
noticias.resumen: Two other French citizens have been sentenced to 15 years in prison, while the verdict has been postponed for 10 additional French nationals by the court.
noticias.texto:
Two other French citizens have been sentenced to 15 years in prison, while the verdict has been postponed for 10 additional French nationals by the court.
Eight French nationals who joined Islamic State (IS) have been sentenced to life imprisonment, while two others have received 15-year prison terms. The Iraqi judiciary has postponed the announcement of the verdict for ten other French citizens.
Romain Garnier, who worked on IS radio operations, is among the French nationals sentenced to life.
Adrien Guihal, also known as Abou Oussama al-Faransi, is one of the defendants whose sentence will be announced at a later date. This man in his forties, originally from the Paris region (Seine-Saint-Denis), lent his voice to the audio recording of the Nice attack in which 86 people were killed on 14 July, 2016.
The same applies to Thomas Collange, whose wife is serving a ten-year prison sentence in France, and to Quentin Le Brun, who appeared in an IS propaganda video; for both of them the Iraqi judiciary has postponed the announcement of the verdict.
During the trial, most of the defendants pleaded guilty and expressed remorse. Some had asked to be repatriated to France.
France has repatriated hundreds of relatives of jihadists, mainly women and children held in Syrian camps.
The sentencing of the ten French nationals comes as Iraq continues to prosecute thousands of people suspected of having joined IS.
The Islamist group seized vast territories in Iraq and Syria in 2014 and was responsible for massacres, also forcing women and young girls into sexual slavery.
Many European citizens travelled to take part in IS's "jihad".
Last year, 47 French nationals were transferred from Syria to Iraq to be tried there.
In that group, 15 French nationals had already been sentenced to life imprisonment and another to 15 years in detention.

noticias.titulo: From volume to value: making tourism work for more of Europe
noticias.resumen: Tourism deserves a central place in European policymaking, writes Peter Lochbihler of Booking.com in an opinion piece for Euronews. The EU should support lesser-known destinations in attracting visitors worldwide, fostering local revitalisation, growth and prosperity.
noticias.texto:
Tourism deserves a central place in European policymaking, writes Peter Lochbihler of Booking.com in an opinion piece for Euronews. The EU should support lesser-known destinations in attracting visitors worldwide, fostering local revitalisation, growth and prosperity.
It takes a village to raise a child, but sometimes it takes the world to save a village. The world of travellers, that is, with their spending power layered on top of curiosity to explore.
In the late 1980s, Anento, a medieval village tucked away in Spain’s Aragón region, was all but deserted. A group of determined locals and former residents began restoring abandoned houses, and tourism helped turn their labour of love into an economic lifeline. By 2024, Anento was welcoming some 45,000 tourists annually who dined at new restaurants, stayed at local accommodations, thus supporting employment and livelihoods for new residents.
Regional revitalisation, jobs and growth
Regional revitalisation, jobs and growth rooted in the place itself that can neither be outsourced nor shipped to some low-cost location: that is tourism’s promise. But there is a risk of “too much success”. A landmark goes viral on TikTok; a spectacular sunrise spot becomes too instagrammable to resist.
The EU Sustainable Tourism Strategy, announced in early November, articulates this tension in a crisp phrase: calling for a shift “from volume to value.”
“Value” looks different depending on where you stand. For travelers, it could mean finding the right holiday at a price a family can afford. For the owner of a small agriturismo, it might be enough off-season bookings to keep the team working throughout the year. For a mayor of a town like Anento, it means making sure tourism brings jobs and revenue while still serving the needs of local residents.
Hospitality: a unique, high-value-added product that Europe sells
The paradox of the visitor economy is that its Europe-wide impact is significant, yet it receives little priority in policy discourse. “A foundation of our economy” is how Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas described tourism, “it accounts for nearly 10% of the EU GDP (Editor's note: GDP (Gross Domestic Product) is the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders over a given period), supports more than 20 million jobs and sustains 5 million businesses, almost all SMEs or microenterprises” (Editor's note: SME means Small and Medium-sized Enterprises).
While the EU's GDP growth for 2026 is expected to hit 1.4%, the travel and tourism industry is moving more than twice as fast at 3.5%, as estimated by WTTC (Editor's note: WTTC is the World Travel & Tourism Council).
Even when its economic weight is recognised, hospitality is seldom recognised for what it is: a unique, high-value-added product that Europe sells to visitors. Intuitively, exports are pictured as goods, be they Belgian chocolates, Swiss watches, French aircraft, or lithography machines made by ASML in the Netherlands, destined for foreign markets.
Surely, there are no production lines, packaging or container ships for a travel experience. The flow moves the other way around: the customer crosses the border to consume a service, while a destination exports it.
Spain: foreign visitors spent almost €135 billion in 2025
In Spain, travel made up nearly half of all services exports in 2024. Consider, for example, a more traditional exporter, Germany, which shipped abroad €263 billion in motor vehicles and parts in 2024. This amounted to 6% of my home country’s GDP. In Spain, foreign visitors spent almost €135 billion in 2025, around 8% of GDP. These figures measure different things, goods exports in one case and visitor spending, or service exports, in the other, but I find this comparison instructive.
That said, export value generation emerges in the places that can connect with visitor demand far and wide. “Digitalisation, particularly the growth of online booking platforms, has improved the visibility and accessibility of rural tourism businesses, enabling them to reach wider markets,” noted the staff working document.
Partnerships between SMEs and large Companys
The Commission also calls for “partnerships between SMEs and large companies operating in the tourism ecosystem.” Independent properties, most of them small or micro businesses, can’t always match the marketing reach and digital capacity of major hotel groups. Online platforms help close that gap, connecting a family-run guesthouse with travellers worldwide while leaving the business rooted in local ownership and identity.
A particular way in which digital distribution matches supply with demand produces another surprising result. Research by Tourism Economics, we’ve commissioned, found that rural areas accounted for 16% of European accommodation bookings overall, compared with 38% of bookings made through online travel platforms.
The same channels can help hotels attract guests outside the peak season: in the 2026 European Accommodation Barometer, 81% of the 1,240 executives and managers surveyed rated online travel platforms very effective for securing off-season stays.
Tourism industry draws strength from diversity
The EU strategy places tourism firmly within Europe’s policy agenda: a range of topics spanning tech adoption, sustainability and talent. We strongly support its emphasis on upskilling.
As the sector grows and competition intensifies, hospitality can and should offer its people room to learn, build a career and take on greater responsibility. In our research conducted in partnership with Statista, 83% of hotel employees surveyed said they wanted to move into leadership roles. That ambition deserves more support from business and governments alike.
Our industry draws strength from diversity. In that spirit, the European Commission is right to set a continent-wide strategy and focus on principle and priorities rather than prescriptions. Destinations themselves are where experimentation and innovation will make the biggest difference.
Case studies show how policies can calibrated to local needs
Paris, Vienna and Copenhagen are exemplary case studies showing how policies, from transport to housing to waste management, can be calibrated to local needs. Decisions about zoning or transport infrastructure can determine whether visitors enrich residents’ lives or put more pressure on them.
Complementarity, along with a continuous exchange of ideas across institutions and geographies, is what success in policymaking will look like for a hyperlocalised industry like tourism.
A sector that contributes so much deserves a central place in European policymaking, including a dedicated EU budget line. Part of that support should help lesser-known destinations connect with visitors from the world over. Let us celebrate Anento’s success and empower more places across Europe to follow its example, creating their own paths to local revitalisation, growth and prosperity.

noticias.titulo: Nordic countries: A European gateway to space? | Euronews Tech Talks
noticias.resumen: The Arctic has become strategically important for Europe. But can the region play a central role in helping the EU reach its ambitions in space?
noticias.texto:
The Arctic has become strategically important for Europe. But can the region play a central role in helping the EU reach its ambitions in space?
On 20 October, the European Union presented its updated strategy for the Arctic, highlighting the region’s importance for the bloc’s security priorities.
“The Arctic is no longer insulated from the world’s geopolitical tensions,” Kaja Kallas, the EU’s foreign policy chief, said at a press conference. “Our updated Arctic strategy reflects this new reality by putting security firmly at its core,” she added.
The EU first codified its Arctic policy in 2008, which it later updated in 2021, principally to align with the environmental and climate ambitions of the European Green Deal.
At the time, Russia, a key Arctic player, had not yet launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. And Donald Trump had yet to threaten to annex resource-rich Greenland, before ultimately signing a security agreement with the semi-autonomous Danish territory in September.
The October update reflects these geopolitical shifts and refers to the Arctic as Europe’s “Northern Neighbourhood”, in a bid to stress its strategic importance. Among the topics covered in the document are the economy, defence, energy, the environment and, crucially, space.
But will this strategy change the role of the Nordics in space, or in Europe's overall access to space? In its latest episode, Euronews Tech Talks travels north to find out.
A gateway to space
The Arctic comprises eight countries, three of which are part of the EU (Denmark, Finland, and Sweden) and two of which are close partners of the bloc (Iceland and Norway).
These Nordic countries have played an important role in the space sector since the early days of the space race and are expected to become even more influential thanks to their two launch sites in Andøya, Norway, and Esrange, Sweden.
Andøya saw its first successful orbital launch in September, when a rocket from the German commercial company Isar Aerospace was sent into space, carrying five small satellites and a technology experiment. Esrange is planning its first orbital launch for 2028.
According to René Laufer, chair professor and head of space systems at Luleå University of Technology, Sweden, Esrange and Andøya will not replace Europe’s main spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana, but rather complement it.
“We will see a growth in launch capabilities and launch opportunities, and that means French Guiana will stay busy and additional sites need to get busy because otherwise we cannot address the demand of the market,” he said.
Europe lags behind the United States in the number of satellites it puts into orbit. Still, European governments and private companies are working to launch more, and this’s where the Norwegian and Swedish spaceports could come in hand.
Launching from Northern Europe provides access to polar and sun-synchronous orbits, and having ground stations so close to the North Pole makes it easier to collect data from the satellites.
The updated Arctic policy and space
The Nordic spaceports are also highlighted in the latest update to the EU's Arctic policy.
“What is new now in space, and I think what is also driving a bit of the momentum in northern Norway, at least when it comes to space, is Andøya spaceport, this very first spaceport on the European continent where you can, and already have successfully launched rockets,” said Andreas Raspotnik, director of the High North Centre for Business and Governance at Nord University in Bodø, Norway.
Moreover, according to its revised Arctic policy, the EU aims to procure additional satellites to extend secure connectivity to the Arctic. The bloc also plans to reinforce the EU Space Surveillance and Tracking system with sensors in the Arctic to protect space infrastructure. The EU is also looking to enhance its Earth observation programme for the Arctic and support the development of its spaceports.
“What has happened here with reframing the Arctic, or the European parts of the Arctic, as Europe's Northern Neighbourhood is hopefully a more strategic approach on how to conceptualise, but also on how to take actions in that space,” Raspotnik told Euronews Next.
However, despite the shift in the EU's approach to the Nordics, Raspotnik believes that the practical implications of the strategy remain unclear. “How that [policy] is then executed, how we'll also see or not see high-level interest in the Arctic after October 20th, that will have to be seen.”

noticias.titulo: French presidential candidate Raphaël Glucksmann to Euronews: 'France's vote will shape Europe's destiny'
noticias.resumen: France's future relationship with Europe has emerged as a central campaign issue ahead of elections in spring 2027, amid divisions over European integration, French sovereignty and support to Ukraine.
noticias.texto:
France's future relationship with Europe has emerged as a central campaign issue ahead of elections in spring 2027, amid divisions over European integration, French sovereignty and support to Ukraine.
Presidential candidate and MEP Raphaël Glucksmann told Euronews that France's vote would "shape the destiny of the entire European continent", five months ahead of major elections in spring 2027.
The centre-left hopeful, who leads the Place Publique party, warned that "the entire European project risks being lost if France falls into the anti-European camp", on the sidelines of a mayoral congress held in Paris on Wednesday.
France's future relationship with Europe is a major campaign issue, amid divisions over European integration, French sovereignty and support to Ukraine.
Referring to the trilateral summit held by Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump on 18 November, Glucksmann called out "three masters of the world who are trying to share it."
"The only obstacle in this sharing of the world is a powerful, independent and free Europe," he said.
The backdrop of a divided French left
Polls indicate that the far-right National Rally party's Marine Le Pen is currently heading the presidential race, followed by the hard-left France Unbowed party's Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Glucksmann, who supports a pro-European and social-democratic model is struggling to gain ground, polling around 8 to 11,5% — against the backdrop of a divided left-wing bloc and a broader fractured political landscape.
France's traditional left and right have faced difficulties marking their territory ever since French President Emmanuel Macron was elected on a centrist platform with his En Marche party in 2017.
Glucksmann's political opponents, including those within the hard-left France Unbowed party, portray him as a centre-left politician who offers insufficient political and economic change from Macron.
In an interview with French broadcaster BFMTV in early November, he responded to this criticism by stating "if I were in the slightest bit attracted to Macronism, I would have accepted all the offers made to me over the past ten years."
Divisions over Europe rife in campaign
The future of Europe's long-term budget (2028–2034) has also become tied up with France's upcoming elections. Macron reportedly urged EU leaders to reach an agreement by December, warning that he may withdraw from negotiations if no deal is reached by then.
A senior European diplomat acknowledged that the French election was the "primary concern" hanging over the talks. "The prospect of a potential Le Pen victory — and its consequences — is always in the back of everyone's mind," the diplomat said.
Although the National Rally and France Unbowed parties' positions remain underpinned by different ideological priorities, both parties back greater national sovereignty and challenge aspects of European integration.
Le Pen wants to strip powers from the EU and cap France’s net contribution to the bloc’s budget at €5 billion a year, declaring that "being pro-France does not mean being anti-Europe." Her party has also pledged to scrap a number of EU regulations and standards, particularly those tied to the business sector, agriculture, energy and environmental policy.
Meanwhile, Mélenchon's party backs scrapping rules and regulations that do not align with French interests, including those concerning the EU migration pact and European defence.
He has previously declared that France should "disobey anything coming from Europe that conflicts with the interests of the French people", adding that France should "amend the treaty that forms the basis of the European Union, because otherwise we will perish politically, socially, and industrially, since we are not in a position to resist."
His party has also called for a reduction in France's net contribution to the EU budget by around €9 billion, a proposal reiterated by the party's finance spokesman Eric Coquerel in October.
Questions loom over future Ukraine support
Raphaël Glucksmann advocates significantly strengthening France and Europe's military and financial support for Ukraine.
He proposes seizing approximately €210 billion in frozen Russian state assets to finance Ukrainian assistance, expanding European military cooperation and protecting parts of Kyiv's airspace against Russian missile and drone attacks.
On Ukraine, the National Rally has declared that it will not continue to provide financial assistance to Ukraine, instead pledging to honour "existing commitments", citing the European Union's €90 billion support loan, as well as "material donations, humanitarian aid, and more active diplomacy".
Le Pen has faced criticism over her past ties to Russia, which included a 2017 meeting in the Kremlin with President Vladimir Putin and her party taking a loan from a Russian bank which was paid off by 2023.
The France Unbowed party 2027 presidential programme does not specify a precise amount or annual budget commitment for future funding. It broadly backs supporting Ukraine, but has drawn a red line around delivering long-range missiles, the deployment of ground troops, and Ukraine’s accession to the European Union.
The party has however repeatedly been accused of ambiguities, for instance after Mélenchon declared that it was perhaps worth asking whether the escalation of the Russian threat in Europe was linked to "Ukraine’s deep-strike attacks."

noticias.titulo: Jordan Bardella denies fresh wave of antisemitism allegations
noticias.resumen: Bardella, who is vying to become France's next prime minister on a joint ticket with Marine Le Pen, faced allegations in September that he made conspiracist comments about Jewish people on Facebook in 2013.
noticias.texto:
Bardella, who is vying to become France's next prime minister on a joint ticket with Marine Le Pen, faced allegations in September that he made conspiracist comments about Jewish people on Facebook in 2013.
Jordan Bardella, leader of France's far-right National Rally (RN), is facing renewed scrutiny, after Le Monde and Mediapart published further revelations on Thursday regarding antisemitic messages he allegedly wrote as a teenager.
Bardella, who is vying to become France's next prime minister on a joint ticket with Marine Le Pen, already faced allegations in September about alleged conspiracist comments he made about Jewish people on Facebook in 2013.
He has consistently denied doing these reports, decrying the media's "persecution" campaign on Thursday. He has already filed two legal complaints against Mediapart.
Taking to X, he wrote "for over two months, several media outlets have been investigating my childhood and adolescence, during which time I was a minor, between the ages of 13 and 17. These reports have extensively quoted statements that I formally deny having made."
Thursday's revelations include antisemitic comments Bardella made in private Facebook conversations with a high school acquaintance in the year he turned 18.
At the time, Bardella, now the president of the National Rally, was a teenager and a member of its predecessor, the National Front. The party was founded by Jean-Marie Le Pen, Le Pen's father, who repeatedly made Holocaust-denying remarks and was convicted several times for hate speech before his death in 2025.
Mediapart said it had seen these comments when it broke the story in September but had not published further excerpts to protect the identity of the outlet's source.
The acquaintance then agreed to share the unpublished remarks to show Bardella was lying after he rejected the initial accusations, the investigative outlet and Le Monde said.
In these, he allegedly wrote "it is Zionists who head banks" and seek a "new world order with Jerusalem as capital".
They said elements in the conversations seemed to confirm Bardella as being their author, including comments about his teachers as well as other details about his parents, and a stint teaching French to foreigners that he mentioned in his 2024 autobiography.
In recent years, the National Rally has courted Jewish voters by positioning itself as a bulwark against Islamic extremism in France, as Le Pen has made huge efforts to dissociate herself from her father's legacy.
Bardella has been instrumental in this effort, visiting Israel in 2025 — the first such trip by a French far-right leader — to demonstrate the National Rally's new credentials.
Researchers and critics of the party have dubbed this the "de-demonisation" of the party, after Le Pen expelled her father from the National Front in 2015 and rebranded it in 2018.

noticias.titulo: Temu agrees to change commercial practices in EU, says Commission
noticias.resumen: The Chinese retailer had been found in breach of EU consumer rules for not doing enough to stop the sale of illegal and unsafe products on its website, which could have led to a fine of up to 6% of its global annual turnover. The company has now made commitments to follow EU consumer rules.
noticias.texto:
The Chinese retailer had been found in breach of EU consumer rules for not doing enough to stop the sale of illegal and unsafe products on its website, which could have led to a fine of up to 6% of its global annual turnover. The company has now made commitments to follow EU consumer rules.
Chinese-owned online marketplace Temu has agreed make several changes including tougher action to stop the sale of illegal and unsafe products on its platform, bringing it in line with EU consumer protection rules, the European Commission said on Thursday.
“Temu’s commitments are an important step towards ensuring consumers can shop online with confidence, knowing that prices are transparent, reviews are trustworthy and their rights to returns and refunds are respected,” Michael McGrath, the EU's commissioner for consumer protection, said in a statement.
He added that the Commission will "continue to closely monitor Temu's compliance".
It's the latest turn in the Commission’s investigation into Temu's practices, which was first launched October 2024 to assess whether the company was in compliance with EU regulations for very large online platforms (VLOPs) under its flagship Digital Services Act.
Thursday’s announcement signals that Temu was able to persuade the Commission that it's adequately taking steps to stamp out illegal trade on its marketplace and make meaningful changes to the way it runs its platform to comply with EU rules. Noncompliance could have seen the company face a fine of up to 6% of its global annual turnover.
“We're pleased to have reached a resolution with the European Commission and national consumer protection authorities,” a Temu spokesperson said, adding that the company would "continue to strengthen transparency and improve the shopping experience for consumers across Europe".
In May, the Commission slapped Temu with a €200 million fine after investigators found dangerous baby toys and faulty chargers widely available on its platform. Temu was then asked to present an action plan to address these issues and other DSA breaches.
As recently as early November, the Commission published preliminary findings from its investigation into Temu that showed the company had not made sufficient changes.\
Investigators cited several ongoing issues, including "ineffective controls to ensure safety standards", "weak content moderation" and an "ineffective sanction system".
Temu was given time to review the findings and decide how to proceed.
The Commission on Thursday said Temu had committed to making its company information more accessible, while providing better customer support; simpler withdrawals, returns and refunds; more reliable consumer reviews; clarity on pricing; an end to messages pressing customers to make purchases; a removal of forced gamification features; providing substantiated environmental claims; and a clearer check-out system.
Thursday’s announcement brings the Temu case at European level to a close, leaving it in the hands of national consumer protection authorities to monitor the company’s compliance with its commitments, which apply across the EU and the European Economic Area.
Should Temu fail to comply with the latest commitments, the company would be liable for fines of up 4% or more of its annual turnover in the relevant member states.

noticias.titulo: Eurozone leaders back Hernández de Cos to succeed Lagarde at ECB
noticias.resumen: Eurozone leaders meeting in Brussels backed Hernández de Cos to lead the European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the 21 countries that use the euro.
noticias.texto:
Eurozone leaders meeting in Brussels backed Hernández de Cos to lead the European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the 21 countries that use the euro.
A majority of eurozone countries have backed Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank (ECB), following a summit in Brussels on Thursday.
Hernández de Cos, 55, who heads the Bank for International Settlements, secured more support than former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot. If formally appointed, he would become the first Spaniard to lead the ECB since its creation in 1998.
He served as governor of the Bank of Spain from 2018 to 2024. Both Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo have backed his candidacy, marking Spain's first bid for the ECB presidency.
He is seen as a consensus candidate.
What could Hernández de Cos mean for interest rates?
The ECB has raised interest rates twice this year, while eurozone inflation reached 4% in October, twice the bank's 2% target.
Jefferies economist Modupe Adegbembo told Reuters that Hernández de Cos was considered slightly more dovish than Knot. However, she said a change in leadership alone was unlikely to alter the ECB's approach to interest rates.
MUFG economist Henry Cook described Hernández de Cos as a pragmatic centrist and expects him to broadly maintain Lagarde's approach.
MUFG forecasts a 0.25 percentage point rate rise in March, which would be Hernández de Cos's first interest rate-setting meeting as ECB president.
The Brussels discussions also covered two other vacancies on the ECB's Executive Board.
France's Laurence Boone is expected to take over responsibility for market operations from Isabel Schnabel, who is due to leave on 3 January 2027 to join the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Boone served as Europe minister under Emmanuel Macron.
Germany's Markus Brunnermeier is also in line to replace ECB chief economist Philip Lane, whose term ends on 31 May 2027. These nominations would complete the process of top jobs at the central bank.
EU ambassadors agreed on Thursday on the text of the recommendations for all three candidates, which eurozone governments are expected to adopt in writing by the evening, paving the way for the European Council to make the appointments in December after consulting the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council.
What happens next for Christine Lagarde?
Lagarde announced on 29 October that she would step down on 7 February 2027, almost nine months before the end of her term.
She said leaving the ECB would give her greater freedom to speak out on issues beyond monetary policy.
Speaking at The New York Times' DealBook Summit on 18 November, Lagarde said taking on a leadership role at the World Economic Forum was "one of the options".
She declined to reveal her plans but insisted: "I'm not retiring."
In July, she told Euronews in an exclusive interview that she was "not a candidate for anything" but intended to "explain the importance of the European dimension" ahead of the vote, which could see far-right candidate Marine Le Pen pit against hard left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon. A run-off is seen as a radical scenario by financial markets.
Lagarde has not endorsed anyone yet.
She is also expected to promote a book coming out in January next year.

noticias.titulo: What makes a city attractive? AI ranks Budapest’s centre among the world’s top 10
noticias.resumen: Budapest city centre ranked as the world's 10th most attractive downtown in an international AI study using street views to gauge liveability. The historic core is world class, but poor comfort and struggling suburbs mean the whole capital only came 42nd.
noticias.texto:
Budapest city centre ranked as the world's 10th most attractive downtown in an international AI study using street views to gauge liveability. The historic core is world class, but poor comfort and struggling suburbs mean the whole capital only came 42nd.
Researchers from Corvinus University of Budapest and the Toulouse School of Economics have used artificial intelligence to analyse the popularity of 150 cities worldwide, based on seven criteria. Within a two-kilometre radius of the city centre Budapest ranks 10th, within five kilometres 15th, and across the entire urban area included in the study it comes 42nd.
The research team examined 150 cities in 70 countries by analysing more than three million street images. In the project called StreetPulse they used artificial intelligence to assess the urban environment according to seven criteria: beauty, perceived safety, vibrant urban life, pedestrian-friendly design, historical character, comfort and perceived affluence.
In the ranking based on Google Street View images, which looks at a two kilometre radius around city centres, Paris takes first place with 6.29 points on a 10-point scale. The French capital is followed by Amsterdam, Saint Petersburg, Barcelona and Vienna. With an average score of 5.83 Budapest ranks 10th, ahead of many other cities included in the list.
In the historic inner city of the Hungarian capital Budapest scores 6.38 for historical character, 6.30 for perceived safety and 6.31 for pedestrian-friendly design. Beauty is rated at 6.05, vibrancy of urban life at 4.55, comfort at 4.82 and perceived affluence at 6.40 by the artificial intelligence system. When the five-kilometre radius is taken into account Budapest drops to 15th place, while across the entire urban area examined it ranks 42nd. In this latter comparison Geneva, Amsterdam and Vienna are at the top.
Alongside the ranking focused on European cities and built on Google Street View images, a global comparison is also available that covers more than 160 cities, based on the analysis of open source images from the Mapillary and Panoramax databases. Here Venice, Paris and Amsterdam take the top three inner city places, while Budapest comes 26th.
The two rankings each have different strengths and limitations. Google Street View provides high quality image data collected using a relatively recent and uniform methodology, but using these images involves significant costs.
By contrast, the global ranking is based on openly accessible images, which makes the analysis more cost effective, easier to repeat and allows other researchers to build on the results. However, the quality of open source images can vary and they are updated less frequently, so they reflect the current state of cities less accurately.
Help the research by comparing images!
On the StreetPulse interactive maps available at cities.ccl.center anyone can explore the scores for different parts of a city, compare cities and create their own rankings. By comparing two street images users can also contribute to the research, helping to examine how closely AI assessments match people's impressions. The site also allows cities to be listed on the basis of a global database that studies how people perceive urban environments and seeks to understand human behaviour.
The databases make it possible to analyse the data in more detail and to combine them with other data sources, for example revealing how motorways separate some parts of a city from each other or identifying areas perceived as less safe.
They can be a valuable tool for local authorities, civil society organisations, businesses and everyone involved who wants to understand and improve the urban environment, see how the state of public spaces shapes everyday life and achieve a better quality of life by improving the surroundings.
"We want to continue developing the StreetPulse platform, assessing cities according to an increasing number of criteria so that we can help municipalities improve the quality of urban spaces. To this end we welcome the involvement of researchers, local authorities and civil organisations that are ready to work with us," said César Hidalgo, lead researcher on the project and director of the Center for Collective Learning.
A video overview of the project is available on YouTube:
StreetPulse is based on more than a decade of work by the research group at the CIAS research institute of Corvinus University of Budapest and the Center for Collective Learning at the Toulouse School of Economics. Supported by the Driving Urban Transitions European partnership, the development can help both urban researchers and urban planners in their work.

noticias.titulo: Russia launches ballistic missile and drone barrage on Ukraine, killing at least three
noticias.resumen: Ukraine's air defences downed 87 Russian missiles and drones overnight on Thursday. Meanwhile, Ukrainian drones struck a chemical plant making components for military explosives and a power station in the Stavropol region.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine's air defences downed 87 Russian missiles and drones overnight on Thursday. Meanwhile, Ukrainian drones struck a chemical plant making components for military explosives and a power station in the Stavropol region.
Russian forces struck residential buildings and an educational institution in Kharkiv overnight on Thursday, killing at least three people and leaving others potentially trapped under rubble, as a wider assault combining ballistic missiles and drones caused casualties in Kyiv and several other regions.
The attack involved Iskander-M, Zircon and S-400 ballistic missiles alongside 113 Shahed, Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, 76 of them jet-powered.
Ukraine's air defences shot down or neutralised 87 aerial targets.
Two people were killed when a Russian strike hit a residential building in Kharkiv on Thursday morning, while seven people were injured in a Russian missile strike on Kyiv.
A drone also struck a multi-storey building in the city's Novobavarsky district, injuring three people. Local authorities said others may still be under the rubble.
A third person was killed and several wounded in a strike on an educational institution in the city's Kyiv district.
One person was wounded in Dnipropetrovsk region. In Donetsk region, one person was killed and three injured in a strike on a post office in Bylbasivka on Tuesday evening.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian infrastructure continue
Ukrainian drones struck a thermal power plant and a chemical facility in Nevinnomyssk, Stavropol region overnight on Thursday.
The chemical plant, Nevinnomyssky Azot, is part of the EuroChem company and has been attacked at least six times since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022.
The plant produces around 1.42 million tonnes of ammonium nitrate, 1.16 million tonnes of ammonia and 0.17 million tonnes of acetic acid per year. The facility produces components used to make military explosives octogen and hexogen, which go into artillery shells.
The adjacent Nevinnomysskaya GRES power plant, which supplies electricity to the chemical facility among other consumers, was also struck.
Regional authorities in Stavropol said production and energy facilities had been damaged along with a school building and a university branch, and two people were wounded. Schools, universities and colleges in Nevinnomyssk switched to remote learning.
A new fire broke out at the Kuibyshev refinery in Samara region on the morning of Thursday, a day after Ukrainian forces had already struck it and the nearby Syzran plant.
Ukrainian forces also struck the Subkhankulovo pipeline station in Bashkortostan, a major hub in the Transneft trunk oil pipeline system that pumps crude oil from Western Siberia and Tatarstan.
A fire was reported at a plant in Naberezhnye Chelny in Tatarstan; monitoring sources said it may be the Altynpolymer-NCh facility, which processes plastics. Four people were injured in a drone attack in the Krasnodar region. Authorities in Rostov and Voronezh regions also reported air attacks.
Russia's Defence Ministry said 343 Ukrainian drones had been destroyed overnight across 15 regions, over the Azov and Black Seas and over Russian-occupied Crimea. Euronews could not independently verify these claims.
Russia and Ukraine exchanged the bodies of servicemen killed in Moscow's ongoing all-out war, returning 250 to the Ukrainian side and 22 to Russia, Russian state news agency RBC reported, citing a State Duma deputy.
The exchange was partially confirmed by Khochu Nayti, a Russian organisation that helps families locate missing, dead and captured servicemen.
"Today, 26 November 2026, with the mediation of the International Committee of the Red Cross, the bodies and remains of 22 Russian servicemen were handed over to Russia as part of repatriation," the organisation said.
The previous such exchange took place on 22 October, when 252 bodies were returned to Ukraine and 25 to Russia.
Similar exchanges have taken place regularly since summer last year, when Russian and Ukrainian representatives reached an agreement in Istanbul.

noticias.titulo: ‘Is James Bond conservative?': Trump gives verdict on Robert Pattinson – but asked about 007's politics first
noticias.resumen: Donald Trump has given Robert Pattinson his blessing after the actor was announced as the next James Bond. First, however, Trump reportedly asked whether Bond was a conservative. You can't make this up...
noticias.texto:
Donald Trump has given Robert Pattinson his blessing after the actor was announced as the next James Bond. First, however, Trump reportedly asked whether Bond was a conservative. You can't make this up...
Everyone's got an opinion on the new Bond...
From Hollywood A-listers and Amazon bosses, ex-Bonds and former heads of MI6, we've heard from a lot of people about the casting of Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond... But one person had yet to give his two cents – despite having a track record for co-opting pop culture references and having previously weighed in on who should be the next Bond.
Now, Donald Trump has given Robert Pattinson his seal of approval as 007 and wished him "luck" as the seventh actor to play Bond. First, however, he had to check his political affiliation...
The New York Post asked Trump about Pattinson at an Oval Office interview this week.
Trump apparently needed to know where Pattinson stood politically before answering the outlet’s question about the British actor playing Bond. He reportedly called through the open door of the office to his aide Natalie Harper - who has been nicknamed the "human printer" for printing documents for him to review.
“Is James Bond conservative?” Trump asked.
“He’s been good,” she told the Trump, handing him papers detailing information about Pattinson.
One showed a 2012 tweet in which Trump urged Pattinson to dump his former girlfriend and Twilight franchise co-star, Kristen Stewart.
Indeed, Trump posted repeatedly on Twitter about the couple's break-up after Stewart admitted cheating on Pattinson in 2012. Pattinson has previously called Trump's interest in his former relationship "such a bizarre curiosity", and joked that he felt left out when the posts stopped.
“Robert Pattinson should not take back Kristen Stewart. She cheated on him like a dog and will do it again — just watch,” Trump's tweet read.
Trump read the post aloud, telling the people in the room it was "a long time ago".
Trump was seemingly pleased as he continued looking through clips of himself and the actor.
“That’s cute,” he said, adding: “He says nice things” - without elaborating what those "nice things" were.
Trump added he “always” liked people who liked him and said Pattinson “looks nice”. He concluded by wishing him “luck” in his new role as Bond.
It is understood Pattinson has never publicly shared his political views. Then again, Trump could have been referring to 007 with his "Is James Bond conservative?" question – considering he has referred to Hannibal Lecter as a real-life person before.
To clarify, they're both fictional.
Pattinson, 40, will become the seventh actor to play 007, replacing Daniel Craig, who left the franchise in 2021 after No Time To Die.
In response to his casting, the actor, who has become one of the world’s most famous stars since his breakout roles in the Harry Potter and Twilight franchises, followed by Tenet, The Odyssey and Primetime, called the role the “honour of a lifetime” and “a dream come true”.
Production on the as-yet-untitled Bond 26 is due to start next year, with Denis Villeneuve directing and Steven Knight on script duties.
Before filming can start, Pattinson will have to complete filming The Batman Part II – production on which was temporarily paused after director Matt Reeves was faced with a personal issue. Steven Soderbergh has stepped in to help shoot the final few weeks.
This means that the earliest audiences will get to see the next Bond adventure will be in the second half of 2028 - making it seven years since Daniel Craig's swansong, and the longest gap between Bond films since 1989's Licence To Kill and 1995's GoldenEye.

noticias.titulo: Passenger flights diverted as Kuwait army intercepts Iranian drone attack
noticias.resumen: Kuwait's military said four people were injured after "a number of hostile" Iranian drones were detected and intercepted in its airspace. Flights crossing Iraq toward the Gulf were given new headings ahead of Kuwait, shifting the international corridor.
noticias.texto:
Kuwait's military said four people were injured after "a number of hostile" Iranian drones were detected and intercepted in its airspace. Flights crossing Iraq toward the Gulf were given new headings ahead of Kuwait, shifting the international corridor.
Flights on the key air traffic corridor between Europe, the Gulf region and Asia crossing Iraq towards the Gulf were suddenly redirected south on Thursday afternoon amid reports that Kuwait’s airspace was closed.
The Kuwait military has since issued a statement that four people were injured after "a number of hostile" Iranian drones were detected and intercepted in its airspace.
"The Iranian aggression targeted a vital facility, causing falling shrapnel that injured four people," said a statement by the defence ministry, adding that the injured were taken to a hospital for treatment while the incident caused unspecified "material damage".
Two Italians working for German defence group Rheinmetall died, Italy's foreign ministry said.
Since the war in Iran broke out in late February, most international flights crossing Europe have been flying toward major hubs in Doha, Abu Dhabi, Dubai and other destinations via a route running through Turkey, Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and the UAE.
All flights on the corridor were given a new heading, prompting them to make a sharp turn ahead of Kuwait's airspace and move the entire international corridor toward neighbouring countries, including a flight on which Euronews reporters were travelling.
The drone attack on Kuwait comes just one day after the US Virtual Embassy in Iran said Tehran, Yemen's Houthis and other aligned groups may target US interests and citizens in the region, including companies and institutions.
Washington warned citizens across the Middle East to exercise heightened vigilance after Iran attacked US assets in Bahrain and Kuwait and Yemen's Houthi forces struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district, wounding 11 people.
US citizens in the region were urged to monitor airline and airport operations and prepare for possible flight cancellations and airspace closures.
The war has seen the Gulf states caught in the crossfire, with US military facilities and energy installations on their soil targeted.
The US and Iran are in a standoff over the vital Strait of Hormuz, with the US military working to escort ships transiting the waterway in defiance of Tehran's attempts to close it.
Flights bound for the Gulf countries carry extra fuel for emergency diversions, in case they need to enter a holding pattern near their destinations if airports and airspaces close due to military activity.

noticias.titulo: Fathers' antidepressant use tied to slight blood pressure risk in kids — but drugs may not be why
noticias.resumen: Researchers said their findings should offer reassurance for hopeful fathers who take antidepressants.
noticias.texto:
Researchers said their findings should offer reassurance for hopeful fathers who take antidepressants.
Children whose fathers took antidepressants in the months before conception are at slightly higher risk of developing high blood pressure — but the fathers' mental health, rather than the drugs, may explain the link, a large new study suggests.
About 4.1% of men worldwide experience depression, and antidepressant drugs are a first-line treatment when it is moderate or severe. The share of expectant fathers taking these medications has risen over the past two decades in countries like Denmark, according to the study, which was published in The BMJ.
Researchers tracked more than 1.3 million babies born in Denmark from 2000 to 2023, and then followed them for an average of 12 years. About 18,400 children were diagnosed with a metabolic condition such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol levels, or overweight or obesity.
That includes 364 children whose fathers had used antidepressants in the three months before conception. They were slightly more likely to develop high blood pressure than children whose fathers did not take antidepressants, the study found.
The risks were not elevated for other metabolic conditions, and the extra risk disappeared when researchers compared them to children whose fathers took antidepressants during pregnancy, but not beforehand.
“The mental health conditions for which the fathers took antidepressants may partly explain the study findings,” Prasad Nishtala, a reader in the life sciences department at the University of Bath, said in a press statement. He was not involved with the study.
The findings offer “reassurance for men treated with antidepressants before pregnancy,” the researchers said.
They also accounted for mothers’ and fathers’ age, education level, other medication use, history of metabolic conditions and mental health history. Other factors, such as severity of illness, diet and exercise, may also have played a role.
Other large studies have found no link between fathers’ preconception antidepressant use and preterm birth, birth defects, autism or intellectual disability in their children.
“This study does not challenge the existing evidence. It extends it, cautiously, to metabolic outcomes,” said Alastair Sutcliffe, a professor of general paediatrics at University College London. He was not involved in the study.
“Men who need antidepressants should not stop them because of this study,” he added.

noticias.titulo: Judges in Netanyahu corruption trial urges dropping key charges
noticias.resumen: Israel continues to struggle to form a government after the 27 October election. Netanyahu has denied wrongdoing in all three cases since his trial began in May 2020.
noticias.texto:
Israel continues to struggle to form a government after the 27 October election. Netanyahu has denied wrongdoing in all three cases since his trial began in May 2020.
Judges overseeing the long-running corruption trial of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have urged prosecutors to reconsider major parts of the case.
The Jerusalem District Court suggested prosecutors consider dropping the bribery allegation in one of the cases, known as Case 4000, which alleges Netanyahu used his position to provide regulatory benefits to telecoms company Bezeq in exchange for favourable coverage on the Walla news website.
It is the most serious of the three cases against Netanyahu and the only one involving a bribery charge.
In this instance, the court questioned the strength of the prosecution’s evidence, particularly testimony from former Communications Ministry director-general Shlomo Filber, citing inconsistencies and doubts over whether any quid pro quo had been proved.
In another case, known as Case 2000, concerning alleged negotiations with Yedioth Ahronoth publisher Arnon Mozes over favourable coverage, the judges questioned whether the conduct described actually amounted to a criminal offence.
The court also suggested that prosecutors seek an agreement over the remaining case, Case 1000, which concerns allegations that Netanyahu received expensive gifts, including champagne, cigars and jewellery, from wealthy businessmen.
The court stressed that its comments did not amount to an acquittal and no charges have yet been formally dismissed. Netanyahu has denied wrongdoing in all three cases. His trial began in May 2020.
Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said prosecutors would review the judges’ comments, while Netanyahu’s lawyer has called for criminal mediation.
Still no clarity over last month's election result
The intervention by the judges comes at a sensitive political moment in Israel, with the country still unable to form a government after the 27 October election.
Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot currently has the mandate to form a government, but his four-party bloc holds only 48 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, short of the 61 needed for a majority.
A weakening of the prosecution case could strengthen Netanyahu’s position in coalition negotiations and reduce one of the biggest legal uncertainties hanging over his political future.

noticias.titulo: Watch as rare cloud 'waterfall' cascades over Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro
noticias.resumen: The natural phenomenon went viral on social media, forcing photographers to confirm that it wasn't produced by artificial intelligence.
noticias.texto:
The natural phenomenon went viral on social media, forcing photographers to confirm that it wasn't produced by artificial intelligence.
A rare cloud phenomenon took social media by storm, as thick clouds cascaded around Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, over the weekend.
The weather phenomenon occurs when moist sea air pushes up the slopes and cools, forming clouds that descend and create a water-fall effect.
Only the summit of the mountain, with the iconic statue, and the highest peaks remained visible above a white blanket that gushed down the slopes.
It has been described as Cidade Maravilhosa" (Wonderful City) - an epithet for Rio de Janeiro that gained popularity in the early 20th century and still lives up to the name.
Orographic clouds sweep over Christ the Redeemer
The moment was captured on a mobile phone by filmmaker and photographer Márcio Amaro, from the Santa Teresa neighbourhood, and quickly went viral on social media.
"I had never seen Corcovado like this", wrote Márcio Amaro, making it clear that "the image is real" and not produced by artificial intelligence (AI).
The scene looks as if it has come straight out of a film, but it is very real and has an explanation in atmospheric science. The technical term is orographic cloud, a rare phenomenon triggered by winds coming in from the ocean that push a mass of moist air against a natural barrier.
In this case, that air rose up the slopes of Corcovado. On its way up, it cooled very quickly, a change that leads to the condensation of water vapour and to the formation of dense cloud near the top of the mountain.
As it crosses the summit, the mist is projected over to the other side and, as it begins to descend, it follows the contours of the terrain, creating the illusion of falling water.
As it continues to drop, the air warms up again and the droplets evaporate, which reinforces the effect of a veil or curtain sliding down through the vegetation, until the mist eventually dissolves.
Given that Corcovado Mountain is close to the Atlantic Ocean and covered in Atlantic Forest, the orographic cloud phenomenon is actually frequent in Rio and the surrounding region, especially when cold fronts pass through or in the early morning.
Other photographers had already captured a moment like this in August 2026, showing Christ the Redeemer rising above a tangle of clouds at daybreak. However, that was only the result of static fog trapped in the valleys.
The moving waterfall image depends on a precise combination of factors: the height of the cloud, which has to be exactly at the level of the statue's feet, with Christ clear of the mist, the density of the vapour and a constant current of wind that drives the mass of air down the hillside without dispersing it immediately.
Rio de Janeiro was already an unmissable destination for nature lovers. After this spectacle, there really are no excuses left. You just have to get up early.

noticias.titulo: TUI boss wants EU to cut bureaucracy, attract talent and expand green energy
noticias.resumen: Euronews spoke with TUI's CEO Sebastian Ebel about manure-powered cruise ships, migration, dependence on the US, Artificial Intelligence, and the future of tourism.
noticias.texto:
Euronews spoke with TUI's CEO Sebastian Ebel about manure-powered cruise ships, migration, dependence on the US, Artificial Intelligence, and the future of tourism.
TUI Group is regarded as the world's largest integrated tourism group. The firm includes around 460 hotels, 19 cruise ships, five airlines with 125 aircraft and around 1,200 travel agencies with a total of 67,000 employees.
In 2025 the tourism group, headquartered in Hanover, generated revenue of €24.2 billion and an operating profit before interest and taxes of €1.46 billion.
On 9 December the travel group will present its annual figures for 2026.
Euronews spoke to Sebastian Ebel at an economic and innovation summit on the cruise ship "Mein Schiff Flow" in the northern-German city of Kiel.
Euronews: In your view, what should the EU do to stimulate the economy and strengthen competitiveness?
Sebastian Ebel: Bureaucracy is not only the EU's responsibility, national governments are responsible for it as well. I always use Denmark as an example: just as much a member of the EU as Germany, but with a far lower density of regulation. That is perhaps the first point, that we should organise these things that we can regulate ourselves, ourselves and differently and better. Of course in my view the EU apparatus, and I am a convinced European, it is the best peace model we have ever had, needs to be reformed. That includes streamlining it, cutting back regulation and focusing on guard rails.
Euronews: Businesses also complain about labour shortages. Demographic trends in Europe will make the problem even worse. How do you assess this for your sector and for your company?
Sebastian Ebel: I think we face a demographic factor that is challenging. When an age pyramid turns upside down, far fewer people have to support far more older people. That means that, mathematically, we have to work longer, at least those who want to and are able to. And it also means that we need immigration, specifically talented people who can solve the problems we have here. By the way, that is nothing new. I remember the waves in Braunschweig and Wolfsburg of Italians who came to work for VW. I remember people from the Philippines who came here for medical services. The point is that we bring the right people here who can strongly support us in this demographic transition so that it does not backfire on us.
Euronews: Which political and economic framework conditions, the big levers, do we need in Germany and Europe to boost the economy?
Sebastian Ebel: Cutting bureaucracy is the main point for me. If you work here every day as an entrepreneur, you know what you are talking about. Many people are not aware of the obstacles that exist. This also includes taxonomies, that is, a tax system that is simple, it is not always about cuts, but about it being manageable and understandable. Bureaucracy is a key issue.
Euronews: The economy needs affordable energy and stable energy. It has to be available all the time. But can we really supply an industrial country with sustainable energy?
Sebastian Ebel: Of course. Why not? It is the energy that is produced in the most sustainable and most cost effective way, and increasingly it can be produced even better in the future. Today we are failing because we do not have smart grids, so that we can deal with different situations, a lot of energy when it is stormy outside, little energy when it is dark and there is no wind, and cannot get this to the customer.
Euronews: What about storage capacity? That is needed as well.
Sebastian Ebel: There are three things. First, using the energy we have in such a way that when there is a lot of energy it is cheap and when there is little it is expensive, so that self-regulation takes place. The second issue is expanding the grids. That will increasingly be important. And third, working in large interconnected systems.
Euronews: The EU says nuclear energy is climate friendly and can certainly be used. Do you share that view?
Sebastian Ebel: There are new generations of nuclear energy. However, the question is whether there is majority support for it among the population. I have serious doubts whether this is achievable here. In other countries it is, including for example Sweden. I believe this question is not really on the agenda at the moment. Who today would want to build and put into operation a new nuclear power plant in Brokdorf? I think renewable energy can largely cover demand here and at very, very low prices.
Euronews: What is TUI's position on electric mobility? E-ships will never exist.
Sebastian Ebel: We were one of the first groups to say that we would only have company cars that are electric. We decided that two or three years ago and today we are glad we did. We are electrifying our bus fleets, we operate around 1,000 buses with partners worldwide. And we are now slowly beginning to switch to electric buses. We have the topic of hotels, in other words moving away from fossil fuels towards electric energy or geothermal energy to generate power.
Ships have a major advantage, as we have heard today: LNG-powered ships. They should not run on fracked LNG, but on biogas energy from slurry. We can also produce methanol for traditional e-methanol. The big issue remains air travel. Today it is the most demanding area when it comes to making it carbon neutral in the long or medium term.
Euronews: In your opinion, which fuels currently offer the greatest potential, in other words sustainable fuels?
Sebastian Ebel: For ships, I believe very strongly in e-LNG or biogas LNG. And as a second step, methanol. I think this shift in the way the economy sources energy over a defined short period is perfectly feasible and today there is no longer a contradiction between economics and ecology, they go hand in hand. There are, however, some sectors, such as aviation, where there are still real issues that require technological change. Although I was able to learn again today that perhaps we are not that far away from this. When I see that a country like Denmark is completely independent of fossil gas, and that ships here can be fuelled with Danish e-LNG, then this, produced from slurry from livestock farming, water, slurry, straw, is really a model that we could implement in Germany or other European countries in exactly the same way.
Euronews: An important topic is digital sovereignty. Why do we need to become independent of the US players? We could work well with them.
Sebastian Ebel: I think it is important for security reasons, but also for economic reasons. We have just seen again that Starlink was switched off or reduced for Ukraine. I do not want us in Germany to be dependent on the decision of a single man in America as to whether we get a product or not. I believe it is our responsibility, not only for defence but also for economic enterprises. We must not be vulnerable to blackmail. That is one issue. The other is an economic issue. When I look at the margins of our German car industry and the tourism sector in Germany compared with software companies, the balance of power has been suspended. There high margins, here low margins. And I see that where companies have their own software again, negotiations also go better.
Euronews: How are you using AI, artificial intelligence, at TUI?
Sebastian Ebel: We started with flagship projects. We began with optimising route planning and deployment planning. We have used it very extensively in sales to find new distribution channels. And now, through AI factories, as we call them, we are producing software applications, ideally like in a factory
(Editor's note: AI stands for Artificial Intelligence, German "Künstliche Intelligenz").
Euronews: Tourism, a brief look back. How has 2026 been for TUI so far?
Sebastian Ebel: 2026 was another difficult year. On top of all the economic developments, the war in the east and the challenges in the west, the war involving Iran was added. We had a one off effect because ships were held there and for two or three months we saw a very sharp slowdown in bookings, with long haul travel also heavily affected. Against this backdrop we have performed very, very well. We did not have to withdraw the guidance (Editor's note: the official forecast by the management for future business development) that we issued three months ago. The resilience that we as TUI have shown is something not everyone would have credited us with.
Euronews: What are the trend destinations of the future, if we look a bit ahead?
Sebastian Ebel: Cruises will remain strong. I would say everything related to experiences will grow even more. Whether it is a theme park, the best diving spot or a Dine&Wine course. Market segmentation will become more intense. And then, perhaps as the overarching effect, many people have a fixed budget, especially in economically challenging times. Offering something for this budget, for a single mother or father with one child or for grandparents with their grandchildren, that is one of our main tasks.
Euronews: Overtourism is always an issue. Cruise ships are viewed very critically as well. But what positive effects does tourism have?
Sebastian Ebel: Tourism is seen as extremely positive in the destinations. What we often do here is focus on what happens at two demonstrations in Mallorca. Worldwide, tourism is seen very, very positively. And there are regions, also in Germany by the way, that suffer from overtourism. In such cases it is up to governments to say what kind of tourism they want. Because if the people on the ground are not happy, then the customers are not either.
And the point is that we are told what kind of tourism is wanted. The main point of criticism is often transport and, in particular, housing. Housing is the overriding issue when people still live at home at 25 because they can no longer afford a flat, or houses are always bought by foreigners at higher prices. And there I would recommend that those responsible introduce regulation so that people get the right kind of tourism and in the right quantity.
Euronews: If you could make three or four decisions, if you were the President of the Commission or the German Chancellor, what are the three or four most important decisions where you would say: we have to take these now, otherwise time will run out on us?
Sebastian Ebel: Massive cutting of bureaucracy. Bringing energy prices down to an acceptable level, launching an education offensive for talent, in other words upgrading schools and universities, and making sure that investment pays off again.
Euronews: Thank you very much for the interview.
Sebastian Ebel: My pleasure.

noticias.titulo: Norwegian low-cost carrier Norse Atlantic suspends flights as bankruptcy looms
noticias.resumen: Norwegian low-cost carrier Norse Atlantic, hit by surging jet fuel prices due to the war against Iran, said on Thursday that it was teetering on the verge of bankruptcy as it cancelled all flights for the day.
noticias.texto:
Norwegian low-cost carrier Norse Atlantic, hit by surging jet fuel prices due to the war against Iran, said on Thursday that it was teetering on the verge of bankruptcy as it cancelled all flights for the day.
Founded in 2021 and specialising in long-distance flights, Norse had already warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical", sending Norse shares plunging 85%.
"If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board's intention to file for bankruptcy," the company said in a filing to the Oslo stock exchange.
"There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found," it added.
All of Thursday's flights have been cancelled "pending clarification as to whether a viable financing solution can be established".
Norse said it was "in discussion with investors regarding a possible takeover that would include a financing solution", without providing any details about their identities.
Its shares fell further in early trading on Thursday before rebounding into positive territory, but at 0.04 kroner each, the airline now has a market value of just $9.7 million.
The airline's problems are not new but have worsened following the sharp increase in jet fuel prices resulting from the war in the Middle East.
Spanish airline Plus Ultra announced on Tuesday that it was ceasing operations, and Latvian carrier Air Baltic filed for US Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September.
