noticias.titulo: Feminists march across Spain against violence ahead of general election
noticias.resumen: Demonstrations for the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women come just days before elections in which the far right could approach 20% of the vote.
noticias.texto:
Demonstrations for the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women come just days before elections in which the far right could approach 20% of the vote.
Thousands of demonstrators gathered in cities including Valencia, Barcelona and Seville, as well as the capital Madrid, on 25 November to protest against gender-based violence against women.
The demonstrations came just days before Spain's general election, with the far-right Vox party polling at around 18%, according to the latest polling averages.
In Madrid, the main demonstration followed a route between Cibeles and Puerta del Sol, with Sunday's election featuring prominently in chants and placards.
The march organised by Comisión 8M, which advocates a trans-inclusive and intersectional form of feminism, drew the larger crowd, while another group opposed to that approach held a separate march towards Plaza de España.
Among those taking part in the first demonstration were Frente Amplio candidate Ada Colau and Podemos candidate Irene Montero. Begoña Gómez, the wife of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, also joined the march as part of the Socialist delegation.
This year's demonstrations also came a decade after the 2016 gang rape at the San Fermín festival in Pamplona, a case that became known as "La Manada" and sparked some of the largest feminist protests in Spain in recent years.
Since then, Spain's feminist movement has also experienced internal divisions, including over transgender rights, reflecting debates that have emerged in other countries such as the United Kingdom.
The PSOE's general campaign coordinator, Rebeca Torró, called on women to vote on Sunday in "self-defence", presenting her party as a defender of women's rights against political forces that reject the concept of gender-based violence.
However, Jaime de los Santos, an MP for Spain’s conservative People’s Party (PP), said his party was also committed to combating gender-based violence and accused the PSOE of trying to “frighten” women.

noticias.titulo: ‘The taste layer of the internet ’: Reddit's COO on why AI needs humans
noticias.resumen: Euronews Next spoke to Jen Wong about the threat of AI to the open internet and the importance of human connection on the platform.
noticias.texto:
Euronews Next spoke to Jen Wong about the threat of AI to the open internet and the importance of human connection on the platform.
In the 21 years since its founding, Reddit has played host to some of the strangest, most niche corners of the internet — from knitting groups to discussions about romantic relationships between humans and artificial intelligence.
AI has dramatically transformed the internet for Reddit users in those two-plus decades. Even so, the technology still has the potential to deepen the value of human conversation on the platform, as it “has no inherent taste… and doesn’t know anything,” Reddit’s chief operating officer, Jen Wong, told Euronews Next on the sidelines of Web Summit 2026 earlier this month.
She described Reddit as "the taste layer of the internet", arguing that AI models will always need human communities to understand new products, culture and ways of speaking.
“Reddit — it's fun, it's a place to build together, it's a place where there's something different about getting advice from a group of different people versus having it synthesised by an AI agent,” she said.
Reddit operates on the basis of individually themed groups called subreddits. Users can post links and create their own rules, such as a ban on overt self-promotion or guidelines around authenticity. There are also human moderators who can report extremist or violent behaviour on the platform.
Reddit users increased to 443.8 million weekly active users as of the third quarter of 2025, up from 365.4 million during the same period a year prior. In October, the company said its net income had soared more than 74% on an annual basis in the third quarter of this year.
Still, Wong acknowledged that AI search is harming Reddit's traffic. Search referrals declined in the company's most recently reported quarter, she said, adding that AI search is "not a material traffic driver" in the way traditional blue links were.
Demand for the platform, though, has not disappeared. Reddit remains a top-15 search term, but AI products make it harder for people to reach it. Reddit’s focus now, Wong said, is on logged-in users and those on its application, while also driving traffic to the platform directly.
‘The arms race’
In the interview, Wong argued that AI search is partly to blame for making the internet more closed and siloed than it was 20 years ago.
“I think we have been real believers and beneficiaries of what was an open internet but I think that's changed. I think the internet is not as open,” she said.
Wong also faulted AI for "intensive data stealing and abuse and scraping", which she said has made publishers more guarded.
Reddit currently has partnerships with OpenAI and Google for data sharing. Rather than feeding AI with user content, Wong said the partnerships allow for the company to “lay down guardrails on how our data is being used”.
Data scraping is against Reddit’s terms of service and Wong said it has built-in defences against it. But she acknowledged that “over time that will be an arms race, frankly”. Amid a wave of AI agents and assistants, it could become increasingly difficult to ensure that Reddit users are, indeed, human.
Reddit's approach to AI agents has been to create "clear, sanctioned avenues" for them so their activity is transparent. Bots are acceptable, she said, if they are labelled, and some, such as news feed bots, could even be useful.
When asked about criticism that AI models trained on Reddit data inherit bias, particularly against women, Wong defended the platform as now being "one of the most balanced" on diversity of opinion.
Wong added that while the site's early audience skewed male and tech-oriented, Reddit is now "very gender balanced," with Gen Z women its fastest-growing demographic in some countries, including the United Kingdom.
Reddit in the future
Looking ahead, Wong predicted that over the next five years AI agents will transform Reddit’s business across the board, from user experience to advertising buying. But she insisted the company will maintain its core principles.
“When it seems like everyone's zigging and you're zagging,” she said, “believing in communities, moderation, privacy and anonymity has served us really well.”
Wong added that Reddit’s commitment to human connection would ultimately allow it to adapt to a new technological reality. “When people come together, as we see in real life, it is an incredible trove of lived experience and knowledge,” she said.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has called for expanding the country's nuclear arsenal after inspecting facilities involved in producing nuclear materials and developing weapons, state media reported on Thursday.
Kim visited the sites on Wednesday, including two nuclear material production factories and a nuclear weapons research institute. Their locations have not been disclosed.

North Korea's state news agency KCNA said the country was systematically increasing its capacity to produce nuclear materials to strengthen its nuclear arsenal.

noticias.titulo: Why the Mediterranean is a hotspot for oil spills after tanker sinks near Ibiza
noticias.resumen: Any pollution entering the water could have a possible impact on Mediterranean seagrasses that absorb substantial quantities of climate-heating carbon dioxide.
noticias.texto:
Any pollution entering the water could have a possible impact on Mediterranean seagrasses that absorb substantial quantities of climate-heating carbon dioxide.
Spanish authorities are scrambling to contain any damage to its "vulnerable" Mediterranean waters following a huge oil spill.
On Thursday (26 November), a tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel sank off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one dead.
The Maltese-flagged Med Emre was travelling from the southern port of Algeciras to Barcelona when it sank in the early hours of the morning. 17 crew members were rescued but one was later confirmed dead in hospital.
According to maritime data tracking firm Kpler, the vessel was transporting around 66,000 barrels of refined products.
It is currently unclear what caused the sinking.
A government mechanism designed for marine pollution events had been activated, "but this does not presuppose that pollution has been detected on the coast", Spanish government sources told news agency AFP.
A boat and a plane belonging to Spanish maritime rescue service Salvamento Maritimo had been sent to assess the possible environmental damage, the Balearic emergency services added.
The Civil Protection authority had requested the activation of the European Union's Earth monitoring system Copernicus to obtain images of the area, said the government sources.
'Amplified' potential for pollution
Maritime security expert Emilio Rodriguez Diaz from the University of Cadiz told local news that the area affected by the oil spill was "particularly vulnerable".
Any pollution entering the water could have a possible impact on tourism and on Mediterranean seagrasses that absorb substantial quantities of climate-heating carbon dioxide.
Mediterranean seagrass acts as a major blue carbon sink, trapping carbon in deep rhizome and sediment layers while oxygenating coastal waters - but warming waters from climate change is already fuelling their demise.
The area also includes spaces protected by the European Union's Natura 2000 network and hosts the critically endangered Balearic Shearwater, says SEOBirdLife.
"Contact with the fuel may alter the impermeability and the thermal insulation of the birds' plumage, causing heat loss and hypothermia," the NGO warned.
Marine conservation group Oceana noted that the time of year was "key" for migratory species, including turtles, sharks, red tuna, pilot whales and the striped dolphin.
Oil spills are one of the most concerning sources of marine pollution as they're difficult to clean up and can last for a long time.
"They can severely pollute marine and coastal habitats, causing damage to the natural environment and the economy," says the European Environment Agency.
"The Mediterranean Sea’s highly industrialised nature, characterised by the many extensive ports, refineries and petrochemical plants along its coastlines, amplifies the potential for pollution incidents."
Spain's worst oil spill
But Diaz downplayed comparisons to the 2002 Prestige oil disaster, Spain's worst environmental accident so far.
That spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of fuel and blackened thousands of kilometres of Atlantic coastline, affecting Spain, Portugal and France.
The Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood", he said.
"It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment."
In December 2024, a US-sanctioned Russian cargo ship sank in international waters off Spain's southern Mediterranean coast with 16 people on board -- two of whom were never found.
A Spanish government letter to parliament earlier this year revealed the ship was transporting "components of two nuclear reactors similar to those used by submarines".
The vessel's owner, a company that belongs to the Russian defence ministry, denounced at the time "a targeted terrorist attack", without providing evidence.

EU leaders are meeting in Brussels to discuss the bloc’s next seven-year budget. European Council President António Costa hopes to bring them closer to a deal by the end of the year, but governments are divided over how much to spend and who should pay. Spending priorities include supporting farmers, addressing the high cost of housing and energy, and increased defence spending, particularly for Ukraine.

noticias.titulo: US says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites to build data centres in space
noticias.resumen: The US Federal Communications Commission authorised Elon Musk's rocket company to create a data centre constellation to power AI on earth.
noticias.texto:
The US Federal Communications Commission authorised Elon Musk's rocket company to create a data centre constellation to power AI on earth.
The Trump administration on Wednesday gave Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX the green light to deploy one million satellites that it said would create data centres in space, as governments increasingly look to alternative means to power artificial intelligence.
The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) lauded its authorisation as a historic first amid the AI race. It said that SpaceX's one million "orbital compute modules" — forming a data centre constellation called Starmind — would process massive amounts of data that would be used back on Earth.
"America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, said in a statement. He added that Wednesday's move "opens a bold new frontier".
A lengthier authorisation order published by the FCC noted that SpaceX must deploy at least "one authorised space station" by 2033 — and then gradually add more and more through 2040. Musk welcomed the decision over social media.
In its ruling, the FCC maintained that SpaceX's proposed Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules and that deploying the satellites "serves the public interest". But it acknowledged that it had received a “substantial number” of public comments leading up to its authorisation on Wednesday, including petitions to deny SpaceX's request.
The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centres in space to help run AI tools on Earth. But scientists and industry experts have stressed enormous technical and financial obstacles, as well as a host of environmental concerns like atmospheric pollution caused by launches and reentries.
Proponents of data centers in space argue that capturing the sun’s energy would ease pressure on power grids and cut demand for sprawling computing warehouses on Earth, as well as the resources like water needed to cool them.
European data centres in space?
The European Union is also exploring how to construct data centres in space.
The European Commission’s 16-month, €2 million Horizon Europe ASCEND feasibility study, which was conducted by an industry-led research consortium, found that building solar-powered data centres in orbit is technically and economically viable. It proposed an initial 10 MW deployment by 2036 scaling to 1 GW by 2050.
A review by the European Parliament of the ASCEND proposal in April noted that data centres in space could ease constraints on terrestrial centres, including their high electrical demands. But it also noted that the "main barrier is economic, rather than technical, with future launch costs a key determinant".
Meanwhile, China launched an initial cluster of 12 AI computing satellites in May 2025 as the first phase of its planned 2,800-satellite "Three-Body Computing Constellation" led by ADA Space and Zhejiang Lab.

noticias.titulo: After initial reluctance, Bulgaria says it's 'ready' to join €45 billion Ukraine loan
noticias.resumen: Bulgaria will contribute to the new €45 billion support loan to Ukraine, Prime Minister Rumen Radev confirmed on Thursday. But the country will not help pay for weapons and ammunition.
noticias.texto:
Bulgaria will contribute to the new €45 billion support loan to Ukraine, Prime Minister Rumen Radev confirmed on Thursday. But the country will not help pay for weapons and ammunition.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has confirmed his country will join the European Union's new €45 billion support loan to Ukraine but will refuse to contribute to the purchases of weapons and ammunition.
The loan is meant to cover two-thirds of Kyiv's 2027 wartime deficit.
"We are ready to join it," Radev said on Thursday.
Radev had initially expressed reservations about the financial scheme, arguing his country had to rein in its public spending, which is under intense scrutiny.
As a result, Bulgaria was coupled with Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic in the group that opposes the new loan altogether.
But on Thursday, Radev announced his country would accept the proposal, provided it remained exempt from its military component.
"We have a huge historical diaspora of 300,000 Bulgarians living in Ukraine. And our wishes and our request (are) to concentrate our support in the areas of the Bulgarian population in Ukraine," Radev said at a summit in Brussels.
"So we are going to contribute, but again, no money from Bulgaria for weapons, no money for (the) war in Ukraine," he added.
The European Commission has split the new €45 billion loan into €25 billion for military aid and €20 billion for budget aid. Altogether, it will generate between €2 billion and €2.5 billion in annual payment interests, which will fall on member states.
Kyiv will not be asked to repay the principal until Moscow provides war reparations.
Radev welcomed the loan's dual structure and said his country would chip in the €20 billion allocated for budget aid, intended to cover public services and salaries.
Radev said he would discuss the matter with Commission President Ursula von der Leyen during Thursday's summit, where support for Ukraine is high on the agenda.
Von der Leyen, who presented the loan last week, had publicly offered reluctant member states the option to opt in à la carte depending on their preference. She said she was "very confident" that all 27 countries would back her proposal.
Radev's confirmation comes as political pressure intensifies on Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join the loan.
Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark and Ireland are among those who have said the next EU budget, also under negotiation, cannot be agreed until support for Ukraine is locked in for 2027.
"It's crystal clear that the Russian aggression in Ukraine is one of the biggest challenges that we face. And Ukrainians are fighting for their own freedom, but also for European democracy and values," Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said on Thursday.
"We need to stand shoulder to shoulder with the Ukrainians (who) will need more military and financial support in the years to come. And that is something that no EU country can opt out of. Everyone needs to be in solidarity with the Ukrainians."
It remains to be seen whether leaders can bring Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic into the fold. Unlike Bulgaria, the three countries are already exempted from the previous €90 billion support loan and are bent on continuing their opt-out policy.

noticias.titulo: Less sex, more screens: Britain’s sexual habits are changing
noticias.resumen: One in three 16- to 24-year-olds have never had sex, up from one in five in 2010.
noticias.texto:
One in three 16- to 24-year-olds have never had sex, up from one in five in 2010.
Young people in Britain are having less sex than in the past, but many are sending or receiving sexual images and watching pornography, a large new study has found.
“Britain’s sex lives are changing. While most adults are having sex, people are having sex less often and more young people have never had sex,” said Soazig Clifton, an epidemiologist at University College London and academic director for the National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (NATSAL).
"There is also a higher proportion of people reporting same-sex experiences, and online sexual activity is now part of everyday life for many," Clifton said.
The study, which was published in The Lancet, found that most people in Britain aged 16 to 59 were sexually active, with a median of five lifetime partners. Around two-thirds reported having had one sexual partner in the past year, while women had sex an average of once a month and men twice a month.
The decline is particularly pronounced among younger generations. Among 16- to 24-year-olds, the proportion who said they had never had sex has risen to one in three, compared with one in five in 2010.
Overall, the frequency of sexual activity has declined among people under 45, falling to about twice a month, compared with four times a month in 1990.
The fourth edition of the NATSAL study, which has conducted regular surveys since 1990, is based on responses from 6,719 people aged 16 to 59.
Conducted between 2022 and 2024, the research noted similar trends in other industrialised countries.
Despite the decline in in-person sexual activity, online sexual behaviours are widespread, particularly among younger age groups.
Nearly half of 16- to 24-year-olds said they had sent or received sexual images on their phones in the previous year: 47.1% of young women and 43.5% of young men. The practice was less common among older age groups.
Pornography consumption was also widespread among people under 35. Around half of young women reported having watched pornography, compared with nearly nine in 10 young men.
The researchers found "widespread engagement with pornography and sexting across age groups and genders," a pattern also observed in other countries.
"Together with declines in in-person sex, this might signal a shift away from partnered physical intimacy, towards more solo and online sexual behaviour."
The study also found "increased diversity in the gender of partners" across all age groups.
"Sexual behaviour is a fundamental part of the human experience and changes in tandem with wider social changes," the researchers said.
They stressed that these societal shifts "carry significant implications for sexual and mental health and public health practice".
"We might be tempted to link the decrease in sexual frequency and the increase in childlessness, but we'd be wrong," said Kaye Wellings, professor of sexual and reproductive health research at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.
"People who want to conceive have sex often enough to make sure they do. To understand these trends, we need to look at a complex range of features of the society we now live in," added Wellings, who was not involved in the study.
The researchers said the reasons behind these changes are not yet well understood. However, they pointed to broader societal developments that may have played a role, including rising rates of common mental health conditions, declining alcohol consumption and increasingly online lifestyles.

noticias.titulo: UK sent Sri Lankan refugee to Eswatini in secret deal, the BBC says
noticias.resumen: The United Kingdom reportedly sent a Sri Lankan refugee who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, where he committed suicide, as part of a secret deal, according to an investigation by the BBC.
noticias.texto:
The United Kingdom reportedly sent a Sri Lankan refugee who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, where he committed suicide, as part of a secret deal, according to an investigation by the BBC.
The United Kingdom reportedly sent a Sri Lankan refugee who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, where he committed suicide, as part of an undisclosed deal, according to a BBC investigation.
The man, 35-year-old Kishanth Peramalya, had no connection to the southern African country.
He had left India in 2021 in an attempt to seek asylum in Canada. The Royal Navy rescued him and dozens of other Sri Lankan asylum seekers while their boat sailed in the Indian Ocean, the BBC reported. They were sent to Diego Garcia, an island in the British Indian Ocean Territory that serves as a UK-US military base.
The group of 61 asylum seekers stayed on the island for three years. In 2024, a report from the United Nations refugee agency denounced their detention conditions and said they should be urgently relocated.
By the end of 2024, most of the refugees were allowed to enter the UK but not Peramalya. During his detention, he had committed several crimes and had been convicted of four counts of sexual assault, according to the BBC.
The UK refused to welcome Peramalya due to his criminal convictions but acknowledged he could not return to Sri Lanka, where he had been tortured and sexual assaulted by military officers as a teenager. A UK court upheld the government's decision not to admit him to the country, the BBC said.
In March 2026, the Maldives reportedly agreed to take Peramalya for 30 days. He was then transferred to Eswatini, where his already fragile mental health further deteriotated. He committed suicide on September 13.
The BBC said Peramalya's tranfer to Eswatini was the subject of a draft deal between the UK and Eswatini.
According to the document, which Africanews has not seen, the UK government had agreed to cover the costs of Peramalya's permanent resettlement during three years. The deal was not disclosed to the UK Parliament. Peramalya's sister told the BBC that his family had been unaware that his relocation to Eswatini would be permanent.
"The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances,” Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, told the Guardian.
The UK did not specify why it had chosen to deport Peramalya to Eswatini. Since 2025, Eswatini has accepted several third-country deportees from the United States, a move that has drawn criticism in the southern African country.
"Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people," a spokesperson for the UK government told the BBC. "That includes taking steps to ensure high-harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK."

noticias.titulo: Cheaper, generic HIV prevention drug arrives in Zambia
noticias.resumen: The rollout in Zambia is part of a plan to ensure people in lower-income countries can access the breakthrough HIV prevention drug.
noticias.texto:
The rollout in Zambia is part of a plan to ensure people in lower-income countries can access the breakthrough HIV prevention drug.
The first shipments of a generic version of a twice-a-year HIV-prevention shot arrived on Wednesday in Zambia, and additional deliveries are expected in Uganda in the coming days.
The medication is called lenacapavir and is expected to cost $40 (€36) a year per person. It will eventually be available in 120 countries. The injectable form of pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, is nearly 100% effective at preventing an HIV infection and much more convenient than daily preventive pills that are available now.
“With demand for the injection far outstripping supply, the arrival of generics marks a major step towards making this breakthrough prevention option more widely available and affordable in low- and middle-income countries,” said Tenu Avafia, deputy executive director of Unitaid, a global health agency.
The medications are part of a shipment by the Global Fund, a worldwide partnership to defeat AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria. After going through a clearance process in Zambia, the medications are expected to be used within the next three weeks.
In 2025, the European Commission and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved brand-name lenacapavir, which is made by Gilead Sciences. The FDA approved the generic shot earlier this month, though it cannot be sold in the United States because it is still protected by Gilead’s patent.
Gilead established royalty-free licensing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable greater production of lenacapavir. Those voluntary licenses cover a specific set of countries in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and Latin America.
Gilead officials said the company signed the licenses months before regulatory approval to ensure an early generic supply, and collaborated closely with generic manufacturers and global health partners.
The FDA-approved generic was developed by India-based Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories under an agreement brokered by Unitaid and its partners, which sought to accelerate development and make the drug available at an affordable price.
“Access is a priority because we know that breakthroughs like lenacapavir only matter when they reach the people who need them most,” Daniel O’Day, Gilead’s chairman and CEO, said in a press release.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV and 570,000 died from HIV-related causes last year.
“We have an unprecedented opportunity to reach millions more people at risk of HIV,” Peter Sands, executive director of the Global Fund, said in a press release. “This is how we bring the goal of ending AIDS within reach.”

noticias.titulo: Ebola cases in Congo surpass 12,000 in fastest-growing outbreak
noticias.resumen: The ongoing outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
noticias.texto:
The ongoing outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.
It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.
The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.
Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire (CRP) rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometres north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.
CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.
Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization’s Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.
Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

noticias.titulo: New Danish data breach hits 11,000 despite security upgrades
noticias.resumen: The latest incident comes despite Denmark upgrading its cybersecurity systems after an earlier breach exposed data linked to millions of people.
noticias.texto:
The latest incident comes despite Denmark upgrading its cybersecurity systems after an earlier breach exposed data linked to millions of people.
Hackers broke into Denmark's national registry and accessed the personal information of 11,000 people, the Danish government said on Thursday, two months after another huge data hack.
Danish authorities said they had updated and modernised their security systems since the previous attack in early October, when the data of 8.8 million people was illegally accessed.
Despite that, "the administration of the Civil Registration System (CPR) has discovered a new security breach," the digital affairs ministry said.
"Unauthorised third parties have accessed the CPR data of 11,000 people."
It added: "The incident was stopped thanks to a new technical monitoring system for consultations, introduced after the first incident."
Neither the perpetrators of the latest breach nor those behind the October hack have been identified yet.
But in October an unidentified person contacted Danish newspaper Politiken in English via an encrypted messaging service and claimed responsibility for that breach.
The supposed hacker said they had found an entry point into the register within a few hours by using the login credentials of a former employee of a small Danish company.
They said the employee's password was 123456.
"The hacker says there were no security measures, such as two-factor verification, and that he was therefore able to start carrying out searches in the CPR register," Politiken wrote at the time.
The individual said they made a total of 14,919,352 queries in the database over a 10-day period.
These consisted of checking whether a specific identification number existed.
If it did, the register would provide the name, address, date of birth, gender, date of last move and marital status of the person concerned.
The suspected hacker recorded all the data but told the newspaper they had "no idea how it could be used" and did not intend to sell or disclose it.
In September, the Civil Security Agency raised the threat level for cyberattacks against Denmark to "high".
There has been a surge in cyberattacks, notably targeting supermarket refrigeration systems.
There has also been a series of false bomb threats against schools and planes across Europe, which could potentially be part of a hybrid warfare campaign.
That theory has not been confirmed, however, due to a lack of evidence.

noticias.titulo: Nuclear explosion in space would create 'a huge bell of radiation' to stay for months, says expert
noticias.resumen: Florence Duvellier, military fellow at the Defense Unit of the Security Studies Center at the French Institute for International Relations in Paris, says a nuclear explosion in space by Russia is "technically possible" but also a means to "stay as a big space power".
noticias.texto:
Florence Duvellier, a military fellow at the French Institute for International Relations in Paris, says that it's "technically possible" for Russia to put a nuclear weapon into space. Such a weapon would enable Russia to retain its status as a major space power.
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
          
          ADVERTISEMENT
        
She says that Russia's current focus on the war in Ukraine means it cannot afford to put a large network of satellites into space. However, a smaller nuclear weapon is "not that expensive" and would have a "huge effect".
A nuclear explosion in space would create a huge radioactive field that could cause "a lot of services" such as GPS and weather forecasts to shut down. The radiation would stay in space for months.

noticias.titulo: Huge explosion at Bangkok oil depot sends black smoke over Thai capital
noticias.resumen: A major explosion at a Bangchak oil facility in eastern Bangkok sent flames and thick black smoke into the sky on Thursday. Authorities urged people living nearby to evacuate as emergency services responded to the incident.
noticias.texto:
A major explosion rocked an oil facility in eastern Bangkok on Thursday, sending flames and thick black smoke high above the Thai capital.

The blast occurred at the Bangchak oil depot, operated by Thai energy company Bangchak Corporation.
Bang Na district authorities urged people in the surrounding area to evacuate immediately as a precaution.
The Bangkok city authority later said the fire had been extinguished less than an hour after the explosion, which was reported at around 3pm local time.
No casualties were immediately reported.
The cause of the explosion and the extent of any damage remain unclear.

noticias.titulo: The grapes of wrath: How Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie ended their fight over French vineyard
noticias.resumen: Ownership of Château Miraval, a prestigious estate in the Var, France, was one of the main points of contention in Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie’s divorce.
noticias.texto:
Ownership of Château Miraval, a prestigious estate in the Var, France, was one of the main points of contention in Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie’s divorce.
Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have resolved a long-running legal battle, a decade after the A-list celebrity couple split.
The actors have ended a dispute over the ownership of a French winery, saying in a joint statement: “We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further.”
Pitt, 62, and Jolie, 51, had bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.
In the lawsuit, Pitt argued that Jolie acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to Russian oligarch Yuri Sheflzer, stating that he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes without the permission of the other.
Jolie counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.
Pitt was not charged following an FBI and child services investigation into the incident and he denied the allegations.
They reached a divorce settlement in 2024 after an eight-year legal battle.
All six of the Pitt-Jolie children are now adults, with many of them having dropped their father's surname.

noticias.titulo: EU Commission offers little in response to US drug pricing pressures
noticias.resumen: Some members of the European Parliament suggested the EU should consider its Anti-Coercion Instrument.
noticias.texto: EU lawmakers hoping for a stronger response from the European Commission to U.S. pressure on capitals to raise drug prices got little in the way of new commitments on Thursday. Addressing the European Parliament plenary for the first time on the matter, Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen said there were “too many uncertainties” to assess the impact of Washington’s drug pricing push on Europe. The Trump administration has been pressuring European countries to pay more for new medicines, arguing that American citizens disproportionately shoulder the cost of pharmaceutical innovation through higher drug prices. In response to the Trump administration’s use of trade measures to push countries to raise drug prices, she also said European industry was protected by last year’s transatlantic trade truce struck at President Donald Trump’s Turnberry golf resort in Scotland. The subsequent joint statement that put the deal in writing set a 15% tariff ceiling on most European exports to the U.S., including branded medicines. Berlin faces possible additional tariffs after Washington launched a Section 301 investigation in June into Germany’s alleged “ persistent underpayment ” for innovative pharmaceuticals. Washington’s aim is to strike a deal to raise drug prices, similar to an agreement signed with the U.K. “We have to have a coordinated response,” European People’s Party MEP Tomislav Sokol told the debate in Strasbourg. Bilateral deals “would weaken the European position.” Some EU countries — including France and Ireland — recently asked the Commission to set up a task force bringing together national trade and health officials to assess the U.S. demands and explore a joint response. Renew MEP Stine Bosse, who initiated the plenary debate, warned that other capitals could find themselves in Washington’s crosshairs. “Today it is Germany,” she said. “Member states must work closer together than ever before on joint clinical assessment and yes, on pricing and reimbursement.” Drug pricing is a sensitive national matter, while trade policy falls within the EU’s remit. Belgium’s Deputy Prime Minister and Health Minister Frank Vandenbroucke recently published a paper arguing that the Commission should consider deploying its Anti-Coercion Instrument — the EU’s trade “bazooka” — in response to U.S. pressure. Socialist lawmaker Vytenis Andriukaitis and Renew MEP Vlad Vasile Voiculescu backed consideration of the instrument. Virkkunen, however, did not address that option. Romana Jerković, another socialist, warned that EU legislation such as the Critical Medicines Act would take years to yield benefits. The Trump administration’s policy of tying U.S. drug prices to those paid elsewhere, known as most-favored nation pricing, has prompted pharmaceutical companies to delay medicine launches in Europe. “What are the projects the Commission is planning to respond to the decline [of medicine launches] in the short term?” Jerković asked. Virkkunen cited legislation such as the forthcoming Biotech Act and said the Commission “fully respects” national powers over pricing but that “we can also provide support when needed” — without specifying what that support would entail. She also stressed the need for continued cooperation with Washington. “I believe that there is more that connects us than divides us,” she said. The topic is expected to come up again when EU health ministers meet on Dec. 8.

noticias.titulo: EU leaders clear path for Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos to lead ECB
noticias.resumen: Madrid's victory came after the Netherlands threw in the towel for the central bank's top job.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Spain has a clear path to the most powerful economic job in Europe after the Netherlands gave up the chase for the presidency of the European Central Bank. At the EU leaders’ summit, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten agreed to back a political deal that France, Germany and Spain had crafted in recent weeks to decide the ECB’s leadership for years to come. The Netherlands had initially put forward its former central bank governor, Klaas Knot, for the top job. But the political deal leaves Knot empty-handed. The deal will see Spain’s own ex-governor, Pablo Hernández de Cos, succeed ECB President Christine Lagarde when she steps down on Feb. 7. In return, Germany will appoint Markus Brunnermeier as the ECB’s chief economist, while the markets portfolio on the bank’s six-person executive board will go to France’s Laurence Boone. The ECB sets interest rates, which dictate borrowing costs across the single-currency bloc, with a mandate to keep inflation steady at 2% over the medium term. “Based on the conversation today” among EU leaders, “the Netherlands will support the consensus for the three nominations for the ECB board,” an EU diplomat said. Such consensus would be “an important signal to financial markets.” EU ambassadors have since formally recommended the three candidates for the ECB posts, another EU diplomat said. That will allow EU leaders to kick-start a “consultation process” today with the European Parliament and the ECB, which have the right to give their views on the three candidates. “The Council texts agreed today recommend Pablo Hernández de Cos as ECB President and Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier to the Executive Board,” the diplomat said. A hearing in Parliament is scheduled for Dec. 7, followed by a committee vote, which needs to be rubber-stamped in the plenary the week after. Leaders will then formally cement the deal at their next meeting in Brussels on Dec. 17.

noticias.titulo: US to delay overhaul of military presence in Europe
noticias.resumen: Washington will not meet the Dec. 1 deadline to outline the overhaul, its deputy ambassador told fellow envoys, according to diplomats.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — The U.S. has told NATO allies it will postpone an overhaul of its force presence in Europe beyond a provisional Dec. 1 deadline, according to two NATO diplomats. At a meeting of NATO envoys on Wednesday, U.S. deputy ambassador Scott Oudkirk told allies Washington would not present the Europe force posture review in time for a meeting of alliance foreign ministers next Wednesday, said the diplomats, who were granted anonymity to speak freely about the classified meeting. The review, announced by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in June, is designed to examine U.S. force levels across Europe, including troop levels, military access, basing rights and overflight permissions, as Washington seeks to pivot its military engagement toward other regions, such as the Western Hemisphere and the Indo-Pacific. “We’re still hopeful to meet the Dec. 1 deadline — at least for [U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth] to have the final review,” U.S. deputy Pentagon chief Elbridge Colby told reporters in Brussels last week, praising “enormous progress” by nations like Germany, Poland, the Netherlands and Scandinavian countries for “stepping up” and spending more on their own defense. The U.S. did not give a new date for when it would announce the revamp, the diplomats added, but cited the fact that it was still processing allies’ various offers for supplying military capabilities to replace Washington’s existing equipment and forces as one reason behind the delay. The U.S. delegation to NATO did not respond to a request for comment. Allies had previously suggested the review might be delayed amid uncertainties around Hegseth’s future in the administration, following an attempt to oust him after the U.S. midterm elections. The closed-door announcement marks the first confirmation that Washington would push back the review. In recent months, Colby and other U.S. officials have toured countries like Romania, Poland and Germany in preparation for the overhaul. The U.S. currently has around 80,000 troops stationed on the continent, mostly in Germany, Italy and the U.K.

noticias.titulo: Europe’s food security starts with resilient farms
noticias.resumen: Regenerative agriculture supports farmers’ livelihoods, biodiversity and food resilience. It is a win-win situation.
noticias.texto: Growing up in Brittany, France, food was never simply about what was on the plate. My grandparents were farmers, so I grew up understanding the connection between the food we eat, the people who produce it and the land on which we all depend. That connection has stayed with me. Yet that foundation is under pressure. Climate change, volatile input costs and geopolitical uncertainty are putting growing strain on Europe’s agri-food chain, raising a fundamental question: how do we build a food system capable of withstanding shocks while continuing to provide safe, nutritious and affordable food? Agriculture depends on assets we cannot replace: healthy soils, water and functioning ecosystems. Protecting and restoring those assets is not simply an environmental benefit. It is an economic and resilience imperative. And the scale of the challenge is significant. According to Eurostat, the EU is home to 8.8 million farms managing more than 156 million hectares of agricultural land. 1 At that scale and diversity, there can be no one-size-fits-all solution. This is where regenerative agriculture can make a difference. It is an outcome-based approach, adapted to local conditions, that puts soil health at its core and aims to preserve the land’s productive capacity and strengthen farms’ resilience. But farmers cannot carry the cost and risk of the transition alone. Research published in 2025 found that transitioning to regenerative agriculture can require upfront investments of €2,000-5,000 per hectare, while the business case can take three to five years to turn positive. 2 Agriculture depends on assets we cannot replace: healthy soils, water and functioning ecosystems. Protecting and restoring those assets is not simply an environmental benefit. It is an economic and resilience imperative. Public and private financing must therefore work together to give farmers the confidence to invest for the long term. At Nestlé, we have already seen what long-term investment can deliver. At a global level, Nestlé sources 6.9 million tons of agricultural raw materials from Europe every year. By 2030, we aim to increase the volume sourced from farms adopting regenerative agriculture practices across key ingredients from 21 percent in 2025 to 50 percent in 2030. Through initiatives such as our Nestlé Dairy Plan in Europe, and our Cereal & Grains regenerative agriculture programs, we combine financial support, agronomic expertize and digital tools to help farmers adopt and validate regenerative practices. There is growing evidence that this transition can work economically for farmers. In Spain, dairy farms receiving Nestlé support recorded an 11 percent increase in milk yield following investment. This reflects the impact of the broader program, which combines regenerative agriculture with measures to improve farm efficiency and resilience. Farms applying minimum tillage also reduced diesel use by 41 percent, while farms with covered manure lagoons reduced their share of synthetic fertilizer by 26 percent. In the UK, our Fresh Milk Plan with dairy cooperative First Milk is already showing encouraging signs. After four years, soil carbon stocks measured on three participating farms showed an average gain of 8.9 tons of carbon per hectare. 3 But resilience is about more than productivity and economics. European farmland bird populations have declined by 58 percent since 1980, underlining the pressure on agricultural ecosystems and the need to understand which interventions can make a measurable difference. That is why Nestlé has partnered with BirdLife Europe on a science-led program using farmland birds, butterflies and wild bees as indicators to measure how regenerative agriculture practices can support biodiversity. The aim is to understand what works and focus investment where it can deliver the greatest impact. A five-year study with SEO/BirdLife across Nestlé’s fresh-milk farms in northern Spain recorded 116 bird species, including 25 species in national decline, showing how dairy landscapes can provide vital refuges for biodiversity while continuing to produce food. Evidence, however, is only part of the equation. To bring regenerative agriculture to scale, the economics must work for farmers. As the post-2027 CAP takes shape, Article 10 should provide a strong framework for Transition Payments that help de-risk the transition and enable public and private funding to work together effectively. Resilience is a shared responsibility. Farmers, manufacturers, retailers, policymakers and consumers all have a role to play. That requires balanced and fair relationships across the food chain, where every actor has the means to adapt, innovate and invest for the future. A competitive food system must balance affordability today with resilience tomorrow. On December 2, in Brussels, we will bring these voices together to discuss what is needed to make regenerative agriculture work for farmers and strengthen Europe’s food resilience. For me, Europe now needs to get three things right. Resilience is a shared responsibility. Farmers, manufacturers, retailers, policymakers and consumers all have a role to play. First, put farmer economics at the heart of the transition. Farmers need a viable business case, not simply additional expectations. Second, align public and private investment behind measurable outcomes. We should reward what works: stronger farm economics, healthier soils, more efficient use of inputs and greater resilience. Third, protect the ability of every part of the food value chain to invest and commit for the long term. Europe will not strengthen its food security without fairness for all. Europe cannot have a resilient food system without resilient farms. Healthy land supports stronger farms; stronger farms underpin resilient food supplies. The task now is to move from individual successes to change at scale. References Eurostat (2026): Farms and farmland in the European Union – statistics . Statistics Explained, European Commission. noticias.titulo: Mandelson failed to sell shares in company after becoming US ambassador, latest files show
noticias.resumen: The former U.K. ambassador to Washington also attempted to influence a Cabinet reshuffle by former Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
noticias.texto: LONDON — Peter Mandelson failed to sell his stake in his lobbying firm Global Counsel and attempted to influence No. 10 decisions after becoming ambassador to the U.S., according to a newly released tranche of documents relating to his appointment. The files, published Thursday, lay bare the civil service’s frantic efforts to smooth the process of his unorthodox recruitment as the U.K.’s envoy to Washington, as well as his attempts to exert influence beyond his official role. Mandelson was sacked in September 2025 over the depth of his past friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The emails show that at the time of his appointment Mandelson retained his shares in Global Counsel and that, despite having received an offer to buy them in March 2025, had failed to divest them six months later. The company collapsed in February 2026 after it lost a series of accounts amid coverage of Mandelson’s relationship with Epstein. Senior civil servants exchanged emails late into the Christmas period at the end of 2024 and early 2025 discussing propriety questions, with then head of the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office Philip Barton seeking clarity about what arrangements could be made if Mandelson did not immediately sell his shares, such as placing them in a blind trust. A person with knowledge of Mandelson’s situation said the peer was not asked to divest his shares before taking up the appointment and a blind trust was ruled out by the Foreign Office. In April 2025, Mandelson emailed a U.S. official to propose a lunch meeting to discuss how to approach trade with China and suggested bringing an unidentified “former trade colleague” who could “lead off” the discussion, specifying: “It would be best to keep this under the radar.” The person with knowledge of Mandelson’s situation said that his proposal was to invite a Global Counsel former colleague to a trade trade think in — but that it never took place. While serving as ambassador, Mandelson also said he would water down language relating to China in a speech after receiving feedback from an unnamed director at Global Counsel, the files reveal . In an email, the director said: “As you will see, I have made suggestions on toning down some parts of your apologia of the Trump administration. Scepticism of it is now so deep — at least in the public policy-interested world outside government — that it would be counterproductive/unpersuasive if you came across as having drunk the Kool-Aid.” Mandelson also attempted to intervene in a Cabinet reshuffle by then Prime Minister Keir Starmer in September 2025 via texts to Morgan McSweeney, then No. 10 chief of staff. He suggested moving Darren Jones to lead the science and technology department as a way to “solve your Darren issue.” McSweeney did not respond until the reshuffle had concluded and Jones was given a newly created role as chief secretary to the prime minister. Starmer — who was replaced as prime minister by Andy Burnham in July — found his authority severely weakened over accusations he didn’t take enough enough care to ensure Mandelson, a known friend of Epstein, was a suitable person to be U.K. ambassador to the United States. A spokesperson for Burnham said that while the appointment had been made under the previous administration, “we are clear nothing like this can ever happen again, which is why we will ensure lessons are learnt.” During a statement in the House of Commons, Security Minister Dan Jarvis said Mandelson’s appointment had raised questions about the government’s appointments, vetting and conflicts of interest processes and ministers will respond to an Ethics and Integrity Commission lobbying review before the Christmas recess. Jarvis said further documents have been withheld at the request of the Metropolitan Police, which is currently investigating Mandelson on suspicion of misconduct in public office. Mandelson has not been charged, and his lawyers have said he is cooperating with the investigation and that his overriding priority is to clear his name. This developing story has been updated. Isabel Loubser contributed to this report.

noticias.titulo: 10 key faces of Spain’s next (likely) right-wing government
noticias.resumen: Some right-wing and far-right figures who might enter Spain's next government are already well known. Others fly under the radar.
noticias.texto: MADRID — Spain is heading towards a conservative coalition of the center-right People’s Party and the far-right Vox, polls suggest. But who will sit in government is harder to predict. Spain’s political parties are opaque organizations that keep potential ministers in the dark — including the candidates themselves. PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo , who ran the Galician government for 13 years, prides himself on never having had regional ministers’ names leaked to the press in advance, while a Vox official told Madrid Playbook on condition of anonymity: “There hasn’t been a single mention within the party of potential ministers or positions. Anyone who says otherwise is lying.” Although neither party has named any names, there are several individuals who will likely play a significant role in the next government if the PP and Vox win the Nov. 29 election. Here are 10 of them. 1. Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo Love her or hate her, Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo always leaves a mark. Feijóo picked her for the politically significant number two spot on the PP list for Madrid. Party lists in Madrid are usually headed by the candidate for prime minister, with leaders signaling their closest allies in the following spots. Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo, the People’s Party’s number two candidate for Madrid to the Congress of Deputies delivers a speech in Madrid on October 27, 2026. | Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images Many see the well-known conservative and marchioness as a potential minister, possibly of foreign affairs. But she’s also not someone who toes the party line: In 2020, she was sacked as the PP’s parliamentary spokesperson by then-party leader Pablo Casado after she clashed with the leadership. She said at the time that Casado “believes that my conception of freedom is incompatible with his authority .” She has also been critical of some of Feijóo’s decisions and broken ranks in some votes. 2. Borja Sémper If Álvarez de Toledo is the yin, Borja Sémper is the yang. The standard-bearer of the PP’s more liberal wing holds the equally significant third spot on the list for Madrid. MP Borja Sémper (left) and People’s Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo (right) look on after a parliamentary debate ahead of a vote to elect Spain’s next premier, at the Congress of Deputies in Madrid on Nov. 16, 2023. | Javier Soriano/AFP via Getty Images Sémper is the PP’s national spokesperson and the only figure from outside Feijóo’s inner circle, made up almost entirely of old aides from his 13 years running Galicia, to stand alongside the leader at the head-to-head debate with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. 3. Ildefonso Castro Castro, a Galician like Feijóo, is a classic Atlanticist and could play a key role in La Moncloa, the prime minister’s office. He worked as an adviser during the first years of the last PP government, led by Mariano Rajoy. Ildefonso Castro talks to the media during a press conference during the 13th Asia Europe Foreign Ministers Meeting (ASEM) in Naypyitaw, November 21, 2017. | Hein Htet/EPA The veteran diplomat who has been Feijóo’s right-hand man on foreign policy inside the PP since 2022 is seen as another possible foreign affairs minister. 4. Alma Ezcurra The EU lawmaker has taken on a growing role in the PP and has overseen the party’s manifesto. She’s now the third-highest-ranking official in the PP and someone Feijóo trusts. But she was also seen as an ayusista — someone close to Isabel Díaz Ayuso, Madrid’s hard-line regional president. Alma Ezcurra at the European Parliament’s plenary session on September 15, 2026. | Christian Creutz/European Parliament She holds fourth spot on the list for Madrid, behind Feijóo, Álvarez de Toledo and Sémper, and completes the trio who make up today’s PP: traditional conservatives, liberals and ayusistas . 5. Francisco Conde Conde was a key economic figure in Galicia’s government under Feijóo from 2012, and he later became Galicia’s first vice president. The PP leader has described Conde as “one of [his] best collaborators” and he is part of his closest circle of confidants. His name was floated for Feijóo’s Cabinet in 2023, but the PP ended up falling short on seats to form a government . 6. Marta Varela Marta Varela has been Feijóo’s chief of staff since 2020 and is a key figure in his day-to-day work, including negotiations with Vox. Like the rest of his largely Galician inner circle, she keeps a low profile, but is part of Feijóo’s trusted group of confidants. Mar Sánchez, another lesser-known Galician in that small group, has been at the PP leader’s side since the early 1990s and is also one to watch. 7. Montse Lluis Vox’s deputy secretary-general holds the second spot on the far-right party’s list for Madrid and was the key negotiator with the PP on the regional coalition deals, with Varela on the other side of the table. Both are former journalists. Lluis, who only joined the party in 2022, is the troubleshooter for Vox leader Santiago Abascal and handles the party’s thorniest issues. 8. Carlos Hernández Quero Hernández Quero isn’t your typical Vox figure: He’s young and swaggers about in casual dress with an ear piercing. A rising star in Vox, he focuses on migration and housing. MP of the VOX party Carlos Hernández Quero speaks during a plenary session at the Lower Chamber of the Spanish Parliament in Madrid October 2, 2026. | EPA/J.J. Guillen He’s Abascal’s pitch to young people and the disillusioned working class, and hopes to sway voters on the left in the same way as French far-right leader Marine Le Pen. He’s also an alumnus of ISSEP, a political training school founded by Le Pen’s niece Marion Maréchal, which opened a branch in Madrid in 2020. 9. Jorge Buxadé After Abascal, Buxadé is one of the best-known faces of Vox outside of Spain . He has been an EU lawmaker since 2019 and is head of the Vox delegation in the European Parliament, acting as a bridge between the party and Patriots for Europe. He played a key role in Vox’s departure from the European Conservatives and Reformists Group. Even after losing his post as Vox vice president in 2024 and ceasing to be Abascal’s second-in-command, Buxadé remains one of the party’s key hard-line voices. Jorge Buxadé in the European Parliament in Brussels on July 16, 2025. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images A former Falangist — he ran a fringe offshoot to the Franco-era fascist party in the 1990s — Buxadé is also a state attorney, a senior civil service post that could prove useful for Vox inside a government. 10. Kiko Méndez-Monasterio Kiko Méndez-Monasterio is unlikely to take up a position in the next government but is crucial to understanding Vox. Widely considered Abascal’s chief strategist, he is the uncle of Vox member Rocío de Meer and largely unknown to much of the Spanish public. Méndez-Monasterio co-founded communications consultancy Tizona with Gabriel Ariza, another key figure in Abascal’s inner circle, often seen by his side on trips outside Spain. Neither man currently holds a formal party post.

noticias.titulo: USA warnen EU vor einer Steuer auf Big Tech
noticias.resumen: Beim EU-Gipfel sprechen die Mitgliedstaaten über eine europäische Digitalsteuer. Sie wird zum Teil des Zoll-Konflikts.
noticias.texto: BRÜSSEL – Die Trump-Regierung hat die EU vor einer Besteuerung der „Big Tech“-Unternehmen gewarnt. Parallel beraten die europäischen Staats- und Regierungschefs in Brüssel über um neue Optionen zur Finanzierung des nächsten EU-Haushalts – eine Digitalsteuer ist eine davon. „Wir lehnen den EU-Vorschlag für eine EU-weite Digitalsteuer ebenso ab, wie wir andere Steuern auf digitale Dienstleistungen abgelehnt haben (und weiterhin ablehnen), die US-Unternehmen diskriminieren und gleichzeitig auch den Verbrauchern schaden“, erklärte ein Sprecher des US-Außenministeriums in einer Stellungnahme gegenüber POLITICO und bekräftigte damit Washingtons seit Jahren bestehende Ablehnung. Der Präsident des Europäischen Rates, António Costa, hatte am Samstag vorgeschlagen, die Gespräche über eine europäische Digitalsteuer wieder aufzunehmen. Sie soll zur Finanzierung des langfristigen EU-Haushalts in Höhe von 2 Billionen Euro beitragen. Die Steuer würde für Unternehmen mit einem weltweiten Umsatz von über 750 Millionen Euro gelten, davon mindestens 50 Millionen Euro in Europa – ein Schwellenwert, der US-Technologiegiganten wie Google, Meta und Amazon erfassen würde. Die US-Warnung erfolgte, als die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU am Donnerstag in Brüssel einen zweitägigen Sondergipfel eröffneten, um sich mit der Finanzierungsgleichung des nächsten Haushalts zu befassen: Wie viel soll ausgegeben werden und wie lässt sich die Belastung der nationalen Haushalte verringern, indem durch sogenannte „Eigenmittel“ neue Einnahmen generiert werden? Die Europäische Kommission hatte schon 2018 eine EU-weite Digitalsteuer vorgeschlagen. Der Vorschlag wurde aber zurückgestellt, um den von der Organisation für wirtschaftliche Zusammenarbeit und Entwicklung (OECD) vermittelten Verhandlungen Zeit zu geben, eine globale Einigung zu erzielen. Länder wie Frankreich, Österreich und Italien führten nationale Abgaben ein, was ihnen Vergeltungsmaßnahmen seitens der ersten Trump-Regierung einbrachte. Die Idee einer EU-weiten Steuer gewinnt nun wieder an Fahrt, wobei Frankreich, Dänemark, Spanien und Italien zu den Befürwortern zählen. Der Vorstoß erfolgt vor dem Hintergrund, dass Washington am Mittwoch nach einer separaten Untersuchung zu Überkapazitäten in der Industrie mit neuen Zöllen gegen die EU gedroht hat. „Dies ist ein geeigneter Bereich, da die Unternehmen, die dieser Abgabe unterliegen würden, enorm vom Binnenmarkt profitieren und einige ihrer Tätigkeiten und Dienstleistungen derzeit deutlich zu gering besteuert werden“, erklärte ein EU-Diplomat am Mittwoch bei einer Pressekonferenz im Vorfeld des Gipfels. Er wies Bedenken zurück, der Vorschlag könnte Washington verärgern. „Wir können nicht sagen, dass unser amerikanischer Partner Rücksicht auf unsere Gefühle nimmt, wenn er Maßnahmen zu seinem eigenen Vorteil ergreift“, fügten Diplomaten hinzu und berichteten von „sehr geringem Widerstand“ in den ersten Gesprächen über den neuen Vorschlag. Irland, Schweden, Malta, Deutschland und die Niederlande zeigen sich laut drei EU-Diplomaten jedoch weiterhin zurückhaltend. Da eine neue EU-Steuer einstimmig beschlossen werden müsste, ist es nach wie vor unwahrscheinlich, dass Costas Idee umgesetzt wird. Deutschland hingegen wird den Vorschlag „unvoreingenommen prüfen“, wie aus einem internen Vermerk hervorgeht, der POLITICO vorliegt. „Es muss geklärt werden, ob sie rechtzeitig Mittel für den EU-Haushalt bereitstellen und damit zur Lösung der Finanzierungsfrage beitragen kann“, heißt es darin. In dem Vermerk wird zudem Klarheit hinsichtlich „des internationalen Kontexts“ gefordert. Als Vorreiter im Kampf gegen den Vorschlag bekräftigte Taoiseach Micheál Martin Irlands „entschiedene Ablehnung“ einer Digitalsteuer. Als er zur Sitzung der europäischen Staats- und Regierungschefs ging, erklärte er, eine solche Abgabe stehe „im krassen Widerspruch“ zu den Bemühungen um die Wettbewerbsfähigkeit Europas. Auch Lobbygruppen der Technologiebranche wehren sich gegen den wieder aufgegriffenen Steuervorschlag. Eine Koalition aus elf Branchenverbänden, darunter die in Brüssel ansässigen Organisationen CCIA Europe, DOT Europe und ITI – zu deren Mitgliedern auch die US-amerikanischen Technologiegiganten zählen –, warnte am Donnerstag, dass „Steuern auf digitale Dienstleistungen wiederholt Drohungen mit Vergeltungsmaßnahmen seitens Drittländern ausgelöst haben“. Thibault Krause und Pieter Haeck haben zu diesem Bericht beigetragen.

noticias.titulo: Heathrow expansion plans fail climate tests, MPs warn
noticias.resumen: The government should "go back to the drawing board" on third runway proposals, a parliamentary committee said.
noticias.texto: LONDON — Plans for a third runway at Heathrow are “not currently compatible” with the government’s legally-binding climate commitments, MPs have warned the government. Heathrow expansion should therefore be “grounded” until ministers put in place policies to mitigate its climate impacts, a parliamentary committee said. In a report published Thursday, the House of Commons Transport Committee said the government should put in place “all policies necessary to account for the climate impact of Heathrow expansion before a Development Consent Order is granted.” The report said the government should publish a “contingency plan” in the event the expanded airport smashes through U.K. decarbonization goals. “Plans for a third runway should be grounded for now and the government should go back to the drawing board before proceeding any further,” said Labour MP and Transport Committee Chair Ruth Cadbury. Cadbury said ministers should provide “robust analysis to fill in the gaps in the [Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement] and start putting in place all the policies necessary to accommodate the climate impact of expansion, as well as setting out what will happen if decarbonisation goals are missed.” The warning comes after a report from the government’s independent climate advisers , the Climate Change Committee, warned in September that expanding Heathrow would make it harder to achieve future legally-binding climate goals. The CCC’s advice “is a clear signal that, at present, the government is failing that [climate] test,” the MPs said. The report added: “Heathrow expansion is not currently compatible with the U.K.’s legally binding climate targets, and it seems impossible for the additional carbon dioxide emissions to be offset elsewhere in the economy.” POLITICO reported last year that the Department for Transport’s own data showed a third runway could result in pollution equivalent to an additional 2.4 million tons of carbon dioxide being released into the atmosphere each year by 2050 Then Chancellor Rachel Reeves backed a third Heathrow runway in January last year, citing its potential boost to the British economy. But the MPs said ministers had “failed to make the case” for expanding Heathrow, citing modeling commissioned by the Department for Transport which showed only “relatively modest” levels of additional economic growth. It also urged the government to “strengthen both the air quality test and the noise test.” The Department for Transport has been contacted for comment. Heathrow Chief Executive Thomas Woldbye said: “The case for expanding Heathrow has been examined more thoroughly than almost any infrastructure project in modern Britain. “Successive governments, independent commissions and industry experts have repeatedly concluded that you either expand Heathrow so the U.K. can compete and grow, or you accept a steady erosion of the U.K.’s connectivity and global competitiveness.” This story was updated to include comment from Heathrow .

noticias.titulo: US warns EU leaders against Big Tech tax
noticias.resumen: Washington’s opposition to the idea of a bloc-wide digital services tax complicates efforts to find new revenue sources for the EU’s €2 trillion budget.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — The Trump administration is warning EU leaders against taxing Big Tech as they gather in Brussels to consider new options to fund the bloc’s next budget. “We oppose the EU proposal for an EU-wide digital levy just as we have opposed (and continue to oppose) other digital services taxes that discriminate against US companies while hurting consumers as well,” a spokesperson for the U.S. State Department told POLITICO in a statement, reiterating Washington’s years-long opposition . European Council President António Costa on Saturday proposed reviving talks on a European digital tax to help finance the EU’s €2 trillion long-term budget and unlock a deal on its final size. It would target companies with global turnover above €750 million, including at least €50 million in Europe — a threshold that would catch U.S. tech giants such as Google, Meta and Amazon. The warning came as EU leaders opened a two-day extraordinary summit in Brussels on Thursday to grapple with the next budget’s complex funding equation: how much to spend and how to reduce the burden on national coffers by raising new revenue through so-called “own resources.” The European Commission proposed an EU-wide digital tax in 2018, then shelved it to give talks brokered by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development time to reach a global deal . Countries such as France, Austria and Italy went ahead with national levies, drawing threats of retaliation from Trump’s first administration . The idea of an EU-wide tax is now gaining traction again, with France, Denmark, Spain and Italy among the countries in favor. The push comes as Washington threatened new tariffs on the EU on Wednesday following a separate investigation into industrial overcapacity. “This is a suitable area because the companies that would be subject to this contribution benefit enormously from the single market, and some of their activities and services are heavily undertaxed today,” an EU diplomat said Wednesday, briefing reporters ahead of the summit. The diplomat dismissed concerns that the proposal could antagonize Washington. “We cannot say that our American partner thinks about our feelings when it takes measures for itself,” they added, reporting “very little strong opposition” in the preliminary talks about the new proposal. Ireland, Sweden, Malta, Germany and the Netherlands, however, remain cautious, according to three EU diplomats. Since a new EU tax would require unanimous approval, it’s still unlikely that Costa’s idea would fly. But the German government will examine it “with an open mind,” according to an internal note seen by POLITICO. “It must be clarified whether it can provide resources for the EU budget in a timely manner and thus contribute to solving the financing equation,” it says. The note also calls for clarity on “the international context.” Leading the charge against the proposal, Taoiseach Micheál Martin repeated Ireland’s “strong opposition” to a digital tax. As he walked into the meeting of European leaders, he said such a levy “flies in the face” of the push for European competitiveness. Tech lobby groups are also pushing back against the revived tax proposal. A coalition of 11 trade associations, including Brussels-based groups CCIA Europe, DOT Europe and ITI — whose members include the U.S. tech giants — warned Thursday that “digital services taxes have repeatedly triggered threats of retaliation measures from third countries.” Thibault Krause and Pieter Haeck contributed reporting.

noticias.titulo: France’s Jordan Bardella faces fresh antisemitism accusations
noticias.resumen: The far-right leader has already denied the allegations and said they are part of “a manhunt” against him.
noticias.texto: PARIS — French far-right leader Jordan Bardella is facing new accusations that he was the author of antisemitic messages as a minor. The investigative website Mediapart , which reported similar allegations against Bardella in September , and the newspaper Le Monde on Thursday published a raft of new correspondence allegedly between Bardella and an unidentified school friend on Meta’s Messenger platform that contains antisemitic comments. In the messages, Bardella reportedly wrote that “zionists are at the top of all the banks” and that important French ministries were run “by people for whom Israel and the banking interests are more important than French interests.” “The banks are all owned by Jews,” he wrote, according to Mediapart. The messages were allegedly sent in 2013, when Bardella was 17 and a member of the National Front, the predecessor of the party he currently leads, the National Rally. Bardella has repeatedly dismissed previous allegations of antisemitism leveled against him, and in a statement released by the National Rally on Thursday, Bardella said he “categorically denies being the author” of the new batch of messages. Bardella also attacked the reports as part of “a manhunt” against him. “Former school friends, high school teachers … face repeated and pressing requests to collaborate in this persecution project,” Bardella said. The accusations against Bardella threaten to undermine his longtime mentor and party’s presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen. She is the front-runner ahead of next year’s presidential election, with POLITICO’s Poll of Polls putting her at 34% in the first round of voting — far ahead of her nearest challengers. The fresh allegations could again test the relationship between Bardella and Le Pen, who has said that the 31-year-old would become her prime minister if she came to power. Le Pen has worked to try to rid the party of the racist and antisemitic reputation it developed under her father, Jean-Marie, who was convicted multiple times for racist comments and downplaying the Holocaust. This week, National Rally lawmaker Laure Lavalette also faced allegations she contributed to a student newspaper in the 1990s which contained antisemitic caricatures. Lavalette dismissed the accusations in a TV interview, saying she would not try to justify something that happened “30 years ago” in “a climate that was very different.”
